studyMethodsSummary: Seven supervised learning models (linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net, decision tree, support vector regression, and random forest) were trained to predict wind speed at 102.2 m using mesoscale data, meteorological-mast observations, or both data sources. Their performance was assessed using five-fold cross-validation and compared with the power-law method.
studyKeyFindings: Machine-learning models trained with mesoscale data, observed data, or both were reported to outperform the power-law method for MAE, MSE, RMSE, and R2. Random Forest achieved the best reported result for scenario A using mesoscale data only. For scenario B, Random Forest had the highest tabulated R2, but linear regression was recommended because its performance was similar while its computational cost was substantially lower. For scenario C, Ridge regression was recommended because Random Forest and SVR did not provide considerable improvement relative to their computational cost.
studyFutureWorks: Determine the confidence level and uncertainty of wind-resource assessments using machine learning instead of the power law, assess whether measurement campaigns can be partially avoided when modeled data alone are used, investigate optimized coarse-resolution mesoscale models, and improve Random Forest using high-performance computing or ensemble approaches.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared seven supervised-learning algorithms for the same vertical wind-speed extrapolation task and incorporated modeled data from the New European Wind Atlas into the training data.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Few studies have focused on vertical wind-speed extrapolation in the temporal domain, and further comparison of representative supervised-learning algorithms and the use of modeled mesoscale atmospheric data were needed.

studyMethodsSummary: The study trained and compared LASSO, Random Forest, and XGBoost transfer methods for constructing 3-hourly 100 m wind speed from ERA5 near-surface wind and other meteorological, geographical, terrain, and time features.; The methods were evaluated against ERA5 using a 2004–2005 test set, and the best-performing Random Forest method was applied to 19 Euro-CORDEX regional climate projections under RCP8.5 and to two mast stations.
studyKeyFindings: The machine-learning methods produced more accurate 100 m wind-speed estimates than the traditional power-law method, with Random Forest having the highest overall simulation accuracy among the three tested machine-learning algorithms.; Random Forest and XGBoost reproduced the diurnal and seasonal changes of 100 m wind speed more accurately than the traditional method.; The regional mean Random Forest RMSE was 0.525, corresponding to a reported 64.1% reduction relative to the traditional method.; Under RCP8.5, the study found significant negative trends in European hub-height wind speed and wind energy during 1979–2019 and projected further reductions in wind-power production.; At the SAC mast station, the transfer-model predictions systematically underestimated 100 m wind speed by about 40%, indicating limitations when local surface conditions differ from the ERA5 grid representation.
studyFutureWorks: Future developments could apply more elaborate bias-correction methods to climate projections.; Performance at specific sites could be improved using smaller-scale models and additional local information.; The method could be combined with short periods of 100 m wind measurements and long periods of surface-wind measurements to produce long-term hub-height wind-speed series for site assessment.
studyLimits: ERA5 has known near-surface wind mismatches and a general underestimation bias.; The transfer-model accuracy decreases near coastlines, suggesting that distance from the coastline could be included as an additional feature.; Only two long-term mast stations were used as examples because long mast records are rare.; The ERA5-trained transfer model may be inaccurate at sites where adjacent vegetation, buildings, altitude, or local land use cause surface-wind observations to differ from ERA5.; The climate-model application used a simple bias-correction technique, although more elaborate methods are available.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study develops a data-driven transfer method to construct gridded hub-height wind speed from commonly available climate-model variables over a large region.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hourly hub-height wind-speed output is rare in global and regional climate models, which often provide only 10 m wind speed, while constant-exponent extrapolation does not represent the nonlinear, spatially and temporally varying relationship between surface and hub-height winds.

studyMethodsSummary: The study developed an LSTM-based vertical wind-speed extrapolation procedure trained first with the Levenberg-Marquardt method and enhanced using particle swarm optimization. Measured 10-minute-average LiDAR wind speeds from 10 to 40 m were used iteratively to estimate wind speed from 50 to 120 m. PSO-LSTM was compared with standard LSTM, FFNN, Log Law, and several alternative optimization algorithms.
studyKeyFindings: PSO-LSTM outperformed standard LSTM, FFNN, and Log Law in most performance measures at all evaluated heights. Its R2 values were 96.35%, 88.12%, and 78.26% at 60, 90, and 120 m, respectively. Errors generally increased and performance deteriorated with increasing extrapolation height. PSO-LSTM's superiority did not apply uniformly to MBE: FFNN had the lowest MBE at 60 and 80 m, while PSO-LSTM performed better at the remaining heights.
studyFutureWorks: Further explore the applicability of PSO-LSTM at other sites if measured data is available.
studyLimits: Only measured wind speeds between 10 and 40 m were used to estimate wind speeds at all higher heights, and deviations from measurements increased with height.; Applicability at other sites was not established in this study.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study proposed and evaluated a particle-swarm-optimization-enhanced LSTM method for vertical wind-speed extrapolation and compared it with standard LSTM, FFNN, Log Law, and alternative optimization methods.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The utilization of machine-learning methods to predict wind speed at hub height from measured wind speed at lower heights is limited, and most prior vertical wind-speed extrapolation studies used classical methods.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data from 27 INMET automatic monitoring stations in Mato Grosso do Sul were cleaned, grouped using Ward cluster analysis, and fitted with a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Six numerical parameter-estimation methods were compared using RMSE, R2, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic.
studyKeyFindings: Maximum likelihood and modified maximum likelihood were the most accurate methods for most analyzed stations, although the best of these two depended on month and station group. Modified maximum likelihood performed best for most months in Group 3, while maximum likelihood performed best at Três Lagoas. At low-wind-speed stations, method accuracy decreased; the graphical method was best at Coxim from September to February. The Weibull distribution was not recommended for Coxim and Miranda, which were characterized by low monthly average wind speeds.
studyLimits: The number of monitoring points was below the recommended number for an area of this extent.; The Weibull distribution showed reduced suitability at stations characterized by low monthly average wind speeds.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared six Weibull parameter-estimation methods using similar wind-speed series separated into calibration and accuracy-analysis series.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Further studies were needed to evaluate the best methods for determining Weibull distribution parameters applied to historical wind-speed series in Mato Grosso do Sul.

studyMethodsSummary: Fourteen methods for estimating the shape and scale parameters of a two-parameter Weibull distribution were compared using hourly wind data from 2005–2014 measured or represented at 10 m for three slightly, moderately, and very windy sites. Performance was assessed with RMSE, R2, and relative error; skewness, kurtosis, wind power density, mean wind speed, standard deviation, and height extrapolation were also analysed.
studyKeyFindings: Among the methods assessed at the three selected sites, the Energy Pattern Factor Method had the best RMSE and R2 performance and was the most suitable method for determining Weibull parameters.; The Wind Variability Method and Moroccan Method were not appropriate for estimating Weibull parameters at the three sites.; The Moment Method produced the lowest relative error when estimating standard deviation at the study sites.; The calculated distributions had positive skewness and were skewed to the right, while their kurtosis coefficients were negative.; For the extrapolation methodology used in this study, the Weibull shape parameter decreased with height above ground level while the scale parameter increased with height.
studyFutureWorks: Assess the impact of site roughness and topography on wind-potential estimation.
studyLimits: The comparison was restricted to three sites categorized as slightly, moderately, and very windy.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study investigated how a site's wind-speed level affects the choice of Weibull-parameter estimation method.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous comparisons indicated that the preferred Weibull-parameter estimation method may depend on the site and data, leaving open the relationship between a site's wind-speed level and the method that should be used.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data for 1992–2010 from twelve Nigerian meteorological stations at 10 m above ground level were analyzed with Weibull, mixture Weibull, Gamma, lognormal and normal distributions. Parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood, and model performance was compared using Kolmogorov–Smirnov, RMSE and chi-square goodness-of-fit tests. Although the paper consistently describes five distributions, the conclusion refers to a comparison of four distribution models.
studyKeyFindings: Across the twelve study stations, mixture Weibull was ranked first by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and was also ranked first by chi-square at all stations except Minna and Ikeja. RMSE ranked lognormal first at all stations except Minna. In the overall ranking, mixture Weibull ranked first under Kolmogorov–Smirnov and chi-square, whereas lognormal ranked first under RMSE. The authors selected mixture Weibull as the best method overall and concluded that the conventional Weibull and Gamma methods performed poorly for the study locations.
studyFutureWorks: Use more estimation methods and more goodness-of-fit tests in future studies to identify the estimation method with the best effectiveness.
studyLimits: The performance of Weibull-parameter estimation methods varied from station to station and depended on the goodness-of-fit measure used.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared five statistical distribution methods for estimating Weibull parameters at twelve Nigerian stations and evaluated their accuracy with three goodness-of-fit tests.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Studies comparing different methods for estimating Weibull parameters in Nigeria are very scarce, and the accuracy of the available estimation methods has received little attention.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind data for 2008–2010 at Catalca were measured at 10 m and extrapolated to 30, 60, and 80 m. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was fitted using graphical, method of moments, energy pattern factor, mean standard deviation, power density, and genetic algorithm methods. Performance was compared using MAE, RMSE, NMAE, Chi-square error, R2, and Net Fitness.
studyKeyFindings: All six estimation methods almost fitted the measured data, although the 2010 Weibull PDF and CDF curves deviated considerably from the real-data curve.; GA and GM were respectively the first- and second-best methods in terms of MAE, RMSE, and R2, whereas EPF outperformed the other methods in terms of NMAE and Chi-square error.; Based on the aggregate Net Fitness ranking, the methods ranked from best to worst as GA, PD, GM, MOM, MSD, and EPF.; No method ranked best for all cases, and the suitability of an estimation method depends on factors including data size, data shape, and the selected goodness-of-fit measures.; The reported annual average power densities indicated that the Catalca site is suitable for wind power generation.
studyLimits: Results at different extrapolated heights are not independent because the data depend only on wind extrapolation.; The conclusions are based on one site and three years of wind data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compares six Weibull parameter estimation methods using multiple goodness-of-fit measures and an aggregate Net Fitness test at Catalca.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Accurate estimation of wind-speed distributions and selection of suitable methods for Weibull parameter estimation remain challenging tasks in wind-power planning and operation.

studyMethodsSummary: Three-hourly wind-speed and wind-direction measurements collected at 10 m at Mehrabad International Airport over 1995–2005 were statistically analyzed. Weibull parameters, characteristic wind speeds, wind power density, wind energy density, and wind-direction frequencies were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: For the years considered, yearly mean wind speeds were generally between 4 and 5 m/s, with a maximum of 4.50 m/s in 2004 and 2005.; The Weibull distribution agreed reasonably well with the measured wind-speed distribution in the relevant wind range.; The site studied was not considered suitable for large-scale wind-electric applications under the current wind-turbine technique and cost conditions, but its wind potential may be adequate for small-scale, non-grid-connected electrical and mechanical applications.; The highest monthly wind power density was reported for April and the lowest for August.; The most probable wind direction over 1995–2005 was reported as 180°, described by the authors as west winds.
studyFutureWorks: A comprehensive wind database and improved predictions should be developed prior to construction and installation of wind-energy conversion systems.; Future assessment and turbine selection should consider terrain, different reference heights, site circumstances, and new wind-energy generation technology.
studyLimits: The work is described as a preliminary study.; The assessment used measurements at 10 m in an open area, while terrain, other reference heights, and site circumstances should also be considered when selecting wind-energy conversion systems.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed whether wind energy could provide an alternative energy source in the Tehran region.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The government was reported as unable to provide 100% of Tehran's energy-consumption needs, motivating investigation of an alternative regional energy source.

studyMethodsSummary: Twelve months of 10-minute wind measurements at 10 m height in Koronos village, northeastern Naxos Island, were statistically analysed. Wind speed and direction, availability, duration, diurnal variation and wind power density were assessed, and Weibull and Rayleigh distributions were fitted and compared using RMSE, chi-square and modelling efficiency.
studyKeyFindings: The annual mean wind speed was approximately 7.4 m/s and the estimated annual mean wind power density was 420 W/m2.; The measurement site was classified by the authors as Class 7 and considered suitable for large-scale electricity generation.; The prevailing directions were northeastern, north–northeastern and west–southwestern.; For the measured dataset, the Weibull distribution represented the actual data better than the Rayleigh distribution.; March and July were the windiest months, with mean wind speed reaching approximately 9 m/s, while in June the mean wind speed did not exceed 6 m/s.
studyFutureWorks: Further investigation of the wind regime and diurnal wind patterns should be carried out because only 1 year of data was available.
studyLimits: The available data covered only 1 year, so the authors stated that no conclusive results should safely be drawn and that further investigation was needed.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated real wind data from a remote location in northeastern Naxos Island to assess its wind potential.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Only very broad information had been available on wind potential in the Aegean Sea, especially at remote locations.

studyMethodsSummary: Three-hour wind-speed data from 2003–2007 at 10 m for five sites in Semnan province were analyzed, with wind speeds at 30 m and 40 m obtained by Power Law extrapolation. Ten-minute wind-speed and wind-direction data collected during 2007 at Moalleman, Haddadeh, and Kahak were also statistically characterized. Weibull distributions, wind power density, wind roses, turbulence, and annual energy capture by five wind-turbine models were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: Damghan had the best wind conditions among the five towns, and Moalleman was the best of the subsequently examined sites. At Moalleman, reported power-density ranges were 172–177 W/m2 at 10 m, 257–277 W/m2 at 30 m, and 303–329 W/m2 at 40 m. Prevailing winds were generally from the southwest. The larger turbine considered could produce more than 2000 MWh during 2007. Moalleman was explicitly classified as a class 3 wind-power site and considered suitable for grid-connected and stand-alone applications.
studyLimits: The detailed Moalleman assessment and turbine-energy calculation were based on data for the year 2007.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Assessment of wind-energy potential and wind-turbine feasibility in Semnan province.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind-energy potential had previously been assessed for some Iranian provinces, while the present study addressed another potentially suitable province.

studyMethodsSummary: Five years of three-hourly wind-speed data for Zahedan (2003–2007), measured at 10 m, were statistically analysed using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Weibull parameters were estimated with the standard deviation method; wind speeds were extrapolated to 20 m and 30 m; four small wind turbines were simulated using Windographer; and costs of electricity were estimated.
studyKeyFindings: For the 2003–2007 period, the average Weibull shape parameter, scale parameter, wind power density, and wind energy density were 1.155, 3.401 m/s, 89.184 W/m2, and 781.252 kWh/m2, respectively. Zahedan falls into PNL wind power class 1 overall, and the potential for wind-energy development is limited, although it may be appropriate for low-capacity wind turbines in rural and small communities. Proven 2.5 kW was the most economical of the four assessed turbine models, while Bergey Excel-R produced the highest annual electricity output.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured wind-speed data from three Taiwanese wind farms for 2006–2008 were converted from 10-min measurements to hourly data and averaged over 3 years. Conventional Weibull, Gamma–Weibull, Normal–Normal, Normal–Weibull, Weibull–Weibull, and maximum-entropy-principle probability density functions were compared using Kolmogorov–Smirnov maximum error, RMSE, Chi-square error, and relative percent error of wind potential energy.
studyKeyFindings: For the unimodal wind-speed distribution at station A, superiority of the four mixture probability density functions and the maximum-entropy-principle function relative to the conventional Weibull function was not significant. For the bimodal distributions at stations B and C, all mixture functions and the maximum-entropy-principle function described wind characterizations better than the conventional Weibull function for both wind-speed and wind-power-density analyses. The proposed Gamma–Weibull probability density function performed best in the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test for wind-speed analyses, while the maximum-entropy-principle and Gamma–Weibull functions performed best for wind-power-density analyses.
studyLimits: The maximum-entropy-principle probability density function has a more complex mathematical expression for computer programming, requires more computation time to determine parameters, and its cumulative distribution function could not be expressed in a closed form.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared four mixture probability density functions and a maximum-entropy-principle function with the conventional Weibull function using wind-speed data from three wind farms with different climatic environments.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Systematical analysis about the suitability of mixture probability functions and maximum-entropy-principle functions together with conventional Weibull function in a single study had rarely been found in the literature.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly mean wind-speed data measured at 10 m for Enugu, Owerri and Onitsha were analysed using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Weibull parameters were calculated using the standard deviation method, wind speed was extrapolated to turbine hub heights, and selected wind turbines and a rotodynamic wind-powered pump were simulated.
studyKeyFindings: Among the three locations considered, Enugu had the highest annual mean wind speed and annual mean power density. Based on capacity factor, POLARIS 15-50, POLARIS 62-1000 and WWD-1-60 models, or turbines with similar characteristics, were identified as best suited for electricity generation in Enugu. The three sites were also reported to have strong potential for wind-powered water pumping.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated wind energy potential at Enugu, Owerri and Onitsha and assessed selected small- to medium-size commercial wind turbines.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Although several studies have investigated wind-speed characteristics and patterns across Nigeria, less attention has been given to sites in the south-east region, and the few reported studies there were limited to wind-speed distributions with less attention to wind-energy-potential evaluation.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically assessed offshore wind characteristics and wind energy potential using wind observations from three offshore-island meteorological stations in Hong Kong. Wind speeds were adjusted to an 80 m hub height using a power-law model, and Weibull distributions were fitted using the moment method; the maximum likelihood method was also used to revisit Weibull-model validity.
studyKeyFindings: Waglan Island had the highest reported whole-period annual mean wind speed and wind power density among the three stations. The Weibull distribution gave an adequate description of the offshore wind-speed data, with no significant discrepancy between the moment-method and maximum-likelihood Weibull prediction curves. The southeastern waters near Waglan Island were identified as the most promising location for offshore wind-farm development among the locations assessed.
studyLimits: Because the measurements were collected from meteorological masts on offshore islands, surrounding topographic effects may introduce measurement errors and may influence the representativeness and veracity of the offshore wind characteristics. Measurements from offshore platforms or remote-sensing techniques would be preferable, but such data were not readily available.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Inadequate understanding of offshore wind characteristics had limited the harvesting and utilization of offshore wind energy potential in Hong Kong.

studyMethodsSummary: The study develops probability models for air density, wind velocity, Weibull parameters, surface roughness exponent, MCP long-term wind-speed prediction residuals, and turbine power performance, then combines them in a crude Monte-Carlo based simulation to assess annual energy production uncertainty at Kwangyang Bay.
studyKeyFindings: For the Kwangyang Bay case study, the Monte-Carlo approach produced a long-term AEP of 4.550 GWh, compared with 4.713 GWh from the conventional approach. The standard deviation of generated AEP normalized by its average value was 11%.
studyFutureWorks: Further research will include additional improvement of probability models for meteorological variables developed from limited data.
studyLimits: The orographic directional effect and the stability of the boundary layer are not considered in this study. Topographical effects cannot be generalized because they are too local and are beyond the scope of this study.
studyResearchGapAddressed: A framework for uncertainty analysis of wind energy potential at a specific site based on probability models for each parameter.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The IEC method does not allow complicated relationships between different uncertainty sources, and a more sophisticated stochastic method is needed to simulate the behavior of a physical system.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data measured at 10 m at five locations in southern Algeria were analysed using Weibull probability density functions. Weibull parameters were extrapolated to turbine hub heights, turbine output was estimated by cubic-spline interpolation of manufacturer power-curve data, and annual energy output, capacity factor, and unit electricity cost were calculated for four commercial wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: The sites in southern Algeria, except Tamanrasset, have important wind-energy potential. Adrar was the best location among the sites considered for energy production and capacity factor, while Ghardaia was second. The maximum annual energy output was 9429.8 MW h for the Fuhrlander FL 2500 at Adrar. The Suzlon S82/1.5MW had the highest capacity factor among the considered models and was identified as the most attractive model in terms of cost per kW h for the same hub height of 70 m.
studyFutureWorks: This work should be extended to study the wind energy at different locations; this will help to identify the most favorable areas for wind development in Algeria.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data measured at 10 m were obtained for six north-central Nigerian locations. The authors used a two-parameter Weibull probability density function to analyse wind data, extrapolated wind characteristics to turbine hub heights, assessed annual energy output and capacity factor for five commercial Polaris America wind turbines, and performed an LCOE-based economic analysis.
studyKeyFindings: Among the locations considered, Minna was the most promising site in terms of energy production and capacity factor, followed by Makurdi and Ilorin; based on unit electricity cost, Minna was the most viable site.; The capacity factor ranged from 2.86% for the P17-50 model in Bida to 36.10% for the P50-500 model in Minna.; Average LCOE ranged from 0.0660 $/kWh for the P50-500 model in Minna to 1.2872 $/kWh for the P17-50 model in Bida.; For the P15-50, P19-100, and P50-500 models in Minna, increasing the operating-and-maintenance escalation rate from 0% to 10% increased estimated LCOE by about 7%, while increasing the inflation escalation rate from 0% to 5% decreased LCOE by about 29% and decreased return on investment from 11.54% to 6.23%.
studyLimits: The assessment used wind-speed data measured at 10 m and estimated turbine performance using Weibull distribution parameters extrapolated to turbine hub heights.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated wind-energy potential at six selected north-central Nigerian locations and performed performance and economic analyses for selected small- to medium-size commercial wind turbines.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Although wind-speed characteristics and patterns across Nigeria had been studied, the economic and performance of wind energy conversion systems in north-central Nigerian sites had not been thoroughly investigated.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed 10-minute wind-speed measurements collected during 2007 at 10 m, 30 m, and 50 m above ground level in Zwara, Libya. A Weibull distribution was fitted using the standard deviation method to estimate wind-resource characteristics, mean wind power density, and wind energy density. Wind speeds were extrapolated to turbine hub heights using a power-law exponent function, and MATLAB was used to simulate annual net energy output and capacity factors for four selected wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: Annual average wind speeds were 4.51, 5.86, and 6.26 m/s at 10 m, 30 m, and 50 m, respectively. Annual mean wind power densities were 113.71, 204.19, and 243.48 W/m2, respectively, and the site was classified as wind power class 2. The selected turbines produced simulated annual energy outputs from 969.12 MWh to 5155.70 MWh, with capacity factors from 21.83% to 39.80%.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study constructed a wind rose and estimated mean wind power density and wind energy density for Zwara.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Although several wind-energy-potential studies had been reported, there had not been a representation of the wind rose. The paper also states that Elmabruk et al. did not present wind energy density in their study.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured wind-speed data from 2007 at 10 m, 30 m, and 40 m were statistically analysed for four sites in North and South Khorasan. The study calculated mean wind speed, fitted Weibull wind-speed distributions, evaluated wind direction and wind roses, calculated turbulence intensity and surface roughness, and evaluated wind power density.
studyKeyFindings: Esfarayen and Fadashk had the highest annual mean wind speeds at the three measured heights among the four studied sites. The authors reported that Weibull distributions gave a good fit to the experimental data and that annual power-density results from measured data and the Weibull distribution had little difference. Bojnourd was evaluated as a class 2 wind-power site, while Esfarayen, Nehbandan, and Fadashk were evaluated as class 3 sites.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily wind-speed data measured from January 2006 to December 2010 at Katsina, Warri, and Calabar were fitted using Gumbel and Weibull probability distributions. Model fitting performance was evaluated using correlation coefficient and Nash-Sutcliffe coefficient of efficiency. Weibull-model results were used to simulate wind-turbine electric-power output at hub heights from 10 m to 110 m and to evaluate present value cost and cost per kWh.
studyKeyFindings: Katsina was identified by raw-data, Gumbel, and Weibull wind-speed and power-density models as a higher wind-speed-class site, whereas Warri and Calabar were identified as low wind-speed sites. For Katsina, the simulated least electricity-generation cost per kWh occurred at a 50 m turbine hub height. For Warri and Calabar, modeled cost per kWh decreased with increasing hub height up to 110 m. The authors stated that modeled electricity-generation costs could support off-grid rural electrification, although initial procurement and installation costs could still be cost intensive for the rural populace.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed wind-energy potential at selected Nigerian sites to gain insights into the usage of wind-energy systems for sustainable rural electrification.
studyResearchGapIdentified: While many studies have deliberated on wind characteristics and energy potential from different parts of Nigeria, none have undertaken such study for establishing how wind energy could have been applicable as a solution for rural-electrification problems in the country.

studyMethodsSummary: Continuous wind-speed and wind-direction records from five meteorological stations in Hong Kong were statistically analysed. Wind speeds were transformed to an 80 m turbine hub height using a power-law exponent of 0.14. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was used to characterize wind speed, estimate wind-power density, and calculate wind-turbine operating probabilities. Moment, maximum-likelihood, and power-density methods were compared for Weibull-parameter estimation.
studyKeyFindings: Across the five stations for the 2005–2010 study period, Tai Mo Shan had the highest whole-period mean wind speed (9.04 m/s) and Hong Kong Observatory had the lowest (2.55 m/s).; The annual Weibull scale parameter ranged from 2.85 m/s to 10.19 m/s, while the annual shape parameter ranged from 1.65 to 1.99.; Tai Mo Shan had the highest reported average wind-power density, reported as 915.53 W/m2 in the Results section and 915.23 W/m2 in the Conclusion; these values conflict.; Hong Kong Observatory had the lowest reported mean wind-power density, 24.20 W/m2.; Hilltops and offshore islands were concluded to be the most promising locations for wind-energy exploitation in Hong Kong, whereas available wind-power potential in urban areas was relatively rare.; The Weibull distribution function was found to give a good representation of the measured wind data, and little difference was observed among the moment, maximum-likelihood, and power-density methods for Weibull-parameter estimation.
studyFutureWorks: Extend the analysis to more weather stations across Hong Kong, particularly offshore areas, and integrate statistical analysis of field measurements with Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations for spatial wind-speed distributions.
studyLimits: Long-period wind measurements are often unavailable; the study introduced relative error to account for possible bias originating from insufficient wind data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Statistical assessment of wind characteristics and potential wind energy at five typical weather stations with different terrain conditions in Hong Kong.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind energy exploitation in Hong Kong is still rare.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed wind-speed data from Kudat and Labuan for 2006–2008. Wind speeds recorded at 10 m were converted to 100 m using the wind profile power law, and a 2-parameter Weibull distribution was used to assess wind characteristics, wind power density, wind energy density, most probable wind speed, and wind speed carrying maximum energy. WRPLOT software was used to show wind direction.
studyKeyFindings: The maximum wind power density was 67.40 W/m2 at Kudat in 2008, while the maximum wind energy density was 590.40 kWh/m2/year at Kudat in 2008.; The highest most probable wind speed was 2.44 m/s at Labuan in 2007, and the highest wind speed carrying maximum energy was 6.02 m/s at Kudat in 2007.; For wind speeds greater than 2 m/s, the maximum deviation between observed and Weibull frequency distributions was about 5%; at wind speeds below 2 m/s, the maximum percentage error was 25%.; The most probable wind directions were 190 degrees at Kudat and 269 degrees at Labuan through the study years.; The authors concluded that the sites are unsuitable for large-scale wind-energy generation, but that small-scale wind energy can be generated at a turbine height of 100 m.
studyLimits: The Weibull distribution function is unable to represent the probabilities of observing zero or very low wind speed.; The analysis used three years of data, and the paper notes that wind data from periods shorter than 30 years may inherit variations from the long-term average.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study estimated wind energy potential at two Malaysian sites using more recent wind-speed data for 2006–2008.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is very limited research on the assessment of wind energy potentiality in Malaysia.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data from Jhampir-FFC were preprocessed into hourly averages and analyzed at monthly, seasonal, and yearly scales. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was fitted using Maximum Likelihood Method, Modified Maximum Likelihood Method, and Energy Pattern Factor Method. Their performance was evaluated using RMSE, R2, Chi-Square tests, and Monte Carlo simulation. Directional wind-power densities and wind-energy production using a selected wind turbine were also estimated.
studyKeyFindings: Maximum Likelihood Method was found to perform better than Modified Maximum Likelihood Method and Energy Pattern Factor Method based on the reported performance evaluation and Monte Carlo results. The annual mean measured wind speed at 80 m was 7.77 m/s and the annual mean measured wind power density was 287.48 W/m2. The annual actual wind energy extracted using the selected turbine was 10054.27 kWh. The authors concluded that Jhampir is suitable for setting up wind farms for green and clean energy utilization.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly mean wind-speed and wind-direction data from Bayan Lepas for January to December 2008 were analysed. Wind speeds were extrapolated to 50 m using a power law with exponent 1/7, wind-speed data were fitted with a Rayleigh distribution function, and wind power density and wind energy density were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: The Bayan Lepas measurement site has limited wind potential and falls under Class 1 wind classification.; The annual mean wind power density was estimated to be 24.54 W m−2 and the annual mean wind energy density was estimated to be about 17.98 kWh m−2 month−1.; A grid-network-connected wind turbine-generator system may not be commercially viable in Penang because of the cost factor; small-scale wind turbine generation applications are described as still promising in the long run with wind-turbine-technology development.; Most prevailing wind was from the N, NNE, SW and SSW directions, whereas directions contributing higher energy included SSW, SW, WSW and NE.
studyFutureWorks: Small-scale wind turbine generation applications are described as promising in the long run with the development of wind turbine technology.
studyLimits: The wind-speed data measured at 12.5 m above ground level were stated to be unsuitable for predicting wind-power potential at a higher altitude without extrapolation.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed wind potential in Bayan Lepas, Penang Island using real-time wind data.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Malaysia possesses high wind-energy potential; however, exploitation and feasibility study of clean and sustainable renewable energy are still insufficient.

studyMethodsSummary: The study combined experimental wind measurements at the GS mast, wind-resource analysis using Wind Rose and WAsP software, Weibull and Rayleigh probability-density analyses, and calculations of agricultural irrigation-pump demand that could be supplied using wind-farm energy subject to alternative curtailment rates and wind-farm layouts.
studyKeyFindings: The authors found that wind turbines would need to be installed near the mast on the north-east side of the mapped area because wind resources elsewhere were too low for exploitation. Under the 0.8% curtailment case, WF1 could meet 120.6 MWh of annual pump demand, equal to 18.16% of average annual pump energy consumption; under the 4.3% curtailment case, WF1 could meet 500.6 MWh, equal to 75.37%. Comparing system, environmental and independent-power-producer perspectives, the authors concluded that WF4, with three wind turbines, should have been the final wind farm built.
studyLimits: Data loss was significant for May and June 2009. The authors state that apparent insufficient production to meet pumping demand during these months is more a matter of missing data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study examined agricultural flexible energy demand, especially irrigation pumping, as a demand-response strategy for wind-energy integration.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The paper states that there was not a study using agriculture and agricultural needs as a demand-response strategy.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data for 2000–2006 from Ankara and Polatlı were analyzed using Weibull and Rayleigh distributions. Wind power density at 10, 30, 50, and 70 m, turbine capacity factors, and energy output for selected wind turbines were calculated.
studyKeyFindings: The highest monthly mean wind speed was 6.40 m/s in July for Ankara and 5.84 m/s in August for Polatlı. The highest capacity factor was 45% for the V82-1.65 MW turbine in Ankara in January; the highest capacity factor in Polatlı was 37% for the same turbine in February.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted a two-parameter Weibull distribution to wind-speed data from four Northern Tigray locations and compared the energy pattern factor, least-squares regression, method of moments, and mean standard deviation methods for estimating Weibull parameters. Performance was assessed using relative percentage error, RMSE, mean percentage error, mean absolute percentage error, Chi-square error, and R2.
studyKeyFindings: Least-squares regression method (LSRM) presented better performance than the other selected methods for the four selected locations. EPFM, MOM, and MSDM were reported as less efficient for fitting Weibull distribution curves at these locations. The authors reported poor-class wind power at all selected locations.
studyLimits: Using monthly mean wind speed can lose extremely high or low wind speeds within a month and does not allow observation of diurnal wind-speed variations.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated four methods for estimating Weibull parameters for wind-energy applications at Chercher, Maychew, Mekele, and Senkata in Northern Tigray, Ethiopia.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Very few studies had investigated wind-speed characteristics and patterns across Ethiopia, with less attention given to sites principally in Northern Ethiopia.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed 10-min wind-speed data from 2011 at 10 m, 30 m and 40 m at four Bushehr Province locations. Weibull probability distributions were fitted using the standard deviation method, wind power and energy densities were calculated, wind direction was analyzed using wind rose diagrams, surface roughness and power-law exponents were estimated, and twelve wind turbines were evaluated using annual capacity factor and annual energy output.
studyKeyFindings: Bordkhun had the highest annual mean wind speed among the four sites, at 5.93 m/s at 40 m, and an annual mean wind power density of about 265 W/m2 at 40 m. The Weibull distribution matched the experimental data considerably well. Bordkhun was considered the best site for wind-energy development in Bushehr Province, whereas Asaluyeh, Delvar and Haft-Chah were not particularly suitable for large-scale turbines; small-scale wind turbines could be a good alternative for those sites. Proven 15 had the highest capacity factor at all sites, while Northern Power 100-24 produced the highest annual energy output.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analysed hourly wind-speed and wind-direction data for six Moroccan coastal sites over 2011–2015. Weibull distributions were fitted using least squares, maximum likelihood, and WAsP methods; R2 was used to assess goodness of fit. Wind power density, turbine capacity factor, and annual output energy were evaluated for selected turbines.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull model provided an accurate description of actual wind-data frequencies independently of the parameter-estimation algorithm used, with R2 values ranging from 0.899 to 0.996 at 50 m.; Dakhla had the highest annual mean wind speed and Weibull scale parameter among the best-fitting results, while Tetouane had the lowest.; Dakhla and Laayoune had the highest annual wind power densities and were concluded to be suitable for grid-connected wind-power systems.; Assila and Essouira were concluded to be suitable only for stand-alone wind-power applications, although their reported annual power densities are below 200 W/m2 and Table 3 classifies 0–200 W/m2 as "Not Suitable".
studyFutureWorks: For a final decision on establishing a wind farm, detailed analysis of these sites must be investigated.
studyLimits: This study was conducted as a preliminary assessment of the wind sites.

studyMethodsSummary: NASA wind data for Kribi, Douala and Limbe covering 31 years (1983–2013) were sorted into mean monthly data and fitted to a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Weibull parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood, and mean power density, maximum power density, most probable wind speed, maximum-energy-carrying wind speed, and wet- and dry-season cumulative wind-speed distributions were analysed.
studyKeyFindings: Kribi was found to be the better of the three sites for wind-farm installation in terms of monthly and seasonal variation of mean wind speed, mean power density, most probable wind speed, and maximum-energy-carrying wind speed. Average wind speeds at all three sites were relatively low compared with the cut-in wind speeds of most modern wind turbines. Wind speeds and power densities were higher in the wet season than in the dry season.
studyResearchGapAddressed: A Weibull analysis of data over Cameroon’s coastal cities was carried out for the first time to estimate and compare power densities, maximum-energy-carrying wind speeds, and most probable wind speeds.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analyzed offshore wind characteristics and wind-energy potential at Bohai Bay using one-second wind data. Weibull, Nakagami, Rician, and Rayleigh distributions were fitted using nonlinear least-squares methods and compared using RMSE and R2; wind-potential indicators were also estimated.
studyKeyFindings: Wind in Bohai Bay mainly blows from the east and is mostly below 12 m/s. Weibull, Nakagami, Rician, and Rayleigh distributions performed well against observed wind speed except in August, when high null-wind occurrence reduced fitting accuracy. Nakagami performed best for forecasting wind power density according to error-sum values. Bohai Bay can be considered a wind class I region according to the study's assessment.
studyFutureWorks: The inaccurate fitting of observed wind speeds in August due to the high percentage of null winds will be improved in future work.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Nakagami and Rician distributions were introduced for wind-speed-distribution fitting and wind-potential assessment at Bohai Bay.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Prior to this study, there had been no relevant research regarding Nakagami or Rician distributions in wind-energy resource assessment.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analysed ten years of wind-speed data from N’Djamena using a two-parameter Weibull distribution to assess wind characteristics, seasonal variation, prevailing wind direction, wind power density and wind energy density.
studyKeyFindings: Wind speeds were higher during the dry season from November to July and lower during the wet season from August to October. The authors concluded that the wind potential at the site is promising but adequate only for small-scale applications.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The paper states that, despite significant wind-power potential in most regions of Chad, no study had undertaken this resource for power generation up to that time.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used the Weibull distribution method to analyse wind-speed data from Medan and determine wind-energy potential that could be converted into electrical energy.
studyKeyFindings: The average wind speed at Medan was reported as 3.159273 m/s. The authors concluded that the wind-energy potential could be used to generate small-scale electrical energy.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used NASA MERRA-2 hourly wind-speed data at 10 m for 01/01/1990–31/12/2019, fitted Weibull distributions using the EPF method, extrapolated wind speed and Weibull parameters to heights from 10 m to 100 m, calculated wind power density, and evaluated four wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: Over 30 years, the reported average annual wind speeds at the two sites varied randomly between 4.7 m/s and 5.4 m/s over an average period of 2 years. Wind power density and available energy were reported to be higher in Amdjarass than in Fada. The paper reports capacity factors of around 25.46% in Amdjarass and 26.33% in Fada for the Vergnet GEV MP 275/32 turbine. The conclusion recommends a "Vergnet GEP MP 275/33" aerogenerator, whereas the evaluated-turbine table identifies "Vergnet GEV MP 275/32"; these turbine designations are conflicting.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed wind speed and direction data measured at Ain Salah over a reported 10-year period, fitted a Weibull distribution using the standard deviation method, evaluated WGT 850 kW turbine and wind-farm energy production, and conducted a cost evaluation.
studyKeyFindings: For Ain Salah, the reported Weibull parameters at 10 m were k = 2.48 and C = 6.0 m/s, with an annual mean wind speed of 5.4 m/s. For a WGT 850 kW turbine, reported annual average power, capacity factor, and energy production were 204.12 kW, 24.01%, and 1.79 GWh, respectively. For the reported wind farm, these values were 2327.02 kW, 23.27%, and 20.38 GWh. The reported energy cost was 0.1603 USD/kWh in the text, while the table and conclusion report 0.1603 USD/KW.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind data from 25 Eritrean sites in the Wind and Solar Monitoring Network were analysed. Mean wind speed, standard deviation, Weibull parameters, prevailing wind direction, and wind power density recalculated for 100 m above ground were assessed. Measured values were also compared with Global Wind Atlas values.
studyKeyFindings: The coastal region sites typically have the highest wind power density, followed by the central highlands.; Assab Airport and Gahro, situated in the far southern part of Eritrea near the mouth of the Red Sea, have the highest mean wind speeds and wind power density among the studied sites.; Some central highland sites, including Gizgiza and Dekemhare, also show potential for wind power, while Kerkebet is the only western-lowland site deemed to have potential.; For good sites, seasonal variations are most prominent in the coastal region, with a peak during November–March, while year-to-year variations are generally small.; Measured mean wind speeds and wind power densities are typically higher than Global Wind Atlas values; the difference is especially large for complex-terrain central-highland sites where Global Wind Atlas results are more uncertain.
studyFutureWorks: More in-depth analyses should be performed before planning the erection of wind turbines at any studied site.; The potential of AI-based forecasting could be studied in the context of increasing wind power in Eritrea.
studyLimits: Extrapolation of wind speed from 10 m measurements to 100 m using the logarithmic wind profile provides significant uncertainty because local orographic and roughness speedup effects and uneven land stability can make the profile inaccurate.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides a comparative assessment of conventional measured wind data from 25 sites distributed over Eritrea's three topographic regions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is a lack of more site-specific wind resource studies which cover the different regions and topographies of Eritrea.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analysed 11 years of daily mean wind-speed data from Akure using Weibull and Rayleigh probability distributions, Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests, wind-speed and power-density extrapolation with height, wind-turbine power-output simulation, and econometric modelling.
studyKeyFindings: The wind-speed data followed the Weibull distribution more than the Rayleigh distribution according to the reported goodness-of-fit criteria.; Monthly mean wind speed ranged from 1.41 m/s in November 2005 to 4.24 m/s in July 1999 under the Weibull model, and from 1.40 m/s in November 2005 to 4.16 m/s in July 1999 under the Rayleigh model.; For the combined January–December 1999–2009 period, mean wind speed was modelled as 2.71 m/s by Weibull and 2.70 m/s by Rayleigh, while mean power density was 18.51 W/m2 by Weibull and 22.26 W/m2 by Rayleigh.; The rainy season, defined as April–October, was windier than the dry season, defined as November–March, and July was identified as the windiest month while December was the least windy month in the reported Weibull and Rayleigh model agreement.; The selected low-wind-speed turbine simulation indicated that increasing hub height from 10 m to 110 m reduced the modelled electrical-energy cost per kWh for both distributions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study used 11 years of daily average wind-speed data to investigate wind characteristics, energy potential, and econometric modelling for Akure metropolis.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Although wind characteristics and energy potential had been studied for other Nigerian sites, the authors stated that no such study was available in the literature for Akure, Nigeria. The authors also identified that prior Nigerian assessments commonly used monthly data rather than daily or hourly data.

studyMethodsSummary: The study introduced the method of multi-objective moments (MUOM) for estimating Weibull-distribution parameters and compared it with MLM, MMLM, MM, GM, and EPFM using actual hourly averaged wind-speed data from four Turkish stations, including annual, long-term, and selected monthly data.
studyKeyFindings: For all considered wind sample cases, MUOM gave smaller power-density error than the other considered methods. It also showed comparable good performance for most considered data with regard to criteria other than PDE.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is no generally agreed upon consensus on the best estimation method for Weibull-distribution parameters in wind-energy studies.

studyMethodsSummary: Seven numerical methods were compared for estimating Weibull shape and scale parameters from wind-speed data recorded in Zuwara, Libya during 2007 at hub heights of 10 m, 30 m, and 50 m. The methods were evaluated using MAPE, MABE, RMSE, and correlation coefficient under bin widths of 1.3 m/s and 1 m/s.
studyKeyFindings: The empirical methods of Justus and Lysen provided the highest performance when the Weibull distribution was well fitted with observed wind-speed data.; The maximum likelihood method gave better accuracy if the Weibull distribution was not matched well to observed wind-speed data; otherwise, its accuracy was not desirable.; The graphical method was found to be inefficient in determining Weibull parameters, and its accuracy was affected by bin width in the cumulative frequency distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared graphical, empirical, energy-pattern-factor, maximum-likelihood, moment, and proposed hybrid methods for estimating the shape and scale parameters of a two-parameter Weibull distribution fitted to hourly wind-speed data at Lomé, Accra, and Cotonou. Model fit was evaluated using RMSE and R2, while predicted wind-speed mean, standard deviation, and wind-power density were assessed using relative percent error and relative root mean square error.
studyKeyFindings: GPM did not yield acceptable adjustment errors on the three sites. MLM often had the lowest distribution-histogram adjustment error. The authors recommend Weibull parameters estimated by EMJ, EML, EPFM, MOM, and HM for predicting mean wind speed, wind-speed standard deviation, and mean wind-power density at Lomé, Accra, and Cotonou; MLM is recommended for the best fit of wind-frequency-distribution histograms.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated numerical methods for estimating Weibull K and C parameters and identifying an appropriate method for fitting wind-speed probability-distribution histograms at three coastal West African locations.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is a lack of study in the literature on determining the most accurate Weibull parameter estimation methods to fit wind speed probability distribution histograms.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analyzed mean hourly wind-speed data recorded in 2018 at İzmir–Aliağa, Turkey; compared least-square, standard deviation–mean wind speed, maximum likelihood, and energy pattern factor methods for Weibull-parameter estimation using RMSE, R2, and Chi-square tests; and performed a present-value cost analysis for wind turbines ranging from 800 to 4200 kW.
studyKeyFindings: The standard deviation–mean wind speed, maximum likelihood, and energy pattern factor methods produced better fitting results for the site wind-speed data than the least-square or graphical method. The annual mean wind speed was 7.53 m s−1, and the annual mean power density calculated by the Weibull distribution using parameters predicted by the standard deviation–mean wind speed method was 520.71 W m−2. The minimum unit-energy cost was obtained with the Enercon E-82 E2 turbine model.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted a Weibull distribution to hourly 2016 wind-speed data from Agadir Al Massira station using seven numerical parameter-estimation methods: graphical method, maximum likelihood method, empirical method of Justus, empirical method of Lysen, energy pattern factor method, Mabchour's method, and method of moments. The methods were compared using R2, RMSE, chi-square error, and error in annual wind-power-density estimation.
studyKeyFindings: For five months (May to September), the maximum likelihood method was the most effective, while the empirical method of Justus was ranked first for January, October, November and December and ranked second for February. For annual wind-power-density estimation, the maximum likelihood method had an error of -0.51 per cent, compared with -4.56 per cent for the empirical method of Justus; the authors concluded that the maximum likelihood method was the most effective and accurate method at Agadir.

studyMethodsSummary: The study developed the PWMBP method for estimating two-parameter Weibull distribution parameters and compared it with MLM, MMLM, MOM, GM, PDM and PWMM using monthly, seasonal and yearly hourly wind-speed data from Cide and Keban, Turkey. Suitability and accuracy were evaluated using R2, RMSE, KS, PDE, graphical comparison, and estimated wind-turbine energy output using Weibull distributions and power curves.
studyKeyFindings: PWMBP apparently outperformed the other methods for power-density estimation for all considered data according to PDE. PWMBP had the highest efficiency for most considered data with respect to R2, RMSE and KS. For energy-production estimation, PWMBP yielded the best performance for 5 time periods of Keban wind-speed data and for 6 of 16 considered time periods for Cide according to EPE.
studyLimits: The analyses used wind-speed data from two Turkish regions, Cide in 2006 and Keban in 2007, and considered the selected seven Weibull-parameter estimation methods.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Development and evaluation of the PWMBP method to estimate Weibull parameters more accurately for wind-energy applications.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The literature contains studies focusing on Weibull parameters for accurate wind-resource prediction, yet there is no consensus on the most accurate estimation method.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared Maximum Likelihood Method (MLM), Modified Maximum Likelihood Method (MMLM), and the newly developed Wind Energy Intensification Method (WEIM) for estimating Weibull shape and scale parameters using hourly wind data measured at 50 m mast height for sixty locations in Pakistan. The methods were evaluated using Wind Energy Error (WEE), RMSE, and R2, and wind energy density estimates were compared with values based on the actual wind-data distribution.
studyKeyFindings: WEIM was found to be the most accurate method in the overall ranking, while MLM was the least accurate. WEIM was found better than MLM with respect to WEE, RMSE, and R2; it was found better than MMLM with respect to WEE and R2, while WEIM and MMLM were comparable with respect to RMSE. Wind energy density values estimated by WEIM were closest to actual energy density values among the three methods. Chaghi, DI Khan, Rahim Yar Khan, and Thatta were identified as the amplest sites in Balochistan, KPK, Punjab, and Sindh, respectively.
studyResearchGapAddressed: R705211__problem_001
studyResearchGapIdentified: R705211__problem_001

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted a Weibull distribution to wind-speed data from Imphal, Guwahati, Shillong, and Kolkata. It compared the method of moments, empirical method, power density method, maximum likelihood method, and the proposed non-iterative energy variance method using R2, RMSE, and power density error.
studyKeyFindings: The proposed energy variance method provided the least error for Guwahati and Kolkata stations, while the maximum likelihood method and power density method showed the least error for Shillong and Imphal stations, respectively.; Across the four stations, Kolkata had the highest reported wind-speed and wind-power potential, whereas Shillong had the lowest reported potential.; The authors identified the energy variance method as the superior estimation method based on the overall ranking analysis and comparison with the existing methods.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study introduced and evaluated a non-iterative energy variance method alongside four conventional methods for estimating Weibull parameters in four cities in Northeast and East India.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous wind-energy assessment studies in various areas of India were limited, and existing works used only one or two methods to estimate Weibull parameters. The authors also identified the time consumption of iterative estimation methods as a limitation.

studyMethodsSummary: Meteorological wind-speed data for Jeddah were assessed using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Monthly, annual and hourly wind-speed characteristics, Weibull shape and scale parameters, wind direction, and wind power and energy densities were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: The reported annual Weibull shape parameter ranged from 1.398 to 1.763 and the scale parameter ranged from 3.146 to 4.329 m/sec. The authors reported that average wind speeds were not sufficient for large-size wind turbines and suggested small wind turbines instead. The paper reports that wind power density was maximum in March and minimum in February. Reported annual wind-power-density values are inconsistent across the paper: Table 4 reports a meteorological maximum of 83.78 W/m2 in 2006, whereas the text reports a highest value of 77.99 W/m2 in 2003.
studyFutureWorks: Future work is indicated as identifying Weibull parameters after the initial wind assessment stages.
studyLimits: The current study covers initial stages of wind assessment to find the best location to identify Weibull parameters.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data from nine offshore buoys in the Ionian and Aegean Sea were fitted with a two-parameter Weibull distribution and a two-component Weibull-mixture distribution. Parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood using a Newton–Raphson numerical method implemented in MATLAB, and fits were evaluated using R2 and RMSE against experimental cumulative frequencies.
studyKeyFindings: For most of the selected sites (six stations with either unimodal or bimodal frequency distributions), the two-component mixed-Weibull distribution provided the highest degree of fit. At Athos, Kalamata and Santorini, p = 0, so the mixed-Weibull distribution was transformed to the simple Weibull distribution. The authors conclude that the two-Weibull mixture is more suitable for such wind conditions and could offer less relative errors in determining annual mean wind power density.
studyLimits: Because all samples were offshore, the utility of some findings for onshore data may be limited.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared maximum likelihood, modified maximum likelihood, and least-squares estimators for Inverse Weibull distribution parameters through Monte-Carlo simulation, then fitted Inverse Weibull and Weibull distributions using ML and MML estimates to seasonal hourly wind-speed data from Bursa and Sakarya, Turkey.
studyKeyFindings: In the simulation study, the ML estimator was overall the most efficient, while the MML estimators had similar bias and MSE performance to ML for large sample sizes and were explicit functions of sample observations.; The LS estimator showed the worst joint performance according to the Def criterion and was not included in the wind-speed-data modeling stage.; For Bursa, Inverse Weibull fitted winter and autumn wind-speed data better, whereas Weibull performed better for spring and summer.; For Sakarya, Inverse Weibull fitted the wind-speed data better than Weibull for all seasons according to RMSE and R2.; MML-based RMSE values were lower, and MML-based R2 values higher, than the corresponding ML-based values for both data sets.

studyMethodsSummary: Eight probability distribution functions—Exponential, Weibull, Gamma, Lognormal, Inverse Gaussian, Log-Logistic, Generalized Extreme Value, and Nakagami—were fitted to wind-speed data from five stations in east and southeast Iran. Maximum-likelihood estimation was used to calculate distribution parameters, and fitting performance was assessed using R2, RMSE, AIC, and BIC.
studyKeyFindings: No single distribution function was suitable for all examined stations. Nakagami provided the best fits at Chabahar and Khaf; Gamma, Generalized Extreme Value, and Inverse Gaussian provided the best fits at Lutak, Rafsanjan, and Zabol, respectively. Nakagami ranked first at two stations and third to fifth at the other three stations. Skewness may be an important parameter affecting Nakagami accuracy, but the influence of the identified parameters requires further investigation for conclusive conclusions.
studyFutureWorks: More examinations of Nakagami effectiveness should be conducted using more case studies with different wind-speed characteristics.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study appraised the capability of different probability distribution functions to fit wind-speed data at five stations in east and southeast Iran and applied Nakagami distribution for the first time in the selected case studies.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is a lack of detailed study about determining the suitable probability distribution models for estimating wind speed distribution in windy locations of Iran.

studyMethodsSummary: Five numerical methods were used to estimate the shape and scale parameters of a two-parameter Weibull distribution fitted to synoptic wind-speed observations from Maroua: maximum likelihood, modified maximum likelihood, energy pattern factor, graphical, and empirical methods. Performance was compared using RMSE and R².
studyKeyFindings: Based on the collected data in the district of Maroua, the maximum likelihood method was the most accurate method overall, followed by the energy pattern factor method and the graphical method. The empirical method followed by the modified maximum likelihood method were the least precise. RMSE and R² values had very close magnitudes for all numerical methods used for the collected data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Selection of a Weibull-parameter estimation method that gives more accurate estimates at Maroua in order to reduce uncertainties related to wind-energy-output calculation from wind energy conversion systems.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analysed 28-year wind-speed data measured at 10 m AGL using the Weibull probability density function. Weibull parameters were estimated using the iterative moment method and extrapolated with an empirical power-law relationship to exposed ridge-tops from 100 to 300 m AGL. Five commercial wind turbines were assessed using computed capacity factors, power outputs, energy outputs, and costs of electricity.
studyKeyFindings: The selected ridge-tops around Kousseri and Maroua, from 100 to 300 m AGL, were assessed as suitable for wind-turbine applications.; YDF-1500-87 was identified as the preferred wind turbine for large communities because it showed the highest capacity factor and the lowest cost of energy among the explored turbines.; P-15-50 was identified as an interesting option for small communities or wind farms, with the highest capacity factor and the lowest cost of energy for its range of specific cost based on rated power.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured hourly wind-speed data from Garoua for 2007–2012 were fitted with a two-parameter Weibull probability density function using six parameter-estimation methods. The methods were evaluated with chi-square, R2, RMSE, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests.
studyKeyFindings: The Energy Pattern Factor method ranked first and the Moment Method second for estimating the Weibull scale and shape parameters. Globally, the Empirical Method, Maximum Likelihood Method, and Modified Maximum Likelihood Method ranked third, fourth, and fifth, respectively, while the Graphical Method was inadequate. Garoua's wind-energy potential was concluded to be not fitted for generating electricity; the authors stated that windmills for community water supply, livestock watering, and farm irrigation could produce a fruitful result.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed the wind-speed distribution and compared six two-parameter Weibull parameter-estimation methods for wind data collected in Garoua.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Due to the absence of a reliable and accurate Cameroonian wind atlas, wind-resource evaluation had received limited attention in Cameroon and further wind-energy assessment studies were necessary.

studyMethodsSummary: The study introduced the upper-truncated Weibull distribution (TWD) for wind-speed modeling, estimated TWD and Weibull-distribution parameters using maximum likelihood, compared fitting results using AIC, RMSE, KS and R2, and compared wind-power-density errors using hourly wind-speed data from three Turkish stations.
studyKeyFindings: Maximum likelihood among the considered methods seems to be a more efficient estimator for TWD parameters in terms of MSE.; TWD outperforms WD for most of the wind-speed data measured in the considered regions of Turkey.; TWD yields less mean power error than WD for most of the considered wind-speed data.; TWD can alternatively be used to evaluate the wind-energy potential of a specified region.
studyLimits: Different model-selection criteria may provide inconsistent ranking orders of fit performance among candidate distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The Weibull distribution is unable to model all wind structures encountered in nature, and selecting the most appropriate distribution is necessary to minimize errors in wind-power estimation for a specific area.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed time series from four urban weather stations in Palermo were divided into monthly and seasonal subsets. Preliminary statistics were calculated, and Weibull, Rayleigh, Lognormal, Gamma, Inverse Gaussian, Pearson type V, and Burr probability density functions were fitted using maximum likelihood estimators. Goodness of fit was ranked using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
studyKeyFindings: The authors state that the Burr PDF achieved better agreement with the empirical wind-speed data. However, the total-period Kolmogorov-Smirnov ranking table ranks Burr first for Merlino and Cassandra, while Gamma ranks first for Morgana and Pizia.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study tested seven probability density functions, including the Burr PDF, for fitting wind-speed data recorded in an urban environment.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Urban wind conditions can be strongly influenced by natural or artificial obstacles, making accurate assessment of wind-energy plant performance more difficult and requiring better local anemometric information.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted Weibull, elliptical, non-Gaussian, and Rayleigh–Rice wind-speed distributions to NOAA ISD-Lite observations from 89 French weather stations for 2010–2013. Fits were obtained by minimizing the right-tail Anderson–Darling statistic, and compared using Cramer–von Mises and right-tail Anderson–Darling of second degree scores.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull distribution was generally accurate near the centre of wind-speed distributions in northern France but tended to underestimate distribution tails and performed less accurately in complex southern terrain. The Rayleigh–Rice distribution generally outperformed the other tested distributions, especially in valleys and at stations affected by persistent channelled flows. Where wind components were close to Gaussian and without much anisotropy, all fits were relatively close, except that only the non-Gaussian distribution did not underestimate strong-wind probability in the tail.
studyLimits: The non-Gaussian wind-speed distribution assumes statistically independent wind components with similar parameters b and c; the authors state that this assumption is debatable and not generically true. The Rayleigh–Rice distribution has four parameters and is not easily fitted.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The widespread use of the Weibull distribution to model wind-speed statistics is empirical rather than physically justified, and the distribution may fit poorly when wind components are non-isotropic or non-Gaussian or when multiple wind regimes occur.

studyMethodsSummary: The study constructed and compared seven bivariate joint-distribution models for wind speed and wind direction: angular-linear (AL), Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern (FGM), and anisotropic lognormal approaches. AL and FGM models used either truncated-below-Normal and Weibull (TNW) or inverse-Gaussian and lognormal (IGL) wind-speed mixtures and mixtures of von Mises distributions for wind direction. Fit was compared using adjusted R2 and RMSE.
studyKeyFindings: Across the North Dakota sites considered, the anisotropic approach generally provided poorer adjusted R2 and RMSE results than AL and FGM approaches, although it could produce close joint-distribution results for some sites. AL- and FGM-based distributions had similar performance, and the simpler FGM approach could be used instead of AL models for representing wind characteristics. IGL and TNW models had comparable performance for representing wind speed and for joint distributions.
studyFutureWorks: Future research may develop more efficient anisotropic-model construction procedures, use multiple directional sectors and prevailing directions, investigate independence between longitudinal and lateral wind-speed components, consider statistical dependency using concepts from FGM models, and incorporate meteorological approaches, seasonality, and spatial effects for uncertainty assessment.
studyLimits: Only Green R had an additional complete record for 2005 for cross-validation. The cross-validation discrepancies were not significant, but they indicated the existence of a potential over-fitting issue when parameters and goodness-of-fit metrics are determined from the same dataset.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted nine parametric wind-speed distributions to hourly wind-speed data from 67 Malaysian stations using maximum likelihood estimation, derived wind-power distributions using a transformation technique, computed theoretical mean wind power using raw moments or Monte Carlo integration, assessed spatial dependence using semivariograms, and produced inverse-distance-weighting maps.
studyKeyFindings: Gamma, Burr, Weibull, Erlang, and Inverse Gamma distributions were selected as the most appropriate distributions across stations. The semivariogram analysis indicated a lack of spatial correlation of wind power in Malaysia. The maps indicated comparatively higher wind-power potential in northeast, northwest, and southeast Peninsular Malaysia and in southern Sabah, while the authors stated that more comprehensive analysis with more stations is needed.
studyFutureWorks: A more comprehensive analysis with more stations is needed to obtain a better map of wind-power potential in Malaysia and to identify specific areas with good wind regimes.
studyResearchGapAddressed: A nationwide rough spatial assessment of wind-power density based on suitable wind-speed probability distributions and geostatistical mapping.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The authors observed that wind-energy research in Malaysia was not widespread and stated that more in-depth studies were needed to explore the opportunity.

studyMethodsSummary: The study derived theoretical wind-power-density functions from Weibull, Gamma, and Inverse Gamma wind-speed probability density functions using a transformation method. Maximum likelihood estimation and Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit statistics were used for wind-speed distribution fitting, and Monte Carlo integration was used to determine power-density statistical properties for Gamma and Inverse Gamma cases.
studyKeyFindings: The wind-power-density function derived from the Weibull probability density function follows a modified Weibull probability density function, allowing its mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis to be obtained from Weibull properties.; For power density derived from Gamma and Inverse Gamma probability density functions, the resulting equations are difficult to match with existing statistical models; Monte Carlo integration was proposed as an efficient and reliable flexible solution for determining their statistical properties.; Among the stations considered, Weibull was the best wind-speed model at Cameron Highlands, Kudat, and Putrajaya, while Gamma was better at Mersing, Malacca, and Sandakan.; The theoretical wind-power-density functions fitted the histograms of empirical wind-power data well under the reported assumptions of unit airstream area and constant air density.
studyLimits: The study does not involve real wind turbines; therefore, the airstream area was assumed to be 1 m2.
studyResearchGapAddressed: A transformation method and Monte Carlo integration approach were presented to derive and evaluate wind-power-density statistical properties.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Difficulty in obtaining statistical properties of wind power density from wind-speed probability density functions, particularly for Gamma and Inverse Gamma distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted eight parametric wind-speed distribution models to hourly data from two Malaysian meteorological stations. Parameters were estimated by maximum likelihood, with the Nelder–Mead optimization technique used for selected distributions. Goodness-of-fit information from the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic, Akaike’s information criterion, deviation in skewness/kurtosis, and 1-R2 was standardized through a standard normal CDF transformation and combined through multiplicative aggregation.
studyKeyFindings: The multiplicative aggregation of standardized goodness-of-fit scores selected the Gamma distribution as the best statistical distribution model for wind-speed data collected at both Kuantan and Balok Baru.; For Kuantan, graphical representations indicated that Gamma, Weibull, and Burr models fit the data better than the other distributions, although the differences among Gamma, Weibull, and Burr were relatively small; the probability difference graph indicated that Gamma was more precise than Weibull and Burr.; The graphical representations agreed with the analytical results obtained through multiplicative aggregation.
studyResearchGapAddressed: An integrated multi-criterion approach using standardized scores and multiplicative aggregation was proposed to obtain a conclusive distribution-model selection.
