studyResearchGapIdentified: Different goodness-of-fit criteria can provide inconsistent answers for the selection of a wind-speed distribution model, causing confusion and a lack of consensus on the best selected model.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted a mixture of two truncated normal distributions (MTTND) and six conventional probability density functions to experimental wind-speed distributions from six locations. Parameters were estimated using non-linear least-squares regression with a trust-region algorithm. Goodness of fit was evaluated for PDFs and CDFs using R2 and RMSE, and estimated characteristic wind-speed quantities were compared with experimental values using relative percentage errors.
studyKeyFindings: Across the six locations considered, the MTTND provided the greatest accuracy for representing the experimental discrete PDF and CDF. For the PDF, its R2 was not less than 0.980 and its RMSE was not greater than 0.011; for the CDF, its R2 was not less than 0.996 and its RMSE was not greater than 0.050. The MTTND also gave lower average and maximum relative errors for the characteristic mean wind speeds than the conventional distributions considered.

studyMethodsSummary: The study developed a mixture kernel density model that combines kernel densities with optimal weight coefficients determined by minimizing asymptotic integrated mean squared error using a Lagrangian multiplier method. The model was evaluated against six conventional models using Chi-square and Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests on hourly wind-speed samples from eight North Dakota sites, and was applied to six wind turbine generator types and three wind-energy assessment indices.
studyKeyFindings: The MKD model passed almost all goodness-of-fit tests and had smaller average test statistics than the other tested models. The authors conclude that it provides a better match to the observed wind profile than the compared models and can facilitate identification of a preferable wind turbine generator and a wind site containing richer wind-energy resources among the sites considered.
studyLimits: The MKD model is not applicable for wind-speed probability-distribution estimation in situations where wind-speed data are not available; this shortcoming is inherited from the kernel density model.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly measured wind-speed data from ten stations in Ontario, Canada, were used to fit and compare the two-parameter Birnbaum-Saunders distribution with nine one-component probability distributions. Distribution parameters were computed using the maximum likelihood method, and goodness of fit was assessed using R2, RMSE, AIC, and BIC. Wind-power-density distributions were subsequently estimated from the fitted wind-speed distributions.
studyKeyFindings: The BS distribution showed very favorable performance for estimating wind-speed and wind-power-density distributions at the examined stations. It gave the best fit at six stations. The paper contains conflicting statements regarding its rank at the remaining four stations: the abstract reports third or fourth, whereas the results and conclusions report third or fifth. Weibull was reported as the second-best function for wind-power-density distribution but was not able to give an adequate description of wind-speed-data frequencies at all sites.
studyFutureWorks: Future wind-resource-assessment work could consider the applicability of additional distribution functions to certain sites and should use a number of case studies with different wind-speed and wind-power characteristics.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study introduced and evaluated the two-parameter Birnbaum-Saunders distribution for wind-speed and wind-power-density distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: To the best of the authors' knowledge, no investigation had applied the Birnbaum-Saunders function to estimate wind-speed and wind-power distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted fourteen probability distributions to 10-min mean wind-speed samples from 178 North American ocean buoys. Distributional performance was compared using probability-plot R2, estimates of average wind-turbine power output, and estimates of extreme wind-speed exceedances.
studyKeyFindings: The bimodal Weibull, Kappa, and Wakeby distributions provided significantly better R2 fits than the other distributions considered, with the bimodal Weibull giving the highest R2 values. Kappa gave the lowest mean-square error and bias for average turbine-power estimates, whereas the 2-parameter Lognormal gave the best extreme-wind-speed estimates but still had significant errors. Model selection therefore depends on the wind-energy application.
studyFutureWorks: Further analyses are needed to validate models based on application-specific engineering parameters, including average power output, extreme wind speed, and potentially fatigue loads.
studyLimits: All samples were from ocean environments, which may limit the utility of some findings for onshore data. Confidence intervals for estimated exceedance counts were challenging to construct because the observations could not be considered independent.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study used a larger geographically diverse offshore dataset and compared distribution performance using both goodness-of-fit and engineering-parameter estimation metrics.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous mixture-distribution studies used limited samples from confined geographic regions, and conventional goodness-of-fit measures such as R2 do not necessarily indicate how well a model predicts wind-energy parameters.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed 10-min wind data from Shurje, Iran, evaluated 46 continuous probability distribution functions using Kolmogorov-Smirnov and R2 measures, extrapolated wind speed to 80 m using power-law and logarithmic-law methods, analyzed turbulence intensity and surface roughness, and estimated 50-year extreme wind speed using periodic maxima, a Gumbel distribution, and the Harris algorithm.
studyKeyFindings: Among the evaluated distribution functions, Wakeby had the greatest compatibility with the measured wind data. Estimated 80 m wind speed using the power law ranged from 5.58 to 12.24 m/s, with an annual mean of 7.72 m/s. The estimated 50-year extreme wind speed at 80 m was 44.262 m/s; the authors concluded that this value was lower than typical Ve50 limits and that the site had limited risk from extreme weather conditions.
studyFutureWorks: Future work was proposed to investigate extreme wind speed using the method of independent storms and the EWTS II algorithm; optimize Wakeby coefficients using nature-inspired algorithms; analyze uncertainty in wind-speed extrapolation and relations between shear parameters and atmospheric stability; explore neural networks for stable-boundary-layer wind-speed fitting; assess further meteorological datasets; and apply a measure-correlate-predict method.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted 11 one-component parametric probability density functions, two two-component mixture distributions, and a kernel-density non-parametric distribution to hourly average wind-speed series from nine meteorological stations in the UAE. Suitability was evaluated using log-likelihood, R2 based on P-P and Q-Q plots, Chi-square, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics.
studyKeyFindings: Overall, mixture distributions were generally the best probability density functions according to every statistic, with MWW more suitable than MGG most of the time. KAP and GG were the best one-component distributions overall. W2 was the best two-parameter distribution and performed better than some three-parameter distributions such as GEV and LN3. One-component probability density functions were not suitable for wind-speed distributions presenting severe bimodal regimes.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The UAE region is characterized by a severe lack of studies focusing on the assessment of wind-speed characteristics and distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study reviewed goodness-of-fit criteria used to compare probability density functions for wind speed data, represented 11 selected probability distributions in conventional moment-ratio and L-moment-ratio diagrams, and applied the diagrams and goodness-of-fit criteria to hourly wind-speed series from seven stations in the United Arab Emirates.
studyKeyFindings: For the United Arab Emirates stations, Kappa, Log-Pearson type III and Generalized Gamma distributions covered all station samples in the diagram regions. Among distributions with one shape parameter, Weibull distributions had the most central position relative to the sample coordinates. Conclusions from goodness-of-fit criteria agreed better with the L-moment-ratio diagram than with the conventional moment-ratio diagram.
studyFutureWorks: Future work should focus on non-stationary frequency-analysis techniques for modelling wind-speed series in various regions around the globe. Moment-ratio diagrams could be adapted to analyse temporal evolution of wind-speed characteristics using a moving window through the data series.
studyLimits: Classical frequency-analysis tools used in wind-speed modelling are based on the temporal-stationarity hypothesis, but this assumption is not always met.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study developed and applied moment-ratio and L-moment-ratio diagram approaches for wind-speed-data analysis in the United Arab Emirates.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Despite its advantages, the moment-ratio-diagram approach had never been used for the assessment of wind-speed distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: Observed hourly wind-speed data from 83 meteorological stations in Québec were fitted with one-component and two-component mixture probability distributions. L-moment ratio diagrams were used to assess one-component distributions, and mixture-model parameters were estimated using least-squares and maximum-likelihood methods optimized with a genetic algorithm. Goodness of fit was evaluated using chi-square, R2, RMSE, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics.
studyKeyFindings: Among the probability distributions having one shape parameter and represented as curves in the L-moment ratio diagram, Weibull provided the best fit.; Mixture models provided better goodness of fit than the one-component Weibull and Kappa distributions according to the performance criteria used.; The maximum-likelihood method outperformed the least-squares method according to all criteria.; The mixture of two Gumbel distributions estimated using maximum likelihood was the overall best model.; Mixture distributions can efficiently model both bimodal and unimodal wind-speed behaviors.
studyFutureWorks: Extend the moment ratio diagram approach to bimodal and mixture distributions.; Analyze non-stationarity in wind-speed data in Québec, including trends, jumps, and cycles.; Extend homogeneous and heterogeneous mixture models to the non-stationary case using covariates such as time, climate indices, and low-frequency climate oscillation indices.
studyLimits: L-moment ratio diagrams cannot represent mixture distributions presenting bimodal behaviors.; Mixture models have additional complexity compared with one-component Weibull models and require advanced optimization methods such as the genetic algorithm used in this study.; The genetic-algorithm parameter-estimation method takes more processing time when mixture models are applied to a large number of stations.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated homogeneous and heterogeneous two-component mixture distributions, alongside one-component distributions, for fitting wind-speed data from a large network of stations across Québec.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind-energy assessment and mapping studies remain relatively limited in Nordic environments. Very few studies had evaluated wind-energy potential in Québec, and previous Québec assessments had primarily relied on the Weibull distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed and wind-direction observations from six stations in the greater Chania area were used for regional and seasonal wind-characteristic assessment, wind-power-density estimation, and comparison of Weibull, Rayleigh, Lognormal, Gamma, and Inverse Gaussian distributions for overall and monthly wind-speed frequency distributions. Distribution parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood estimation.
studyKeyFindings: Mean wind speed varied from 2.1 m/s at Souda to 6.034 m/s at Pedio Volis. The study identified two regions for onshore wind-energy applications: the Chania valley and southern Akrotiri area, suitable only for small-scale applications, and the elevated northern Akrotiri area, proposed as a potential site for larger-scale applications. Gamma was suggested as an alternative to Weibull and, at elevated sites, Gamma outperformed Weibull. Although the chi-square null hypothesis was accepted in very few cases, high coefficient-of-determination values and visual inspection indicated that Gamma and Weibull reasonably modelled the experimental wind-speed distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study proposed non-parametric kernel density estimation for wind-speed probability distributions, developed a wind-speed-sample-based technique to calculate an optimal bandwidth, and compared it with ten conventional parametric distributions using hourly wind-speed data from ten Chinese wind-farm sites over 2004–2006. Goodness-of-fit was assessed using Chi-Square and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests, posteriori histogram comparisons, mean-square-root errors, and visualized distribution matches.
studyKeyFindings: For the ten wind-farm sites and the 3-year datasets considered, the statistical and posteriori comparisons indicated that the proposed non-parametric kernel estimation was more accurate and had better adaptability than any of the ten conventional parametric distribution models. The kernel model could fit bimodal probability-density distributions, whereas the conventional parametric distributions considered were unimodal.

studyMethodsSummary: Long-term hourly observed wind-speed and wind-direction data from four Rwandan meteorological observatories were analyzed for periods with monthly hourly mean wind speed greater than or equal to 2 m s−1. Weibull, Rayleigh, lognormal, normal, and Gamma probability density distributions were fitted and compared using graphical comparisons, residual analysis, RMSE, MBE, and a χ2 goodness-of-fit test.
studyKeyFindings: The paper concludes that Gisenyi has suitable wind-energy potential for electricity generation, whereas Kigali, Butare, and Kamembe have sufficient potential for windmills or water pumping. The reported rankings of best-fitting wind-speed distributions are internally conflicting for Gisenyi, Kigali, and Kamembe between Section 3.2 and the conclusion.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared ten two-component homogeneous and heterogeneous mixture distributions, constructed from Gamma, Weibull, Extreme value type-one, and Normal distributions, with Weibull and four-parameter Kappa distributions for hourly mean wind speed data at seven UAE stations. Mixture parameters were estimated using Maximum Likelihood, Expectation Maximization, and Least Squares methods; Genetic Algorithm optimization was used for the Maximum Likelihood and Least Squares objective functions. Goodness of fit was assessed using BIC, adjusted R2, and chi-squared statistics.
studyKeyFindings: Mixture distributions provided the best fit to wind speed data at all seven UAE stations according to the employed goodness-of-fit measures. The Weibull-Extreme value type-one mixture distribution was concluded to be the most appropriate distribution for wind speed data in the UAE. For stations with skewed unimodality, the improvement from heterogeneous mixture distributions was less important than for stations with skewed bimodality and kurtotic unimodality, and non-mixture distributions could compete with mixture distributions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study investigated the applicability of heterogeneous mixture distributions and identified an appropriate distribution for modeling wind speed data in the UAE.
studyResearchGapIdentified: No study adopted heterogeneous mixture distributions for wind speed analysis in the Arabian Peninsula.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted and evaluated Johnson-Wehrly, Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern, and Plackett bivariate distributions for joint wind-speed and wind-direction data from six Mediterranean locations. Wind-speed marginal distributions included conventional and mixture distributions, while wind direction was represented using finite mixtures of von Mises distributions. Bivariate fits were evaluated using seven bin-specific measures.
studyKeyFindings: Across the examined locations and criteria, the Johnson-Wehrly family generally provided the best bivariate fits relative to the Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern and Plackett families. The univariate best-fit wind-speed distribution did not necessarily provide the best bivariate wind-speed--wind-direction fit. The selected Johnson-Wehrly models were applied to estimate wind-power-density distributions at Andros, Pylos, and Mar de Alboran.
studyFutureWorks: The authors suggest investigating suitable bivariate copulas and kernel density functions, and considering alternative circular models such as nonnegative trigonometric sums for modelling the dependence structure in the Johnson-Wehrly model.
studyLimits: The authors note that multivariate goodness-of-fit tools are limited and that the evaluation measures used are bin-specific. Although several wind-speed and wind-direction bin widths were tested, further research on joint distributions is needed to improve goodness of fit.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared three bivariate parametric distribution families at six Mediterranean locations using seven bin-specific goodness-of-fit measures.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A more in-depth assessment and evaluation of bivariate analytic distribution families was needed to investigate their efficiency and capability for modelling in-situ wind-speed and wind-direction data from diverse wind regimes.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted 23 analytic probability distributions to long-term offshore wind-speed time series from 19 Mediterranean buoys. Fits were assessed using Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Anderson–Darling and chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, followed by coefficient of determination R2. Selected fitted distributions were additionally evaluated by relative estimation errors for mean wind power density and average wind turbine power output.
studyKeyFindings: Johnson SB, Kappa and Wakeby distributions accurately described the empirical offshore wind-speed distributions at the examined Eastern and Western Mediterranean locations and had better adaptability than the Weibull distribution. Johnson SB was the only distribution reported to suit very well in all examined cases with consistently fair goodness-of-fit results. However, the distribution providing the best wind-speed fit was not necessarily the best solution for wind-energy characteristics such as mean wind power density or average wind turbine power output.
studyFutureWorks: Johnson SB distribution is used for the first time in this work and further results need to be sought.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Apart from a previous assessment based on US buoy data, the author reports a lack of published works modelling offshore wind speed using several long-term time series from climatically and geographically different sea areas.

studyMethodsSummary: The study extrapolated long-term daily near-surface wind-speed series from 58 DWD stations to 100 m AGL using the Hellman power law, fitted 67 theoretical cumulative distribution functions, selected the five-parameter Wakeby distribution, modeled Wakeby targets using least squares boosting and spatial predictors, and calculated modeled annual wind energy yield using a standard wind-turbine power curve.
studyKeyFindings: The five-parameter Wakeby distribution was the best-fitting distribution on average and was concluded to be a universal wind-speed distribution for the study area. Relative elevation and topographic exposure in the main wind direction were important predictors. Modeled annual wind energy yield varied strongly over short distances in complex terrain; highest and lowest values occurred within distances below 500 m.
studyLimits: The methodology requires near-surface wind-speed time series measured in meteorological networks, a digital terrain model, a land-cover dataset, and wind-speed data not influenced by local topography or land use for portability.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted two- and three-parameter Weibull distributions (WD2 and WD3), a skewed generalized error distribution (SGED), and a skewed t distribution (STD) to hourly wind-speed data from four Turkish stations. Model performance was compared for monthly, seasonal, and yearly wind-speed data using R2, RMSE, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, negative log likelihood, and AIC.
studyKeyFindings: For the monthly, seasonal, and yearly analyses considered, SGED and STD were generally more suitable than WD2 and WD3 according to the considered model-selection criteria. Particularly, SGED provided the best fit to a variety of wind-speed data. For Station 4 yearly data, STD had the highest fit according to R2, RMSE, and KS, whereas WD3 was best according to negative log likelihood and AIC.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study proposed and evaluated SGED and STD as flexible alternative families for describing wind-speed distributions and estimating wind-power-density distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The Weibull distribution does not exhibit good performance for all wind types encountered in nature, such as low and high wind speed.

studyMethodsSummary: The study modeled 23-year offshore wind-speed records using Weibull, Rayleigh and Lognormal distributions optimized by Cuckoo Search (CS) and Chaotic Particle Swarm Optimization (CPSO). Monthly and quarterly maxima were re-analyzed using a GH model, then Gumbel and GEV distributions were fitted to estimate extreme wind speeds for specified return periods.
studyKeyFindings: For the four Bohai Rim study sites, Weibull was the most suitable distribution for observed wind-speed frequencies. GEV performed better than Gumbel for monthly and quarterly offshore extreme wind-speed modeling. CS–GEV was selected in seven of eight extreme-wind cases; CPSO–GEV was selected for quarterly extremes at site D. The study area had estimated extreme wind speeds below 45 m/s for the evaluated return periods.
studyFutureWorks: More detailed work needs to be carried out for each candidate site to gain precise predictions prior to wind farm construction.
studyLimits: The main challenge for extreme wind-speed estimation was insufficient extreme-wind data; the extracted monthly and quarterly extreme-wind samples had sizes of 276 and 92, respectively.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study proposed GH statistical calibration optimized by artificial-intelligence algorithms to re-analyze extreme wind speeds under data shortage.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Little work had been performed to estimate offshore wind energy together with extreme wind speeds in China, and the availability of long-term extreme wind-speed data was limited.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed wind-speed data from four sites in central China, tested long-term wind-speed-distribution stability using Mann–Whitney U and two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests, compared parametric and non-parametric probability-density models, compared parameter-estimation methods including the cuckoo search algorithm, and assessed wind energy and wind-turbine selection using six output-power curves and consideration of wake-related power loss.
studyKeyFindings: The mutation tests indicate that the wind speed distributions at all of the sites do not change.; For sites 1 and 2, the Weibull distribution was superior to the other selected parametric distributions according to the reported comparison criteria; for sites 3 and 4, the normal distribution outperformed the other selected parametric distributions.; The non-parametric kernel estimation provided more accurate and realistic wind-speed-distribution features at all four observation sites than any conventional parametric model according to the reported comparisons.; In the overwhelming majority of cases, the cuckoo search algorithm was superior to the other reported parameter-estimation methods for the parametric models.; The selection of output-power curves significantly affects wind-turbine selection; the JW1500 turbine had the highest reported average capacity factor and modified average capacity factor at all four sites.; Considering wake effects and power loss can lead to better wind-energy evaluation and wind-farm design.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared selected parametric and non-parametric wind-speed probability-distribution models and compared parameter-estimation methods using four sites in central China.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The two-parameter Weibull distribution does not represent some wind regimes well, and parametric-model selection and performance should be analyzed according to the specific statistical characteristics of wind.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily wind-speed data from 2010–2014 at three Bohaiwan sites in China were characterized and fitted with Weibull, Rayleigh, Lognormal, Gamma, and Loglogistic distributions. The five distributions were compared using RMSE. Seven Weibull-parameter estimation methods, comprising GWO, PSO, CS, EMJ, EML, EPFM, and MLM, were evaluated using IA, RRMSE, and R2. Wind power density, effective wind power density, and wind-turbine availability factor were then calculated using Weibull parameters obtained by GWO.
studyKeyFindings: Among the five tested distributions, the Weibull distribution had the minimum RMSE for wind-speed data from all three Bohaiwan sites, whereas the Lognormal distribution had the maximum RMSE in every reported period. GWO outperformed the other parameter-estimation methods for almost all considered wind-speed data according to R2, RRMSE, and IA; however, for site A during Oct.–Dec., PSO produced the best outcomes, and for site C during Jul.–Sep., CS was the best method. The study concludes that wind-energy resources at the three sites are abundant and that wind turbines are highly likely to operate under the assumed cut-in and cut-out speeds.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There was still no consistent conclusion on which method can obtain the most accurate results to estimate the parameters of the Weibull distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: The study proposed a diffusion-based kernel density method (DKDM) for estimating wind-speed probability distributions. The method uses a diffusion partial differential equation on a finite domain for bandwidth selection and boundary correction, and uses discrete cosine transformation and inverse discrete cosine transformation to reduce computational complexity. It was tested using simulated parametric distributions and wind-speed data from six observation stations.
studyKeyFindings: DKDM accounts for both bandwidth selection and boundary correction of kernel density estimation and does a satisfactory job in fitting commonly used parametric models.; For the six wind observation stations, DKDM produced non-negative probability-density domains, whereas SJPI estimates extended to negative wind-speed values near zero.; The preprocessing random-number procedure eliminated repeated data values and produced continuous probability densities for stations with relatively low recording frequencies and resolutions.; In Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, DKDM and SJPI statistics were smaller than the corresponding critical values, whereas most Weibull-distribution statistics were larger than the critical values.; The authors caution that smaller goodness-of-fit statistics for KDE can indicate smaller bandwidths and closer agreement with the empirical distribution function rather than closer agreement with the true probability distribution function.
studyFutureWorks: Extend DKDM to model multivariate wind distributions.
studyLimits: Compared with parametric methods, DKDM may be trapped in situations where no wind speed is available.; It is inappropriate to compare wind resources between different stations because of different measuring conditions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: An improved non-parametric diffusion-based kernel density method was developed to address KDE bandwidth selection and boundary correction when estimating wind-speed probability distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Most kernel density estimation papers concentrate on mathematical theory, while only a few actually model wind-speed probability distributions. Parametric distribution selection may not work well across different wind farms, and conventional KDE has bandwidth-selection and finite-boundary problems.

studyMethodsSummary: The study developed a Multivariate and Multimodal Wind Distribution (MMWD) model based on multivariate kernel density estimation, applied it to univariate, bivariate, and trivariate wind-condition distributions, compared its univariate wind-speed fit with five standard distributions using R2 from Q-Q plots, and estimated wind power density using Monte Carlo integration.
studyKeyFindings: The MMWD model had the largest R2 values among the compared distributions at both Baker and Station 44013 for univariate wind-speed fitting. The onshore Baker wind distribution was found to be multimodal, whereas the offshore Station 44013 distribution was treated practically as unimodal. Strong correlation among wind speed, wind direction, and air density was observed. For the examined nine-turbine farm, MMWD produced a higher WPD estimate but a 5% lower farm-power estimate than Weibull because wind speeds above the turbine cut-out speed do not contribute to farm generation.
studyFutureWorks: Further research is necessary to allow the MMWD model to better represent the periodic nature of wind-direction data. Explicit consideration and characterization of uncertainties in wind conditions and their propagation into overall wind-farm power output is identified as a direction for future research. Implementation of the MMWD model in optimal planning of commercial-scale wind farms is proposed.
studyLimits: The KDE-based model does not account for the frequency of calms.; The periodic equivalence of wind directions 0° and 360° is not captured in the KDE-based model.; KDE can often lead to overfitting of probability distributions.; Prediction of long-term 20-year wind conditions using 10 years of data might introduce greater uncertainties.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study developed an MMWD model capable of representing multimodal data and joint variations of wind speed, wind direction, and air density.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing wind-distribution approaches make limiting assumptions regarding wind-variable correlation and distribution modality, and a robust multivariate probability distribution of wind speed, wind direction, and air density was reported as absent from the literature to the authors' knowledge.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data from five representative North Dakota sites were fitted with eight conventional probability distributions and maximum-entropy-principle-derived PDFs. Six goodness-of-fit statistics and a proposed comprehensive ranking metric were used to compare distribution-fit performance.
studyKeyFindings: No particular distribution outperformed the others for all five sites. Multiple distributions provided good fits for Alfred and Ray/Wheelock; Green River and Olga had lower goodness-of-fit; no tested distribution provided an acceptable fit for Benedict. MEP-derived PDFs outperformed conventional distributions for Benedict's multimodal wind-speed histogram, whereas one or more conventional distributions outperformed MEP-derived PDFs at the other sites with unimodal histograms. Different goodness-of-fit statistics produced different preference orders among tested distributions.
studyFutureWorks: More research is needed regarding approaches that may serve the purpose of fair comparison of statistical distributions better.
studyLimits: The proposed comprehensive metric is described as a first step for fair comparison of statistical distributions; other approaches might serve the purpose better.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study fitted eight conventional PDFs and eight MEP-derived PDFs to data from each of five North Dakota sites and evaluated them using six goodness-of-fit statistics and a proposed comprehensive metric.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A comprehensive and fair comparison of wind-speed probability density functions was missing; many common PDFs had not been studied as potential candidates, and existing studies often used only one to three evaluation metrics.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted 24 one-component probability density functions and 21 two-component mixture probability density functions to empirical wind-speed probability density functions derived from global ERA-Interim reanalysis data. Sixty-nine distribution-parameter-estimation-method combinations were evaluated using eight goodness-of-fit metrics related to probability-probability plots, quantile-quantile plots, and mean wind power density.
studyKeyFindings: Mixture probability density functions, including Burr-Generalized Extreme Value, Dagum-Generalized Extreme Value, Dagum-Weibull and Generalized Extreme Value-Weibull, generally provided superior fits to one-component distributions for probability-probability-plot goodness-of-fit metrics. The Wakeby distribution was suitable for estimating the upper tail of the majority of onshore empirical distributions, whereas the Kappa distribution was appropriate for many offshore regimes. The Johnson system of distributions and Wakeby distributions were very appropriate choices for estimating mean wind power density according to x3 error. The widely used two-parameter Weibull distribution provided similarly good fits only in a few cases.
studyFutureWorks: In future studies it might be sufficient to fit the majority of empirical probability density functions with a few of the presented distribution-parameter-estimation-method combinations. It is preferable using few distributions defined by a larger number of parameters than searching for a two-parameter distribution suitable only in the specific case.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The investigation provided a comprehensive global-scale performance assessment of numerous commonly used probability density functions and compared them with newly introduced mixture probability density functions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The diversity of conceptual frameworks, samples and results in previous studies makes it difficult to identify the most suitable probability density function or mixture probability density function, parameter estimation method and reliable goodness-of-fit metric for optimal empirical probability density function fitting of wind speed data.

studyMethodsSummary: The study developed a system of wind speed distributions comprising Kappa, Wakeby, and Burr-Generalized Extreme Value distributions. It used 10,016 globally distributed hourly wind speed time series, fitted distributions to empirical wind speed distributions, trained a random forests classifier using L-moment ratios, evaluated goodness-of-fit using eleven metrics combined into a comprehensive metric, and assessed average wind turbine power-output estimation.
studyKeyFindings: The system of wind speed distributions had significantly better goodness-of-fit than the individual evaluated distributions and provided high-accuracy average wind turbine power-output estimates for stations with capacity factor at or above 0.20. The random forests classifier correctly predicted the distribution with the highest comprehensive goodness-of-fit metric at 73.6% of stations.
studyFutureWorks: In future wind resource studies, the system of wind speed distributions can be applied to assess the wind resource from local to global scale.
studyResearchGapAddressed: A single system of wind speed distributions was developed to reproduce the large majority of existing near-surface wind speed regimes.
studyResearchGapIdentified: None of the previous studies incorporated the best of the well-fitting wind speed probability density functions into a single system of probability density functions for harmonized modeling of existing wind speed regimes.

studyMethodsSummary: The study introduced the Extended Generalized Lindley Distribution (EGLD) for wind-speed distribution modelling and compared EGLD, Weibull, Rayleigh, Lognormal and Gamma distributions using hourly averaged wind-speed data from four stations in Turkey. Parameters of all considered distributions were estimated using maximum likelihood estimation, and fitting and wind-power-estimation capability were assessed using RMSE, R2, Chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, AIC and power density error criteria.
studyKeyFindings: EGLD provided a better fit than the other considered distributions for all stations considered in Table 4. The conclusions state that EGLD outperformed Weibull and other well-known distributions for most wind-speed data measured in different regions of Turkey, and that its power density error results showed superiority in estimating wind power. EGLD showed significant improvement in fit for most considered annual and long-term wind-speed data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated EGLD as an alternative flexible wind-speed distribution with two shape parameters, one scale parameter and an explicit cumulative distribution function.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Widely used statistical wind-speed distributions may not model all wind-speed data observed in nature.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted eight probability distributions to wind-speed data from four Algerian stations using the Method of Moments, Maximum Likelihood Method, Power Density Method, and L-Moments Method. Goodness of fit was assessed using R2, RMSE, and power density error.
studyKeyFindings: The best PDF/PEM combinations were Gamma/L-MM for Bouzaréah and El-Hamdania, GEV/MLM for Bousmaïl, and GEV/L-MM for Adrar. Across the employed distributions and sites, L-MM was the most accurate parameter-estimation method, followed by MLM, PDM, and MM. GEV/L-MM was the most accurate of the thirty PDF/PEM combinations, whereas LN/PDM gave the worst results. In terms of power density error, PDM with Gamma, Inverse Gaussian, and Log Normal gave different best results from R2 and RMSE.
studyLimits: Given the low wind speed values at the four studied sites, where the mean wind speed does not exceed 3.7 m/s, the results of this study may change for sites with high wind potential.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The Power Density Method and L-Moments Method, previously used only for Weibull-parameter estimation in wind-energy literature, were developed and applied to the other distributions used in this study where applicable.

studyMethodsSummary: Four parametric wind-speed distribution functions (Gamma, Lognormal, Rayleigh, and Weibull) were fitted to actual and rounded/truncated wind-speed data from five stations in Kerman Province, Iran. Maximum likelihood estimation and method of moments were compared using nine goodness-of-fit indices.
studyKeyFindings: For actual wind-speed data, the lognormal distribution yielded the best fit across the five studied stations.; For truncated wind-speed data, Weibull distribution fitted using maximum likelihood estimation performed best for Bam, Arzuiyeh, and Shahrbabak, while lognormal distribution remained best for Bardsir and Rafsanjan.; The Rayleigh distribution gave the least accurate results for both actual and truncated wind-speed data.; The authors recommend Weibull distribution with maximum likelihood estimation when there is uncertainty about wind-speed-data accuracy.
studyLimits: The analysis was based on five stations in Kerman Province and compared actual data with a rounded/truncated version of those data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Sensitivity of four wind-speed distribution functions to the accuracy of anemometer-measured wind data at five locations was evaluated.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There was no comparative research on the effectiveness of wind-speed data with different accuracies on well-known distribution functions, particularly for wind-speed modelling.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly 2009 wind-speed data from four Turkish meteorological stations were fitted with Generalized Lindley, Power Lindley, and Weibull distributions. Maximum likelihood estimates were used for the actual wind-speed data after a Monte Carlo comparison of maximum likelihood, maximum product spacing, and least-squares estimators.
studyKeyFindings: The Generalized Lindley distribution provided the best fitting in most cases considered according to RMSE, R2, lnL, and AIC. However, Weibull and Power Lindley distributions were more preferable than Generalized Lindley in most cases according to PDE; Generalized Lindley showed substantial improvement for Bilecik in winter and Sakarya in summer.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study proposes Generalized Lindley and Power Lindley distributions as alternatives to Weibull for wind-speed modeling.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is little or no literature about modeling wind-speed data by using Generalized Lindley and Power Lindley distributions together.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared Weibull, Rayleigh and lognormal distributions for 10-min average wind-speed time series from ten South African sites, using RMSE and R2 for goodness of fit. Weibull parameters were estimated using the maximum likelihood method, wind speeds were extrapolated to turbine hub heights using a power-law relationship, and capacity factors for 20 commercially available turbines were estimated analytically.
studyKeyFindings: The wind distribution at all sites was best modelled by the Weibull distribution, with the Rayleigh distribution a close competitor.; Among the ten sites considered, WM05 had the highest capacity factors and WM02 had the lowest capacity factors.; Turbine K was reported as the most appropriate choice among the turbines considered for the coastal region of South Africa based on capacity-factor estimation.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study determined the best-fitting wind-speed distribution for ten sites and estimated capacity factors for commercially available turbines using local wind regimes.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Reliable knowledge of wind distributions and appropriate turbine selection based on local wind regimes is needed for different sites in South Africa.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted two-parameter Weibull, Rayleigh, two-parameter Gamma, and Lognormal distributions to daily wind-speed data from four Yangtze River Delta cities. Wind speeds measured at 10 m were extrapolated to a 90 m hub height using empirical extrapolation. Method of moments, maximum likelihood estimation, least-squares method, bat algorithm, cuckoo search, and particle swarm optimization were compared for parameter estimation. Goodness of fit was evaluated using R2, RMSE, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
studyKeyFindings: In this case, metaheuristic optimization algorithm-based distribution models performed better than numerical-method-based models. Weibull was the best-fitting distribution, followed by Gamma, while Rayleigh and Lognormal had the worst performance. No one metaheuristic optimization algorithm dominated the others in this case. The selected optimal models were PSO-Weibull for Shanghai and BA-Weibull for Hangzhou, Taizhou, and Chuzhou.
studyFutureWorks: Future work should compare more wind-speed distributions and parameter-estimation methods, model wind speeds at different temporal scales, and explore and model seasonal wind-speed data.
studyLimits: Only four commonly used wind-speed distributions and three numerical methods and three metaheuristic optimization algorithms were considered. The analysis used daily wind-speed data sampled at 10 m with a temporal resolution of 24 h; hourly and 10-minute wind speeds were not considered. Seasonal wind-speed trends were not considered.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared bat algorithm, cuckoo search, and particle swarm optimization with conventional numerical methods for estimating parameters of wind-speed probability distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Applications of metaheuristic optimization algorithms to estimate parameters of wind-speed distribution models were relatively few.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared single parametric distributions, four mixture distributions, and a proposed hierarchical mixture of multiple distributions (HMMD) for fitting one-year wind-speed records at four Chinese wind farms. Parameters for mixture models were estimated using EM, HMMD parameters were estimated using nested EM, and wind-energy potential and wind-energy conversion-system performance were assessed using the fitted distributions.
studyKeyFindings: The proposed HMMD model had the best goodness-of-fit among the considered models for the four observed regions. Mixture models generally outperformed single distributions, but no single mixture model always produced the best fit under different wind regimes. HMMD-based wind power densities classified Jilin and Ningxia as Class 3 and Gansu and Dongshan as Class 6; the study described wind-energy potential as moderate in Jilin and Ningxia and excellent in Gansu and Dongshan. The WECS using Nordex N131/3000 Delta at 99 m hub height was selected as optimal for Jilin and Ningxia, while the WECS using eno e.n.o. 126 at 117 m hub height was selected as best for Gansu and Dongshan.
studyFutureWorks: The authors state that reliability evaluation of power systems will be analyzed if wind-speed frequency distribution obeys the HMMD model, and that they will try to estimate all HMMD parameters within a Bayesian framework.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The paper develops HMMD, in which each outer component is approximated by a mixture model, and introduces a nested EM algorithm for parameter estimation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing mixture models assume that each component is a unimodal single distribution; this assumption may be inadequate when a component itself has a bimodal or multimodal distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared Weibull, Rayleigh, and multi-peak Gaussian fits to observed percentage wind-speed frequency distributions from 208 sites across India using R2 as a goodness-of-fit measure. The authors also described annual energy output computation using fitted wind-speed distributions.
studyKeyFindings: For the 208 Indian measurement sites analysed, the authors found multi-peak Gaussian functions to provide a better fit to wind-speed distributions than Weibull and Rayleigh functions, particularly for bi-modal and multi-modal distributions. For uni-modal distributions, the three fits had approximately similar R2 values from 0.95 to 0.99, although Gaussian fit was closer to 1.0.
studyFutureWorks: The authors recommend carrying out the exercise for wind-speed data in other parts of the world and establishing additional formulations for wind-speed analysis, height extrapolation, wind-turbine design considerations, and energy assessments.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The suitability of multi-peak Gaussian functions as an alternative to Weibull and Rayleigh functions for representing wind-speed distributions was assessed using data from a large set of Indian sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The two-parameter Weibull distribution is widely accepted for representing wind-speed distributions, although wind-speed distributions are often bi-modal or multi-modal and can present difficulties for fitting to a single Weibull distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: The study maps wind-energy potential in the Far North Region of Cameroon using wind-speed data, Weibull distribution fitting, vertical wind-speed extrapolation, wind-power-density estimation, and an energy-cost analysis.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides a wind-energy potential mapping and assessment for the Far North Region of Cameroon.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The lack of reliable local wind-energy information for the Far North Region of Cameroon.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted Gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh, Normal, and Lognormal probability distribution functions to wind-speed data from Abong Mbang and discriminated them using Chi-square, R2, and RMSE goodness-of-fit tests. Self-written Matlab R2013b codes were used for computational work.
studyKeyFindings: For the Abong Mbang weather station, the Gamma distribution was the best representative of the wind-speed regime and was closely followed by the Weibull distribution. Wind speeds and power densities were very low; the authors concluded that the site is not technically feasible for installation of even small wind turbines.
studyFutureWorks: The authors advise revisiting the site in the future after accumulating a much longer duration of data and measurements at higher heights for a more valid assessment; the best representative PDF may be different at the same site for different heights.
studyLimits: The study used low-frequency daily data and a limited period of data of only two years.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed wind-energy potential and probability density functions for the Abong Mbang weather station.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The paper states that no such wind-energy study had so far been carried out in some other parts of Cameroon, including Abong Mbang.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically analysed 28 years of 10 m AGL wind-speed data from Maroua using a Weibull probability density function with the energy pattern factor method. It extrapolated wind characteristics to hilltops from 50 to 350 m AGL using an empirical power-law correlation, assessed six wind turbines, and estimated costs of wind-generated electricity in Microsoft Excel.
studyKeyFindings: At 10 m AGL, Maroua was classified as wind-power class 1 and deemed unsuitable for electricity generation. The paper reports that hilltops at 100 m AGL are suitable using taller wind towers, that hilltops at 150 m AGL are most suitable, and that hilltops above 200 m AGL are excellent for wind-turbine applications. YDF-1500-87 had the lowest reported electricity costs among the selected turbines. The paper reports conflicting claims regarding the turbine with the highest capacity factor: the results text and tables identify P-15-50 as having the highest capacity factors, whereas the conclusion states that YDF-1500-87 followed by E82-2000 provide the highest capacity factors.
studyLimits: No measurement stations were installed at the selected hilltops; therefore, 10 m AGL wind characteristics were extrapolated to hilltops.
studyResearchGapIdentified: No feasibility studies had been carried out on potential mountainous wind-farm projects in Maroua.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used monthly mean wind-speed data from 2007 to 2012 at Garoua International Airport, fitted a two-parameter Weibull probability density function using maximum likelihood estimation, extrapolated Weibull parameters and mean wind speed to 15 m and 20 m above ground level, and estimated water-pumping performance for hypothetical windmills.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull distribution proved to be a useful tool to predict the wind regime relevant to wind power generating systems.; The wind energy potential in the north region of Cameroon is not fitted for generating electricity.; The authors conclude that the results encourage the use of water-pumping windmills in rural areas for household water use, small-scale irrigation, and livestock.
studyFutureWorks: Further wind characterization studies at different heights above ground level are required.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Studies on wind characteristics in the north region of Cameroon are limited, and there appear to be limited interests and limited previous research on wind energy for mechanical water pumping.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data collected at a 10-m meteorological station in Ambam from November 2012 to October 2014 were fitted with a Weibull distribution. Weibull shape and scale parameters were estimated using graphical, empirical, energy pattern factor, and moment methods, whose performance was compared using RMSE, chi-square, and R2. Wind power density and wind-energy density were estimated from the collected time-series data.
studyKeyFindings: The empirical method had the best overall performance because it ranked first, second, and third across the three years of analysis. Ambam was characterized as unfavorable for effective wind-energy generation considering the mean monthly and yearly wind speed and wind power density. Nevertheless, at 10 m height, the reported potential was described as not negligible in the Cameroonian rural-electrification context for localities far from the national electrical network.
studyLimits: Ambam is not favorable for an effective energy generation system at the assessed 10-m height.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used NASA satellite daily average wind-speed data for Debuncha, partitioned the data into monthly minimum, monthly average, monthly maximum, wet-season, and dry-season datasets, and fitted Weibull, Gumbel, and Frechet distributions using maximum likelihood estimation. The fitted distributions were compared using P values of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and standard-error analysis.
studyKeyFindings: The authors report that the Frechet distribution best fitted the monthly minimum, monthly average, and monthly maximum wind-speed data relative to the Gumbel and Weibull distributions. They also report that monthly average wind speeds fitted the Weibull distribution better than monthly minimum and monthly maximum wind speeds. Wind speed and wind power density were higher during the wet season than during the dry season. Average wind speeds were relatively low compared with the reported 6–10 m/s cut-in wind speeds of most modern wind turbines.
studyFutureWorks: The authors state that they intend to obtain high-resolution or Cameroon meteorological-department ground-station data for Debuncha and to design more adaptive small wind turbines for low wind speeds by considering aerodynamic structure, reduced load, and high-lift, low-Reynolds-number air-foil design.
studyLimits: High-resolution wind-resource data at 10-minute to 1-hour intervals and ground-station data for the site were not available for analysis.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compares Weibull, Gumbel, and Frechet distributions for monthly minimum, monthly average, and monthly maximum wind-speed data from Debuncha.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The study notes that Weibull distribution is commonly considered the best distribution for mathematically modelling wind-energy potential, and investigates whether other distributions in the generalized extreme value family, specifically Gumbel and Frechet distributions, may better describe wind-energy potential at a site.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used ERA-5 daily zonal and meridional wind data at 10 m above ground level from January 2000 to December 2017 on a 0.25° × 0.25° grid of 2745 sites. Weibull, Normal, and Lognormal probability density functions were fitted by the maximum likelihood method, assessed using RMSE, chi-square, and R2, and used to evaluate wind power densities. Wind speeds and power densities were extrapolated from 10 m to 50 m with a power-law exponent of 1/7.
studyKeyFindings: Weibull and Normal probability density functions were found to be more appropriate than the Lognormal distribution for modelling wind speed in the study area; the Lognormal PDF slightly overestimated wind power density. Wind resources across most of the study area were classified mostly as class 1 and, at a few locations, class 2, and were not suitable for large-scale electricity generation. The highest seasonal wind variability occurred in the Gulf of Guinea during the rainy season and in the Lake Chad Basin during the dry season. Annual/interannual wind-speed and power-density patterns were either decreasing at windier sites or relatively constant at less windy sites.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study used data covering the whole Cameroonian territory and compared Weibull, Normal, and Lognormal PDFs across 2745 sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous Cameroon wind-energy studies targeted specific locations and did not simultaneously address the use of Normal and Lognormal PDFs for a large number of sites across Cameroon.

studyMethodsSummary: Three-hourly wind-speed data measured five times per day from 6am to 6pm at 10 m were analyzed using Weibull and Rayleigh probability-density models, goodness-of-fit tests, power-density calculations, and wind-rose plots.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull model was a better fit to the Bafoussam wind regime than the Rayleigh model. Mean wind speeds varied between 1.9 and 3.1 m/s in the cases considered, and Bafoussam was assessed as a poor wind-energy-potential site. Winds were predominantly from the NE first quadrant, mainly at 10 degrees, while most calms occurred at 6am and the highest wind speeds were measured at 3pm.
studyFutureWorks: Evaluate wind energy at higher heights using power laws accounting for surface roughness; collect a longer-duration dataset after a considerable number of years; compare Weibull with a broader spectrum of probability density functions; and use a higher sampling rate with newly installed airport instruments.
studyLimits: The three-hourly time steps diminish the stochastic nature of wind speeds and directions at shorter sampling times; the Beaufort scale is subjective and less accurate; and the energy-potential evaluation assumes zero surface roughness.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared thirteen numerical methods for estimating Weibull parameters using 38 years of average daily wind-speed data for representative towns in the 10 regions of Cameroon. Method effectiveness was assessed through R2, RMSE, chi-square test and relative power density error, including quantitative comparison of Weibull cumulative distribution functions with cumulative data frequencies.
studyKeyFindings: The energy density method was the best method for estimating wind power density at all selected sites, followed by the novel energy pattern factor method. The graphical method was best for the cumulative distribution function at all sites except Ebolowa, where the empirical method of Justus was best. The selected sites were reported as wind power class 1; Maroua had the highest reported wind power density, 33.4806 W/m2, and Ebolowa the lowest, 0.1126 W/m2. The authors suggested that low-start-up wind turbines may be suitable for small applications, while Maroua, Garoua and Ngaoundere were more suitable for wind-power generation systems than the other cities considered.
studyFutureWorks: Future work will be focused on the study of the technical and economical aspect of Savonius wind turbines to produce household energy in rural areas of Cameroon.
studyLimits: For Ebolowa, only two wind-speed bins were observed in the data; the authors associated this limited number of bins with poor performance of several methods.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared thirteen Weibull-parameter estimation methods across representative towns of all 10 regions of Cameroon.
studyResearchGapIdentified: For previous Cameroonian wind-potential studies, the accuracy of the chosen method to estimate Weibull parameters was not clearly justified because of a lack of such works applied to the considered sites.

studyMethodsSummary: The study compared measured and satellite-derived wind-speed data at Garoua using MBE, RMSE, RRMSE, R2 and IOA; used a two-parameter Weibull probability distribution function for wind-speed characterization; extrapolated wind characteristics to a 30 m hub height; simulated four 20 kW wind turbines using a parabolic power-curve law; and estimated costs of energy and water with the present value of costs method.
studyKeyFindings: Satellite-derived data were found sufficiently accurate to provide a reasonable wind-resource assessment during the initial phase of wind-project planning before higher-accuracy in situ measurements are available. The North Region was classified as wind power class 1 at 10 m height above ground level and was deemed unsuitable for large-scale wind-turbine applications. Figuil showed the best combination of capacity factor, cost of energy, cost of water and flow-rate capacity among the sites considered, whereas Poli showed the worst values independently of the wind turbine used. The turbine with the lowest cut-in and rated wind speeds had the highest capacity factors and the lowest costs of energy and water produced.
studyLimits: The satellite-derived-data assessment against ground measurements was performed for Garoua, the only site with measured ground-level data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study explored long-term satellite-derived wind data and statistical accuracy indexes to assess wind resource and electric wind pumping potential in the North Region of Cameroon before higher-accuracy local measurements are accessible.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Satellite-based wind-resource data are valuable in Cameroon because very few meteorological stations are available, while studies on wind power remain very limited.

studyMethodsSummary: Twenty-eight years of up to three-times-a-day synoptic wind-speed observations from Kousseri were analyzed. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was fitted using maximum likelihood, modified maximum likelihood, graphical, empirical, and energy pattern factor methods. The methods were compared using RMSE and R².
studyKeyFindings: The five methods were effective for the available Kousseri data, with RMSE and R² values very close across methods. The energy pattern factor method had the lowest yearly-average RMSE and highest R², followed by the maximum likelihood and graphical methods. The maximum likelihood method had the smaller average relative error for predicted wind-speed standard deviation than the energy pattern factor and graphical methods.
studyFutureWorks: Extension of this study to other locations in the Northern region of Cameroon and over similar study periods is required for a sound conclusion.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The suitability of five numerical Weibull-parameter estimation methods was compared for Kousseri, Cameroon.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A more appropriate Weibull estimation method is needed to provide accurate and efficient evaluation of wind energy potential because the suitability of each method depends on the sample data distribution and is location specific.

studyMethodsSummary: Five numerical parameter-estimation methods for a two-parameter Weibull distribution—maximum likelihood, modified maximum likelihood, energy pattern factor, graphical, and empirical methods—were compared using measured wind-speed data from Maroua, Cameroon, for 1985–2013. RMSE, chi-square, and R² were used for performance assessment, and predicted mean wind speeds and standard deviations were compared with measured data.
studyKeyFindings: The five Weibull methods had RMSE, chi-square, and R² values with magnitudes very close to each other. The paper identifies the energy pattern factor method as the most accurate method based on the statistical tests, but it reports that this method produced the highest standard-deviation errors compared with measured standard deviations. The paper contains conflicting rankings of the graphical and maximum likelihood methods: the abstract ranks the graphical method second and maximum likelihood third, whereas the discussion ranks maximum likelihood second and graphical third. The conclusions recommend the energy pattern factor method for estimating Weibull parameters and state that the maximum likelihood method could be an alternative.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured 10-minute wind-speed data from Alasaba meteorological station in 2007 were statistically analyzed using a Weibull distribution model. The study compared measured and Weibull-estimated monthly wind-speed frequency and cumulative distributions, used R2 goodness-of-fit testing, extrapolated wind speed and Weibull parameters to different heights, and estimated wind power and energy density.
studyKeyFindings: The authors report that Weibull distributions generally fitted the actual monthly wind-speed data well, although November showed a significant difference between actual and estimated monthly cumulative density functions. The reported monthly R2 values include 98.2% for July, 97.7% for September, 96.8% for December, 72% for November, and 85.1% for May. The study concludes that the site wind-speed and energy-intensity values indicate that present technology allows cost-effective wind-power generation.

studyMethodsSummary: The study assessed wind energy potential at Kırklareli University Kayalı Campus using measured wind data, Weibull and Rayleigh statistical distributions estimated by Moment and Maximum Likelihood methods, goodness-of-fit tests, WRPLOT wind-direction analysis, and WAsP-based turbine energy-production and micrositing analyses.
studyKeyFindings: For the examined statistical distributions, the Rayleigh MLE method was estimated to be the most suitable model based on goodness-of-fit tests. At 100 m, annual mean results estimated using Rayleigh MLE reported a scale parameter of 7.15 m/s, wind speed of 6.34 m/s, standard deviation of 3.31 m/s, and power density of 322 W=m2. The annual dominant wind direction was Northeast (NE), with 1407 blowing hours. The GE103 model was suggested as the most suitable turbine and was estimated to generate 7.270 GWh annually.
studyFutureWorks: A techno-economic analysis is planned to determine the investment opportunities at the location.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The authors report that this is the first study to determine the wind energy potential of Kırklareli University Kayalı Campus.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data measured between 2000 and 2006 at six Turkish meteorological stations were analyzed. Weibull distributions were fitted using the mean wind speed-standard deviation method, wind speeds were extrapolated using a power-law formula, and annual energy output and capacity factor were calculated for four commercial wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: The annual mean wind speeds at Erzurum, Elazıg˘, Bingöl, Kars, Manisa and Nig˘de were reported as 8.7, 8.5, 5.9, 6.9, 7.4 and 8.0 m/s, respectively, at 10 m. Erzurum and Elazıg˘ were concluded to be the best regions among the six studied locations for harnessing wind power. The locations investigated can be evaluated as marginal areas for economical electrical energy generation. The conclusion states that annual highest Weibull k and c values occur at Elazıg˘ and Erzurum, respectively, although the yearly k row in Table 3 reports the largest listed k value, 1.96, for Bingöl.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Wind power potential was calculated for Manisa, Nig˘de, Elazıg˘, Bingöl, Erzurum and Kars in Turkey.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The potential sites of wind energy generation of Turkey have not been completely investigated in detail yet.

studyMethodsSummary: Five years (2014–2018) of wind-speed data recorded every 10 min at 10 m at the Djibouti-city weather station were statistically analysed using Weibull shape and scale parameters. Wind characteristics, wind direction, power density, energy density, and the performance of five selected commercial micro wind turbines were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: The annual mean wind speed was 1.652 m/s at 10 m. The monthly mean wind speed was lowest in June (1.247 m/s) and highest in February (2.329 m/s). Eastern winds were the dominant direction (61.3%), followed by western winds (36.05%). Among the five turbines considered, the Polaris P12-25 yielded the highest reported capacity factor (9.629%) and annual energy output (2.1 × 10^4 MWh), although the conclusion describes this energy output as occurring in August. The authors conclude that Djibouti-city has potential for small-scale wind-turbine applications and that turbines with hub heights greater than 30.5 m should be installed for efficient harvesting.
studyFutureWorks: An extensive power-feasibility study should be conducted in larger geographical areas of Djibouti-city to choose the best possible options for different scales of wind-power generation.
studyLimits: The available wind potential for Djibouti-city could not be estimated for other areas because of lack of data. A few days from the 9th to the 30th of September 2015 were missing because of a technical problem of the cup-anemometer.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides one of the first evaluations of wind potential in the Republic of Djibouti using five years of wind-speed data for Djibouti-city.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A wind-energy-potential study in this urban area was not feasible before because of lack of data.

studyMethodsSummary: Eight probability density functions were fitted to measured wind-speed data from two urban and two rural stations in Djibouti. Their goodness of fit was assessed using RMSE, R2, and the index of agreement for monthly, seasonal, and yearly periods.
studyKeyFindings: Based on yearly, monthly, and seasonal analyses, Weibull, Rayleigh, Gamma, and Gumbel were the top four ranked distribution functions for all stations. For the rural stations, Nakagami ranked 1st for Ghoubet and 3rd for Bada Wein in the yearly analysis.
studyFutureWorks: The Nakagami distribution should be conducted and evaluated for more rural sites which have high wind speed.
studyLimits: For Ghoubet, approximately 21 days of data between October and November 2015 are missing; the losses were often due to violent wind at the site.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed eight distribution methods for modeling wind probability distributions using urban and rural wind-speed data in Djibouti.
studyResearchGapIdentified: In eastern Africa, including Djibouti, no detailed analysis had been investigated on the assessment of probability density functions to characterize wind-speed distributions. Weibull and Rayleigh distributions are not always enough and may not be suitable for modeling all wind regimes.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data measured at 10 m were analysed for Illizi and Es senia using Weibull statistics. Weibull shape and scale parameters were estimated using the maximum likelihood method, and mean wind speed and wind power density were calculated for monthly and seasonal analyses.
studyKeyFindings: At 10 m, Illizi had the highest reported annual average wind speed of 6.5 m/s, while Es senia had a middle wind potential with an annual mean velocity of 3.5 m/s. For both regions, spring was reported as the windiest season. Monthly mean wind speed and mean power density were highest in June for both sites among the reported monthly values.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Contribution to the update of the wind map in Algeria through wind-resource analysis in two regions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study processed meteorological and wind-speed data from Laayoune over 369 days, fitted a Weibull distribution using least-squares, standard-deviation, and Mabchour's methods, and compared WES 18-100KW, XANT M-21 100KW, and Northem Power NPS 21-100KW turbines using Excel, ALWIN, and HOMER.
studyKeyFindings: For the Laayoune site, the authors conclude that the XANT M-21 100KW turbine has generally good annual energy production compared with the other turbines and has a low total cost; they identify it as the most efficient, most profitable, and best suited turbine among those compared.

studyMethodsSummary: The study combined 10 m surface-station observations, TerraClimate and ERA5 gridded data, and CORDEX-Africa regional climate-model simulations to assess historical and projected wind speed and wind power density across Zambia. ERA5 was selected for subsequent analysis, three better-performing RCMs were combined into an ensemble, outputs were bias-corrected using linear scaling, ERA5 wind speed was extrapolated from 10 m to 100 m using a power law, and wind power density was calculated.
studyKeyFindings: Observed 10 m winds across Zambia averaged 2.8 m/s and were rarely strong. Extrapolating ERA5 wind speed from 10 m to 100 m increased the mean from 2.5 to 3.4 m/s for 1981–2000. Wind speed generally increased across much of the country, although lowland terrain in Eastern Province bordering Malawi showed negative projected anomalies. Projected annual average wind power density was about 46.6 W/m2, which the study concluded is generally too weak for large-scale wind-power generation. Small-scale turbines accommodating a cut-in wind speed of 3.8 m/s were concluded to be more suitable, particularly in rural and suburban areas where obstructions are few.
studyLimits: Station data covered only 2006–2021; the study used ERA5 in subsequent analyses because of this limited station-data period. Country-level spatial averages could potentially obscure maximum wind power densities across some regions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides a comprehensive assessment of wind-speed projections across Zambia using high-resolution CORDEX-Africa models.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Assessment of wind-speed variables relevant to wind-energy generation across southern Africa, particularly Zambia, has been ignored, and literature on future spatiotemporal wind-speed variations is especially lacking.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind data from the Ngaoundere meteorological airport station were processed using a Weibull distribution with parameters estimated by the modified maximum likelihood method. Wind speed was vertically extrapolated with the Hellmann exponential law, and WAsP together with generated topographic data was used for wind-resource extrapolation and mapping. A hypothetical wind farm of four 1.65 MW Vestas V82 turbines was simulated in a selected high-wind-resource area.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull parameters calculated by the modified maximum likelihood method were very close to those obtained by WAsP, and agreement was observed for the mean wind speed and energy density calculated at 10 m. A hypothetical wind farm of four 1.65 MW turbines in the selected high-resource area had a computed annual energy production of 5,985 MWh and could enable a reduction of 1200 tons of CO2 emissions per year.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study carried out wind characterization for Ngaoundere and provided a wind resource map intended to support selection of suitable areas for wind park installation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind energy remains unexploited in Cameroon despite its theoretical potential in the North of the country, and research in this area is still in its starting phase in Cameroon.

studyMethodsSummary: The study evaluated Taïba Ndiaye wind-farm production data at annual, monthly, daily, hourly, and intra-day scales and compared production with ERA5 wind conditions at 100 m above ground level.
studyKeyFindings: Production peaked between December and May and was lowest between July and November. Night-time production was 43.1% higher than daytime production overall. Farm production showed a strong positive correlation with 100 m wind speed; winter and spring production maxima were associated with strong winds, while low summer production was attributable to meteorological conditions characterized by weak winds.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used ERA5 reanalysis and in situ data from the Ziguinchor meteorological station to characterize wind spatio-temporal variability and available wind power density at 10 m and 100 m. Weibull distribution analysis, wind-rose analysis, turbulence-index analysis, wind-occurrence analysis, and wind-turbine capacity-factor calculations were performed. The abstract specifies five named Basse Casamance sites, whereas the methods and results specify six sites, additionally including Oussouye.
studyKeyFindings: Wind potential was stronger on the coast and in the north-western part of Senegal. At the seasonal scale, wind was higher in winter and spring than in fall and summer. In Basse Casamance, Diembering, Kabrousse, and Kafountine had higher wind power density at 100 m than inland sites. At Ziguinchor and 10 m for 2016–2018, ERA5 gave slightly higher annual mean wind speed and wind power density than station data. Nordex acciona N-100 and EolSénégal/500 W/24 V were identified as more suitable at Ziguinchor at 100 m and 10 m, respectively.
studyFutureWorks: A technical and economic analysis of a wind system for electricity production for Ziguinchor and other Basse Casamance sites would be interesting. The authors also state that the impact of global warming at 1.5 and 2°C on wind power density in Senegal should be studied.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed wind spatial and temporal distributions and wind power density across Senegal, with a case study focused on Basse Casamance.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous wind-potential studies had not covered the whole country, especially the Basse Casamance area in southern Senegal.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used monthly mean wind-speed data measured at 10 m at the NIMET meteorological station in Kano. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was fitted using the standard deviation method, wind speeds were extrapolated to different hub heights using a power-law expression, and wind power density, energy density, and energy efficiency index were calculated.
studyKeyFindings: For the reported 2000–2014 analysis period, the overall monthly average wind speed was 9.13 m/s; June had the highest monthly wind speed of 10.6 m/s and November had the lowest of 6.7 m/s. The maximum monthly power density and corresponding energy density were estimated as 735.925 W/m2 and 529.866 kWh/m2, respectively, in June. The authors concluded that Kano falls under wind power density Class 7 and could be considered for wind-turbine application.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed wind power potential and energy efficiency index for Kano using monthly mean wind-speed data and Weibull analysis.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Kano State has no wind power project currently due to lack of research that could reveal its potentials and benefits; previous studies did not include energy efficiency index formulation.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used daily wind-speed climatic data for Accra from the Tutiempo Network, averaged the daily data into monthly data and the monthly data into yearly data, and applied a two-parameter Weibull distribution function. Weibull shape and scale parameters were calculated using the empirical method or Standard Deviation Method.
studyKeyFindings: For Accra during 2002–2016, monthly mean wind speed ranged from 3.5944 ms−1 to 5.4167 ms−1. The highest reported wind power density was 157.5603 Wm−2 in September 2006. Periods with mean power density greater than 100 Wm−2 were reported as suitable for large-scale electric wind application, while small-scale wind turbines could be a good option during the remaining periods. The monthly mean wind-power-density and mean-wind-speed relationship had a coefficient of correlation of 99.3 %.
