studyResearchGapAddressed: The study employed more wind-speed data for Accra than studies found in the literature and distinguished mean power density for large-scale electric wind application for each month and year during the study period.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The availability of wind resources necessary for exploitation is still a big limitation in Ghana, and wind-data coverage by the Energy Commission is limited to a few regions.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed and wind-direction records collected approximately every 10 minutes during 1998–1999 at five northern Senegalese sites were analysed. The selected-station data were fitted using a two-parameter Weibull probability distribution, with Weibull parameters estimated through linear regression.
studyKeyFindings: The annual average wind speed in the northern coastal region was reported as 3.8 m/s, based on data from five locations, and an annual energy of 158 kWh/m2 could be extracted.; The reported average wind speed is below the 6.0 m/s minimum speed stated for wind-electric generation, whereas wind-powered water pumping appears to be a viable option.; Wind availability was higher during the dry but cold season; the maximum monthly mean wind speed of 5.3 m/s occurred in March, while September and October had the lowest monthly mean wind speeds of around 3.0 m/s.; The Weibull distribution was reported to be well suited for the particular study area and useful for calculating parameters relevant to wind-power-generating systems.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct additional long-term measurements for the region.; Perform more detailed studies separately at each site before construction and installation of wind energy conversion systems.
studyLimits: The work is described as a preliminary study based on approximately two years of data.; The authors state that more detailed site-specific studies are needed before construction and installation of wind energy conversion systems.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated wind-energy potential at five northern coastal Senegalese locations as an attempt to contribute to a prospective Senegalese Wind Atlas.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A reliable and accurate Senegalese Wind Atlas was absent, and further studies assessing wind energy in Senegal were considered necessary.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data for Abeche, Mongo, and N'Djamena were assessed using the Weibull distribution. Wind speeds and Weibull parameters were extrapolated from 10 m to turbine hub heights, and five wind turbines were assessed using capacity-factor, energy-output, and present-value-cost calculations.
studyKeyFindings: N'Djamena had the highest reported wind speeds from 10 m to 105 m, but the Enercon-82 turbine had the highest reported capacity factor among the evaluated turbines at Abeche and Mongo. The authors conclude that Enercon-82 is applicable for Abeche and Mongo, while future work should examine other adaptable turbines for N'Djamena.
studyFutureWorks: Seeing other adaptable wind turbines for the N’Djamena site.

studyMethodsSummary: The study applied ten numerical methods to estimate the shape parameter k and scale parameter c of a two-parameter Weibull distribution using daily wind-speed data from Kano, Maiduguri, Jos, Abuja, and Akure, Nigeria, for 2002–2012. The methods were evaluated using RMSE, R2, chi-square error, MAPE, and MABE, and wind characteristics including mean wind speed, most probable wind speed, wind speed at highest energy, and wind power density were calculated.
studyKeyFindings: The best overall numerical methods for estimating Weibull parameters were MMLM for Kano and Maiduguri, MQM for Jos and Abuja, and EMJ, EML, and AMM jointly for Akure.; MOMAB was the least-performing numerical method for all five studied locations.; Among the locations considered, Jos had the highest reported mean wind speed and wind power density, while Akure had the lowest reported mean wind speed and wind power density.; The authors concluded that Jos was the best location for installing wind turbines, Kano was an excellent location for grid integration, Maiduguri was suitable for a stand-alone application, and Abuja and Akure were unsuitable for wind-energy applications.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study estimated Weibull parameters for wind-speed data from five Nigerian locations using ten standard and rare numerical methods and compared their performance.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Documentation of Weibull-parameter estimation for wind-speed data was reported as lacking for Africa, particularly Nigeria despite its untapped wind-power potential.

studyMethodsSummary: The study assessed 30 years of monthly mean wind-speed and wind-direction data at 10 m for 1984–2013 and five years of daily wind-speed data for 2009–2013. It used a two-parameter Weibull probability density function, estimated wind power density, extrapolated wind speed to 80 m, and evaluated six practical wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: Monthly mean wind speed peaked at 4.62 m/s in August and was lowest at 3.60 m/s in November. Mean wind speed was 4.05 m/s during dry DJF months and 4.32 m/s during wet JJAS months. Maximum estimated wind power density was 145.48 W/m2 in August. AV 928 had the highest reported monthly average power output among the turbines considered, but capacity factors were relatively low, approximately 10% or less, raising concern about the economic viability of a large-scale wind-power project at the study site.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There exists limited evidence of wind-energy assessment studies in Nigeria, where electricity supply is still below demand.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed time-series data for 2002–2011 from three Nigerian offshore locations were averaged to daily and monthly values. Weibull, Rayleigh and Exponential probability distributions were fitted and compared using RMSE, R2 and chi-square. Wind power density, characteristic wind speeds, turbine power output and capacity factor were estimated.
studyKeyFindings: Weibull distribution provided a better fit to the collected wind data than Rayleigh and Exponential distributions based on the reported goodness-of-fit results. The paper concludes that the three considered locations have potential for wind power generation and recommends DeWind D6 and Polaris P62-1000 turbines, or turbines with similar design characteristics, for the three locations.
studyFutureWorks: Up-to-date data should be adopted in future analysis.
studyLimits: The analysis was based on currently available wind data.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind energy has been underutilized in Nigeria, and there was a need to investigate wind-energy potential in offshore regions of Nigeria.

studyMethodsSummary: The study assessed wind resources for sixteen Algerian regions using meteorological data. Wind-velocity characteristics and wind-power potential were determined using the Weibull distribution; annual and seasonal wind-resource maps were established, and wind speed and power density were evaluated at 10 m, 30 m, and 50 m heights.
studyKeyFindings: Among the sixteen studied sites, the highest annual mean wind speed and annual mean wind power density were found in Adrar, while the lowest values were observed in Skikda.; Seasonal average wind velocity and temperature changed significantly from one season to another and from one site to another.; The dominant wind directions for the studied sites were North and West.; Group A regions were reported as suitable for low-power applications such as water pumping and electricity production through small turbines, whereas groups B and C were reported as suitable for high-power applications.
studyFutureWorks: Other power systems may be integrated in the future.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study explored wind resources and energy potential for sixteen regions covering almost all the territory of Algeria.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Only few studies participated in the map actualization of Algeria by adding other sites and other parameters in the assessment of wind resources.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data from six coastal Ghanaian locations were analysed using two-parameter Weibull distributions. Weibull parameters were estimated using the standard deviation method, wind characteristics were extrapolated to turbine hub heights using Weibull-based height expressions, and performance and LCOE were calculated for four commercial wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: The coastal Ghana wind resource was classified as Class 2 or less and was considered marginally suitable for large-scale wind-energy development, suitable for small-scale applications, and potentially useful as part of a hybrid energy system. The CF-100 turbine was considered the most economically viable option across all selected sites. Turbines with cut-in wind speed below 3 m/s and rated wind speed between 9 and 11 m/s were considered suitable for the coastal region.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Extensive analyses had not been performed on the available coastal Ghana wind data to provide energy policy makers diverse viewpoints for better informed decision making.

studyMethodsSummary: The study assessed offshore wind-energy technical potential in the Lagos coastal region using bathymetry data from GEBCO, wind-speed data analysed from existing literature, wind-speed scaling to a 135 m hub height using the log law, turbine-layout calculations, and output and annual-energy-generation calculations for the Aerodyn SCD 8.0/168 turbine.
studyKeyFindings: The paper reports that Lagos annual electricity demand of about 96.36 TWh can be met by annual generation of about 191.2 TWh for a wind farm at the shore and 200 TWh for waters with depth less than 50 m. It concludes that the most efficient depth for the current target energy demand would be between the shore and 50 m deep offshore.
studyFutureWorks: Further work can be done on losses during transmission of power to the system operation unit and the cost of carrying out the proposed work.
studyLimits: Economic and market factors were outside the scope of the study. Exclusive economic zones, Marine Protection Zones, commercial fishing, and other restrictions were not implemented because no such data was obtained.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides a technical assessment of offshore wind resources around Lagos, Nigeria, including a technical turbine layout and potential output.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Onshore wind-energy resources have been fairly explored, whereas offshore wind energy in the Lagos region had not been explored.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analysed 5-min average wind-speed time series collected during 2005–2009 at 10 m in Johannesburg; compared Weibull, Rayleigh, lognormal, and logistic distributions using R2 and RMSE; estimated Weibull parameters and wind power density using the standard deviation method; and evaluated annual energy output, capacity factor, and levelised electricity cost for small commercially available wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: Weibull distribution provided the best fit among the distributions considered. Johannesburg had a whole-period mean wind speed of 4.15 m/s and a wind power density of 62.72 W/m2, and was classified as class 1, which is poor for grid application. However, because monthly minimum wind speeds were greater than 3 m/s, the site can be used for small wind-power applications. Turbine F was reported as the most preferable turbine, with an LEC of 0.25–0.33 $/kWh, although Table 9 reports a lower 2005 LEC for turbine H than for turbine F.
studyLimits: The authors note that weather-service data observed at lower mast heights are not reliable for large-scale wind-turbine assessment, because instrument positioning information is usually unavailable and existing standards may be applied less strictly. They state that these data can be adequate for small-scale wind turbines operating at lower height.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The paper determined the statistical distribution describing Johannesburg wind speeds, evaluated wind power potential, and performed cost analysis of selected small commercially available wind turbines based on the local wind regime.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Very little had been reported on South Africa regarding assessment of wind distribution and wind power potential.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily average wind speeds from 15 Nigerian sites were fitted with a two-parameter Weibull distribution using an empirical method. Wind power density was estimated and classified using the NREL standard, commercially available wind turbines were evaluated using capacity factor, and unit electricity costs were calculated using the present value cost method.
studyKeyFindings: Sites S2 (Jos) and S3 (Kano) had class-7 wind resources and were reported to be economically viable for wind-power grid integration. S8 (Iseyin), a class-5 site, may also be considered for grid application but may require a turbine with lower cut-in and rated wind speeds. S7, S9, and S15 were not considered viable for grid application but were reported as suitable for standalone applications.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides technical information on the feasibility and viability of wind power across wide geographical locations in Nigeria, including wind-resource potential, turbine selection, and unit electricity cost.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Lack of technical information on the availability and viability of renewable energy resources was identified as a hindrance to harvesting wind energy in Nigeria.

studyMethodsSummary: The study modeled the spatial distribution of daily offshore wind-speed data in Benin Republic's Exclusive Economic Zone using a Weibull distribution fitted by maximum likelihood. Weibull parameters were extrapolated to several heights, wind power density was computed, and bathymetric data were used to identify areas providing a compromise between exploitable wind potential and turbine foundation constraints.
studyKeyFindings: Wind power density in Benin's EEZ was reported to vary from 129.1 to 197.3 W/m2 at 10 m, from 409.5 to 575.9 W/m2 at 50 m, from 621.4 to 850.4 W/m2 at 80 m, from 769.6 to 1039 W/m2 at 100 m, and from 924.3 to 1233.5 W/m2 at 120 m.; Wind resource at 50 m falls into Class 4 and reaches Class 5 close to the shore; at 80 m it falls into Class 5 at some locations and reaches Class 6 close to the shore; at 100 m it reaches Class 7 close to the shore.; The region close to the shore in Benin's EEZ represents the best compromise between wind-potential viability and foundation complexity.
studyFutureWorks: More detailed studies should be conducted to assess the techno-economic viability of offshore wind-energy projects and an offshore wind farm in Benin's EEZ.
studyLimits: This study did not cover the economic feasibility of offshore wind energy in Benin's EEZ.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study used satellite wind-speed data to investigate exploitable offshore wind-energy potential in Benin Republic.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is no known published research investigating offshore wind energy potential in Benin Republic, and no wind-data measurement is available from local meteorological offices.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data recorded every 10 min over one year at eight northwestern-coast Senegal sites were used to calculate monthly and annual mean wind speed and wind power density. Weibull distributions were fitted to wind-speed data, wind speeds were extrapolated to turbine hub heights using the power law method, and annual energy output and capacity factor were calculated for three large and three small commercial wind turbines.
studyKeyFindings: Annual mean wind speed ranged from 4.32 m/s at Kayar to 4.80 m/s at Potou at 20 m, and from 4.12 m/s at Dara Andal to 4.49 m/s at Sakhor at 12 m. All assessed wind turbines had their best capacity factor at Sakhor. Repower was considered suitable for grid connection because of the quantity of output energy that could be generated, whereas Yellow-Sand was considered better for isolated application because of its high capacity factor.
studyResearchGapIdentified: In Senegal, the development of new wind projects continues to be hampered by the lack of knowledge of wind potential and the absence of reliable and accurate wind resource data in many parts of the country.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly average wind-speed data for one year at 20 m and 60 m were assessed for Msallata, Espiaa, Alqatrun, and Adirsiyah in Libya. Weibull parameters were estimated using the Empirical Method of Justus, Graphical Method, and Maximum Likelihood Method, and fitted distributions were compared with actual data using R2, RMSE, MBE, and MAE.
studyKeyFindings: At 20 m, GM gave the best distribution performance for Adirsiyah and Espiaa, MLM for Alqatrun, and EMJ for Msallata. At 60 m, EMJ gave the best modeling performance for Adirsiyah and Msallata, while MLM gave the best performance for Alqatrun and Espiaa. Msallata had the maximum wind-power potential and Adirsiyah the minimum among the four sites considered.
studyFutureWorks: Future studies related to wind energy can investigate wind farm layout optimization, economic feasibility, and environmental impacts to develop wind farm projects.
studyResearchGapAddressed: While statistical data are presented in many studies in the literature, this study supported statistical data by comparison with real data and compared results from different Weibull-distribution methods.

studyMethodsSummary: The study applied a two-component mixture Weibull distribution to hourly mean wind-speed data from four weather stations on Gran Canaria and compared parameter estimation by the method of moments, maximum likelihood, and least squares. Fits to wind-speed and wind-power-density cumulative distributions were evaluated using SSE, R2, MSE, and RMSE.
studyKeyFindings: The two-component mixture Weibull distribution provided a good fit at all weather stations under study.; For wind-speed distributions, the least-squares method provided the highest degree of fit at all analysed stations, although the difference with the other estimation techniques was not significant.; For wind-power-density distributions, least squares had a slightly higher fit at the unimodal stations 1 and 2; maximum likelihood and the method of moments had the highest fit at the bimodal station 4 and the bitangential station 3, respectively.; There was no significant difference between the methods employed in describing wind-power probability-density distributions.; If sample data are independent, maximum-likelihood estimators should be used because of their large sampling efficiency, but they require elaborate calculation techniques.; The least-squares method provides a robust and computationally efficient alternative, whereas the method of moments does not always supply a feasible result and lacks the desirable optimality properties of maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators.

studyMethodsSummary: The study applied and compared five wind-energy-potential estimation methods—ANFIS, MLP, SVR, EMJ, and MLM—to wind data from Lomé and Cotonou. It fitted wind-speed probability density functions, calculated available energy, recoverable energy, and wind-turbine energy output, and evaluated method performance using RMSE and R2.
studyKeyFindings: ANFIS and MLP outperformed EMJ, MLM, and SVR for wind-speed characterization and wind-energy-potential estimation at the Lomé and Cotonou sites. ANFIS was reported as the most accurate approach and MLP as the second most accurate. SVR ranked third but was unstable across estimation types and sites and was less recommendable for Cotonou. Weibull distribution-based EMJ and MLM were reported as the least accurate, especially for recoverable energy and wind-turbine energy output.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared five promising wind-energy-potential estimation methods in the regional context of Togo and Benin and recommended methods for future wind-resource assessment projects in the region.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data collected at 10, 20 and 30 m during 2008 and 2009 at Borj-Cedria were used to estimate seasonal mean wind speed, wind-speed distribution and wind-power density. The seasonal net energy production of seven commercialized 1.5 MW wind turbines assumed to be installed at 80 m above ground level was evaluated using manufacturer power curves, air-density correction and a power-loss factor.
studyKeyFindings: The authors report that Borj-Cedria presents a promising wind potential and that the simulation of seven commercialized wind turbines shows about 3.57% difference in annual net energy production. They conclude that the Vensys70 wind turbine is the best type adapted to the site conditions among the turbines studied.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Little studies have been presented in this sector in Tunisia.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly mean wind-speed data for 2013-2017 from NiMet were evaluated at 10 m using a two-parameter Weibull probability distribution function to determine monthly and annual wind-resource potentials for power generation at Yenagoa, Calabar and Port Harcourt.
studyKeyFindings: Computed annual mean wind speeds were 1.74 m/s for Yenagoa, 2.85 m/s for Calabar and 1.38 m/s for Port Harcourt. Computed annual mean power densities were 4.64 W/m2, 7.06 W/m2 and 3.08 W/m2, respectively. The paper concludes that the investigated coastal south-south Nigerian locations have a low wind-energy resource classified as Class 1 and that higher wind speed, power density and wind-energy resource may be achieved if data were collected above the 10 m height used in the study.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind speed and wind-direction data for 2015–2018 from five Moroccan coastal sites were analysed. Weibull parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood, modified maximum likelihood, energy pattern factor, and WAsP methods; RMSE, R2, and chi-square were used to assess fitting. Wind speed and Weibull parameters were extrapolated to hub heights, wind power density was calculated, and five commercial wind turbines were evaluated using annual output energy and capacity factor.
studyKeyFindings: Modified maximum likelihood provided the best Weibull fit for Laayoune, Boujdour, Al Hoceima, and Essaouira, whereas maximum likelihood gave the best results for Tantan. Boujdour and Essaouira recorded the highest monthly wind power densities at 50 m in July. The EWT DW52-500 had the highest reported capacity factors among the evaluated turbines, while the Mitsubishi MWT62/1.0 had the highest reported output energy.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study determined wind-speed distributions at different heights using historical wind-speed data, calculated wind power and energy density, and selected wind-turbine models for the sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The authors state that their work is among the first studies conducted for these Moroccan coastal regions.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analysed 24 years of wind-speed data from ten South West Nigerian stations using a two-parameter Weibull distribution, assessed Weibull goodness of fit, extrapolated wind characteristics from 10 m to turbine hub heights, simulated outputs of five wind-turbine models, and conducted a cost-benefit analysis.
studyKeyFindings: Average wind speeds between 1.9 and 5.3 m/s were reported across the stations. Lagos Island, Ikeja and Ibadan were ranked as the top three stations based on Weibull results. GE 1.5xle produced the highest simulated output among the five turbine models. The authors concluded that, apart from Lagos, Oyo and mountainous locations, lower-wind-speed-rated turbines would be more appropriate and that turbines with cut-in speeds of 2.0–3.0 m/s and rated speeds of 10–12.0 m/s would be excellent for the sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Most recent wind-profile studies focused on northern Nigeria, while more work was required to expose wind-profile characteristics of southern Nigeria using recent wind-speed databases.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used average daily meteorological wind data from National Agency of Meteorology stations at 10 m, fitted a Weibull distribution using the standard deviation method, calculated available and recoverable wind power, extrapolated Medea wind speed to 20, 40, and 60 m, and evaluated four wind turbines for wind pumping.
studyKeyFindings: At 10 m, the selected locations were reported to have relatively low wind characteristics. Tiaret, Batna, and Meliana were identified as having more significant wind power potential among the selected North Algerian sites. The authors concluded that wind power can nevertheless be considered in northern Algeria for pumping at modest drills, despite rather low wind speed.
studyFutureWorks: Investigate many regions of the studied departments in order to identify ideal places for construction of wind power plants to generate electricity.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed a decade-long on-site wind dataset from Naama using Weibull and Rayleigh distribution fitting, Pearson correlation analysis, principal component analysis, wind-turbine simulation in ASHES, and solar simulation using PVGIS-SARAH. Linear regression models were used to predict wind power generation from global irradiance, with an enhanced version additionally incorporating temperature and humidity.
studyKeyFindings: Wind speed and solar irradiation showed statistically significant negative monthly correlations from January to May and from September to December, whereas the correlations during June to August were not statistically significant in the reported monthly correlation analysis. The Weibull distribution provided a slightly better fit to the Naama wind-speed dataset than the Rayleigh distribution. Simulated wind output was generally higher during early morning and late-afternoon-to-evening periods, when solar output was lower or absent.
studyFutureWorks: Future research should explore longer-term climatic data, technological advancements, broader geographical coverage, complex summer atmospheric dynamics, and advanced predictive models incorporating additional relevant parameters.
studyLimits: Seasonal discrepancies, particularly weaker correlations during summer, suggest the need for more comprehensive environmental analyses. The decade-long data may not fully capture long-term climatic trends, findings based on current technology could evolve as technology advances, and the focus on Naama may limit generalizability to other regions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluates whether Naama wind resources can supplement declining solar photovoltaic output, particularly during evening and low-solar-irradiance periods.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Solar photovoltaic generation is intermittent and unavailable at night, creating a need for complementary renewable resources capable of reducing supply shortfalls.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used monthly wind-speed data for 2008-2016 measured at 10 m, fitted a two-parameter Weibull distribution using the energy pattern factor method, extrapolated wind speed and Weibull parameters to hub heights using a power-law model, estimated turbine energy output and capacity factor, and evaluated electricity-generated cost using the present value of costs method.
studyKeyFindings: The reported mean monthly wind speeds were within 4.31-6.04 m/s at 10 m height.; The study reported monthly wind power density values from 61.864 W/m2 in November to 184.792 W/m2 in December.; The conclusion states that the wind potential at the selected area could be considered marginal (class 2) according to wind-power classification.; Table 6 reports that YDF-1500-87 had the lowest electricity-generated cost per kWh and the greatest total annual energy among the listed turbine models.; The source contains conflicting annual wind-speed, turbine-selection, capacity-factor, energy-output, and electricity-cost statements between the abstract, body text, conclusion, and Table 6.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study analyzed wind-speed characteristics and wind potential at Tobruk, Libya, over 2008-2016 and estimated electricity-generated cost for selected wind turbines.
studyResearchGapIdentified: To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to carry out such an analysis of the wind speed of Tobruk, Libya.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted Weibull and Rayleigh probability density distributions to wind-speed data from Medan for 2017–2019, evaluated the distributions using R2, Chi-square, and RMSE, and calculated wind power-density potential.
studyKeyFindings: The paper reports that Weibull was better than Rayleigh based on Pdf comparison and R2. The paper contains conflicting qualitative claims for Chi-square and RMSE: the abstract and conclusion state that Rayleigh was better, whereas Section 3.2 states that Weibull had lower values than Rayleigh. Annual power density was reported between 72.2078 and 79.4618 W/m2.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study proposed Pdf analysis using Weibull and Rayleigh distributions, evaluated the models with R2, Chi-square, and RMSE, and calculated wind-energy potential.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind-speed research in Medan had been conducted, but its renewable-energy potential had not been analyzed and evaluated.

studyMethodsSummary: Eight probability density functions—Weibull, Gamma, Rayleigh, Gumbel, Lognormal, Inverse Gaussian, Nakagami and Exponential—were fitted to measured wind-speed data from two urban and two rural stations in Djibouti. Their fitting accuracies were evaluated using RMSE, R2 and the index of agreement over monthly, seasonal and yearly periods.
studyKeyFindings: Based on yearly, monthly and seasonal analyses, Weibull, Rayleigh, Gamma and Gumbel were the top four ranked distribution functions and provided the best fits for all stations. For the rural stations, Nakagami ranked first for Ghoubet and third for Bada Wein; it was also ranked first at Bada Wein during the cold season.
studyFutureWorks: The Nakagami distribution should be conducted and evaluated for more rural sites that have high wind speed.
studyLimits: For Ghoubet, approximately 21 days of data between October and November 2015 are missing; the paper states that data losses during these months are often due to violent wind at the Ghoubet site.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study assessed eight distribution methods for modelling wind probability distributions using urban and rural wind-speed data in Djibouti.
studyResearchGapIdentified: In the eastern part of Africa, including Ethiopia, Kenya, Eritrea, Somalia and Djibouti, no detailed analysis had been investigated on the assessment of probability density functions to characterize wind-speed distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly wind-speed data for 2008-2016 measured at 10 m were statistically analysed. A two-parameter Weibull distribution fitted using the Energy Pattern Factor method was used to characterize wind speed and wind potential. A power-law model was used to extrapolate wind speed and Weibull parameters to other hub heights. Candidate wind turbines were evaluated for energy production, capacity factor, and electricity-generated cost using the present value of costs method.
studyKeyFindings: The mean monthly wind speeds were reported to range from 4.31 to 6.04 m/s at 10 m height.; Monthly wind power density was reported to range from 61.864 W/m2 in November to 184.792 W/m2 in December.; The paper concluded that the wind potential at the selected area could be considered marginal (class 2) according to wind-power classification.; YDF-1500-87 was reported to have the lowest electricity-generated cost per kWh and maximum energy power compared with the other evaluated models.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Wind-speed characteristics and wind potential at Tobruk, Libya, were analysed for 2008-2016, and electricity-generated costs of selected wind-turbine models were estimated.
studyResearchGapIdentified: To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to carry out such an analysis of wind speed at Tobruk, Libya.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed measurements from Bangui M’Poko Airport were analysed using a Weibull distribution fitted by the modified maximum likelihood method. WAsP was used with topography, roughness, and obstacle information to generate a wind atlas, wind-resource maps, and annual-energy-production estimates for a hypothetical wind farm.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull parameters, mean wind speed, and mean energy density calculated using the modified maximum likelihood method were very close to the WAsP results. The authors reported that the deviation in wind speed extrapolated to 70 m and in annual energy production was relatively small and may be due to determination of surface-roughness height. The estimated annual energy production of the hypothetical ten-turbine wind farm was 42.626 GWh.
studyFutureWorks: Future work is intended to account for interactions between wind turbines, also called wake effects, in numerical simulations and to evaluate turbine-output energy with an economic analysis of the produced kWh.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used 25 years of daily average wind-speed data at 10 m meteorological height for Enugu, Onitsha, and Owerri. Weibull distributions were fitted using double-logarithmic plots and one-dimensional regression to obtain shape and scale parameters, and predicted probability densities were compared with observed distributions using Pearson correlation and root-mean-square error.
studyKeyFindings: Annual mean wind speeds were 5.5 ± 0.6 m/s for Enugu, 3.6 ± 0.4 m/s for Onitsha, and 3.3 ± 0.3 m/s for Owerri.; The fitted Weibull shape factors were 2.0, 1.5, and 1.9 and the corresponding scale factors were 6.4, 5.6, and 5.1 m/s for Enugu, Onitsha, and Owerri, respectively.; All reported correlations between measured and predicted probability densities were statistically significant at the 5% level; within the region of overlap, the Weibull distribution can be used with acceptable accuracy to predict wind potentials for the studied locations.; Within the region of overlap, the theoretical model appears to underestimate the probability density of every speed bin for each location, and the authors associate the large root-mean-square errors with coarse approximations arising from daily averages.
studyFutureWorks: Observations over smaller time-scales, such as hourly averages, may help to improve the results.
studyLimits: Daily averages may produce coarse approximations that fail to account for short time-scale variations of wind characteristics.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study examined frequency distributions of daily average wind speed for Enugu, Onitsha, and Owerri over a longer period of up to 25 years and modeled the observed data using the Weibull distribution.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous assessments of theoretical wind potential at Nigerian locations gave little or no attention to frequency-distribution patterns of wind speed over the studied periods.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily average wind-speed data measured at 2 m above ground level were obtained from the Federal University of Kashere weather station for October 2014 to February 2017. The data were checked for homogeneity, outliers, and missing records; spurious and missing data, wind gusts, and cyclonic winds exceeding 20 m/s were eliminated. Wind speed was analysed using the Weibull distribution through seasonal and annual analyses, and a vertical wind profile was used to estimate mean wind speed at various heights.
studyKeyFindings: Monthly average wind speeds computed for 60 m above ground level ranged from 2.15 m/s to 6.42 m/s; the maximum occurred in June and the minimum occurred in September.; The dry season had the highest Weibull shape-parameter value, K = 2.08, which the authors interpreted as signifying more stable winds during that season.; The modelled average wind speed at 60 m was 4.30 m/s, which the authors stated was beyond a minimum standard of 3.5 m/s.; The authors concluded that part of the energy requirements of the study area can potentially be obtained from wind throughout the year.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed average daily wind-speed data for Kano, Maiduguri, Jos, Abuja, and Akure using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. It compared maximum likelihood, method of moment, power density, empirical, and logarithmic moment methods for estimating Weibull parameters using RMSE and R2. It also evaluated five 25 kW pitch-controlled wind turbines, including capacity factor and cost of energy, at hub heights from 10 to 50 m.
studyKeyFindings: The method of moment was suitable for Kano and Jos, while the empirical method was suitable for Maiduguri and Abuja; both methods were suitable for Akure.; The power density method was the worst numerical approach for assessing Weibull parameters across the five locations.; Jos and Kano were concluded to be viable for grid integration of wind energy, with Jos identified as the most viable location for wind-energy generation applications.; WT3 had the highest capacity factor and the least cost of energy in all selected locations, whereas WT5 had the highest cost of energy.; The cost of energy decreased with increasing turbine hub height under the sensitivity-analysis conditions.; The wind energy conversion systems have the potential to avoid significant carbon footprints when implemented as alternatives to fossil-fuel systems.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared five numerical techniques for estimating two-parameter Weibull parameters and evaluated techno-economic performance of five 25 kW pitch-controlled wind turbines at varying hub heights.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous wind-resource and cost studies discussed by the authors predominantly used the two-parameter Weibull distribution at 10 m and applied individual parameter-estimation methods; the present study compared five numerical techniques and assessed the effect of varying hub height on cost of energy.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured wind-speed data at 10 m above ground level for 2011–2016 were analyzed for thirteen Nigerian sites. A two-parameter Weibull distribution was used for wind-power assessment; average wind-power density and corresponding wind-energy density were estimated. Wind speeds were extrapolated from 10 m to the 25 m turbine hub height using a power-law relationship, and annual electric energy output was calculated for a selected 20 kW wind turbine.
studyKeyFindings: Wind-power densities at the investigated sites were generally poor and class 1, except Jos, which was class 2. Jos had an average wind speed of 5.34 m/s and wind-power density of 133 W/m2. Kano had a wind-power density of 79.96 W/m2. Small stand-alone wind-energy systems in Jos, Sokoto, Kano, and Maiduguri were assessed as quite promising; Jos had the largest reported annual electricity generation, followed by Kano, Sokoto, and Maiduguri.

studyMethodsSummary: Four probability distributions were fitted to wind-speed data collected at Yola Airport, Nigeria: Weibull, exponentiated Weibull, generalized power Weibull, and exponentiated epsilon. Parameters were estimated in R using the fitdistrplus package and its default maximum likelihood method. Wind speeds were extrapolated from the 10 m anemometer height to selected heights, and wind-power estimates were calculated using assumed conversion conditions.
studyKeyFindings: All four distributions provided good fits to the Yola wind-speed dataset. The exponentiated Weibull, generalized power Weibull, and exponentiated epsilon distributions had relative likelihood gains per data point of 5.25%, 5.38%, and 5.50%, respectively, over the Weibull distribution; the exponentiated epsilon distribution had the highest gain. The authors report that an exponentiated-epsilon estimated average wind speed of 3.68 m/s at 120 m above ground level could generate 6.11 W/m2, and that a proposed 20-turbine wind farm configuration could generate 1.57 MW.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared the Weibull distribution with exponentiated Weibull, generalized power Weibull, and exponentiated epsilon distributions for modeling wind-speed data in Yola, Nigeria.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The Weibull distribution may fail to properly describe wind-speed data of certain locations and may not be the best model compared with other probability distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily wind-speed data from four Nigerian locations, measured at 10 m over 11 years, were characterized using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Wind speeds were extrapolated to hub heights from 10 m to 90 m using a power-law expression. Wind power density, turbine capacity factor, and unit energy cost were estimated to assess wind-turbine selection and techno-economic viability.
studyKeyFindings: Jos, Kano and Ikeja were reported as economically viable for grid integration, whereas P/H was reported as viable for standalone application at 10 m. GE/900s was identified as the most suitable turbine for all sites considered because of its high capacity-factor values. Increasing hub height reduced the electricity cost for Ikeja, P/H and Kano, except for Jos, for which 50 m was reported as the optimum hub height.
studyResearchGapAddressed: In contrast to earlier studies focused on identifying suitable locations, selecting turbines and determining unit energy cost, this study also determined the effect of varying hub height on unit energy cost.

studyMethodsSummary: Four groups of 10-minute wind-speed data measured during 2014 at two coastal Zhejiang wind farms and at four heights were fitted with Weibull, Rayleigh, Gamma, logarithmic normal, and Inverse Gaussian distributions. The study compared goodness-of-fit indicators and wind-power-density relative errors, then compared six Weibull parameter-estimation methods.
studyKeyFindings: The four wind-speed datasets were right-skewed and unimodal, with positive skewness and peakedness values.; Weibull and Rayleigh distributions had better fitting performance than logarithmic normal, Gamma, and Inverse Gaussian distributions at the four sites; after wind-power-density analysis, Weibull was concluded to be the best model for the studied Zhejiang coastal regions.; AMLM and GM had the worst Weibull fitting performance, EMJ performance was unstable, and MLE, PD, and MM achieved highly similar goodness-of-fit results and better accorded with the actual wind-speed distribution than the other methods.

studyMethodsSummary: The study introduced the two-parameter Topp-Leone Lindley distribution, assessed maximum likelihood, least squares and maximum product spacings estimators using Monte Carlo simulation, and compared TLL with six parametric distributions for long-term measured wind-speed data from ten stations in Inner Mongolia, China.
studyKeyFindings: The TLL distribution provided optimal wind-speed fittings at five selected stations and ranked second or third at the remaining stations. The weighted Lindley distribution also effectively fitted wind-speed data at the selected stations. Although the Weibull distribution did not provide good wind-speed fits at all selected stations, it provided stronger estimation of wind power density; TLL also presented accurate estimates of wind power density.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The paper constructed a new probability distribution to fit wind-speed data in Inner Mongolia, China.
studyResearchGapIdentified: A unified model for assessing wind speed at all regions of Inner Mongolia had not been proposed.

studyMethodsSummary: The study applied maximum likelihood estimation of two-parameter Weibull distributions to hourly mean wind-speed data. It proposed an iterative sampling-interval procedure using a Box-Cox transformation, Anderson-Darling normality testing, autocorrelation coefficients, and the Ljung-Box test to select an independent wind-speed sample for estimating parameter standard errors.
studyKeyFindings: For hourly mean wind speeds recorded at Amagro station, the selected data-acquisition interval for accepting independence at a significance level of 0.05 was 174 h, slightly more than one week.; Autocorrelated successive hourly mean wind speeds invalidated the usual statistical tests but had no significant effect on the shape of the estimated Weibull probability density distribution in this case study.; The calculated uncertainties for commonly used wind-energy statistic functions obtained from dependent wind-speed data were over-optimistic; the paper recommends using an independent wind-speed sample to estimate these uncertainties.; The root mean square error was 0.029 for both Weibull distributions compared in the study.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted Lognormal, Gumbel, and Generalized Extreme Value probability distributions to monthly wind-speed data for Brasília, Campo Grande, Cuiabá, and Goiânia. Distribution parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood, and goodness of fit was assessed using KS, R2, RMSE, AIC, BIC, and AICc indicators.
studyKeyFindings: For the four cities considered, the GEV distribution was reported as the best overall representation of wind-speed data when compared with LN and GUM distributions. For Campo Grande, GEV demonstrated a better fit for most months, except January, when LN performed better; GEV and LN were tied in July according to the combined ranking.
studyFutureWorks: The estimated distribution parameters and methodology can be implemented in studies concerning renewable-energy-source location, module reliability, power quality, protection systems, harmonics, and noise treatment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated the goodness of fit of probability distributions for wind speed at four central-western Brazilian cities.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The authors state that no detailed statistical analysis of wind-speed characteristics in the Brazilian Midwest area had been carried out to date.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed 1 Hz wind-speed measurements from FINO-1 at 100 m over three years. It compared Weibull, Gaussian, Nakagami, Rician, Gamma, inverse-Gamma, and log-normal distribution models across time windows from 10 min to 1 month using next-point probability, Kullback–Leibler divergence, and square-velocity relative deviation.
studyKeyFindings: For large time windows, including 1 month, Weibull fitted wind-speed distributions better than Gaussian. For shorter windows, Gaussian, Nakagami, and sometimes Rice models performed better than Weibull depending on the metric. Gaussian produced the least errors in energy predictions independently of window size among the compared models.
studyFutureWorks: Future research could study the process across scales, including how standard deviation scales with time-window scale and analyses of correlations and Hurst exponents, to clarify limitations of assigning a particular statistical distribution to wind speed.
studyLimits: One percent of data points that were NaNs were discarded; windows with more than 40% NaNs were discarded. Empirical distributions with two local maxima, representing less than 2% of windows, were discarded for histogram fitting and energy-prediction analyses. For inverse-Gamma fitting, windows producing infinite values below computational resolution, about 0.1% of windows, were discarded.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The paper systematically investigated two-parameter wind-speed distribution models over time windows spanning from 10 min to 1 month.
studyResearchGapIdentified: How the Weibull model holds for shorter time periods remained an open question.

studyMethodsSummary: Three-hourly measured wind-speed data from January 2006 to December 2016 at ten Burkina Faso sites were fitted with Weibull, Hybrid Weibull, Rayleigh, Gamma, and inverse Gaussian distributions using the maximum likelihood method. Model fit was assessed using R2 and RMSE, and annual wind-power-density estimation was compared using relative percentage error.
studyKeyFindings: Based on R2 and RMSE, Weibull was the most suitable distribution at Bobo, Dédougou, Ouaga, and Ouahigouya; Hybrid Weibull was most suitable at Bogandé, Fada, and Po; and inverse Gaussian was most suitable at Boromo, Dori, and Gaoua. For annual wind-power-density estimation, Hybrid Weibull had the minimum error at seven sites, whereas Rayleigh had the minimum error at Ouaga and Ouahigouya and Weibull had the minimum error at Dédougou.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study evaluated the capacity of five distribution functions to fit wind-speed data at ten sites throughout Burkina Faso.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There is a lack of extensive research on determination of appropriate frequency-distribution models for estimating wind-speed distribution across different regions of Burkina Faso.

studyMethodsSummary: Historical wind-speed data for Medan City from 2017 to 2019 were used to estimate and compare Weibull, gamma, and exponential distribution functions. Scale and shape parameters were calculated, and the models' PDF and CDF results were compared with observed cumulative probability.
studyKeyFindings: For the Medan City wind site and the 2017–2019 wind data, the exponential distribution was found to be the best model for determining CDF, followed by Weibull and gamma distributions. The Weibull distribution was found to be the best model for determining PDF. The gamma model gave the worst performance in determining both CDF and PDF values. The observed cumulative probability using the exponential model did not fit the expected values.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compared Weibull, gamma, and exponential distribution models to identify suitable distribution functions for wind-speed characteristics in Medan City.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There was not enough information available about which model among the Weibull, gamma, and exponential distributions is suitable to estimate PDF and CDF of wind speed.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data from 10 Tamil Nadu stations for 1980–2018 were fitted with nine probability distribution models. Model fit was ranked using the Anderson-Darling statistical test.
studyKeyFindings: A single probability distribution did not provide the best fit for all 10 stations.; The generalised extreme value distribution provided the best fit for six stations, whereas the Kumaraswamy distribution provided the best fit for four stations.; The Kumaraswamy distribution ranked between 1 and 3 for 9 of the 10 stations and was therefore reported as more consistent than the other distributions within this study.; The Kumaraswamy distribution provided the best fit even when the wind-speed distribution was negatively skewed, whereas Nakagami performed satisfactorily only for slightly positively skewed distributions.; All stations analysed in this study had platykurtic wind-speed distributions.
studyFutureWorks: Further study should assess the performance of the Kumaraswamy distribution for mesokurtic and leptokurtic wind-speed distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Studies related to the prediction of wind energy potential in Tamil Nadu are limited, though the state has high potential for renewable energy extraction in India.

studyMethodsSummary: Average hourly wind-speed data from the Poprad meteorological station for 2005–2021 were analysed as a whole and split into seasonal and monthly datasets. Two-parameter Weibull, three-parameter Weibull, and exponentiated Weibull distributions were fitted using the maximum likelihood method and compared using KS, AD, AIC, BIC, RMSE, and R2 criteria. Wind direction was also analysed using wind roses.
studyKeyFindings: The exponentiated Weibull distribution provided a better fit than W2 and W3 for the entire period and seasonal wind-speed data. It performed best for monthly data except in February and March, when W3 performed better and EW was second best. The authors conclude that EW is a suitable alternative for wind-speed data with high positive skewness and kurtosis.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Hourly wind-speed data from the Poprad-Tatry airport meteorological station in Northern Slovakia were modelled using W2, W3, and EW distributions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The authors state that no published paper had focused on applying the exponentiated Weibull distribution to model wind speed at a higher-altitude inland location.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly wind-speed data from Bozcaada, Gökçeada, and Bilecik between October 2015 and September 2016 were converted to frequency distributions. A Finsler geometry-based distribution approach was compared with two-parameter Weibull and Rayleigh distributions using RMSE and wind power-density-error analyses.
studyKeyFindings: The authors report that the Finsler geometry model had a better fit with measured probability-density distributions than the Weibull and Rayleigh models in the monthly analysis. The Finsler geometry method had small errors for power-density estimation over 12 months, whereas the Rayleigh distribution had high error rates in both monthly wind-speed modeling and power-density estimation. Weibull provided results similar to Finsler in some months.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study compares the Finsler geometry method with Weibull and Rayleigh models for low- and high-wind-speed regions and evaluates power-density errors.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The performance of the Finsler geometry method at low and high wind speeds had not been compared and had not been investigated in terms of power density.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed time series of hourly daily measured wind-speed data from five Rwandan meteorological stations for 1974–1993, averaged the data monthly, fitted Weibull and Rayleigh probability density functions, estimated Weibull parameters using the Maximum Likelihood method, extrapolated wind characteristics to higher altitudes, calculated wind power density, and plotted wind roses.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull probability density distribution was found to be the best-fitting model for the empirical distribution of measured monthly average wind speeds. At 60 m, Gisenyi had the greatest reported mean monthly wind speed and mean power density among the stations considered. On average, the windy season coincides with the rainy season in most parts of Rwanda, except in the western part where it coincides with the dry season.
studyFutureWorks: The authors recommend more detailed and systematic analyses of wind-speed patterns using continuous wind-speed data for at least one year, with seasonal, monthly, daily, and hourly analyses compared with the present results to obtain more reliable long-term averages.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study investigated wind-energy-resource potential in Rwanda and provided a database intended for users of wind power.
studyResearchGapIdentified: In Rwanda, wind energy had been unexplored and no study had been conducted to explore that resource.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fits an inverse Weibull distribution to wind-speed data using a modified maximum likelihood approach, compares estimation approaches, evaluates goodness of fit using MAPE, RMSE, and R2, and describes sensitivity, calibration, and validation procedures.
studyKeyFindings: The authors report that the proposed method produced d = 2.0082 and z = 6.1962, with RMSE = 0.0002 and R2 = 0.9999 in the reported parameter-estimation computation. They conclude that the inverse Weibull distribution with the modified maximum likelihood function provides a framework for wind-speed evaluation and renewable-energy resource assessment.
studyFutureWorks: Further research can explore additional statistical techniques and models, validate and refine the approach using larger and more diverse datasets from different geographical regions and wind sites, and incorporate machine-learning and artificial-intelligence algorithms for more precise wind-speed predictions and forecasts.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted three original probability distribution functions, six two-component mixture probability distribution functions, and one three-component mixture Weibull distribution to hourly mean wind speed data from a wind farm in Texas. Parameters were estimated using the Aquila Optimizer method with RMSE as the objective function, and distributions were compared using RMSE, R2, and chi-square error.
studyKeyFindings: For the utilized wind speed data, Gamma gave the best fit among the three original distributions. The two-component mixture Weibull distribution gave the best fit among the original and two-component mixture distributions, and the three-component mixture Weibull distribution gave the best fit among all distributions proposed in the study.
studyFutureWorks: More three-component mixture distributions can be investigated and compared with the three-component mixture Weibull distribution.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analyzed wind-speed and wind-direction data collected at 10 m in the Arzew region, fitted a Weibull distribution, used WAsP for wind-resource assessment, mapping and wind-farm simulations, compared four wind-turbine technologies under one-row and two-row layouts, and used HOMER for economic and environmental evaluation.
studyKeyFindings: The Arzew study site had a mean wind speed of 4.46 m/s at 10 m height, with annual mean wind-speed variation between 3.9 m/s and 4.79 m/s during the stated 10-year study period.; The Weibull shape parameter k varied from 1.38 to 2.12, and estimated power density varied from 100 W/m2 to 132 W/m2.; The single-row structure produced more energy for all wind-turbine models than the two-row structure.; Among the technologies evaluated, the Power Wind wind farm had the lowest reported cost of energy, $0.068/kWh, and the lowest reported carbon-dioxide quantity, 3,892,065 kg/year.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used a bottom-up GIS-based offshore-wind resource-assessment approach. ERA5 monthly-average wind speeds were processed, extrapolated from 10 m to 100 m using the logarithmic wind profile law, and used with a Rayleigh wind-speed distribution, the Vestas V164–8 MW power curve, capacity-factor estimation, array-density assumptions, and scenario-specific spatial exclusions to estimate annual energy production. A GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation using capacity factor, bathymetry, distance to the Eskom transmission grid, and distance to commercial harbours identified suitable development regions.
studyKeyFindings: With the minimum wind-quality limitation applied, Scenario 1 was estimated to have 44.52 TWh of annual energy production and Scenario 2 was estimated to have 2 387.08 TWh of annual energy production.; The study identified Richards Bay, Kwa Dukuza, Durban, and Struis Bay as suitable offshore-wind development regions.; The estimated annual energy production for Scenario 1 could theoretically meet 14.9% of South Africa’s annual electricity demand, while Scenario 2 could theoretically satisfy annual electricity demand eight times over.
studyLimits: The ERA5 dataset resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° created small data gaps at points where the dataset met study-area borders, including EEZ and terrestrial boundaries.; The study did not consider the effect of shipping lanes on resource potential and site selection.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Quantification of offshore-wind energy resources under four development scenarios and GIS-based identification of suitable offshore-wind development regions in the South African exclusive economic zone.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The study states that it was the first offshore-wind resource assessment to focus exclusively on the South African context and to identify the most suitable wind-farm development regions within the South African EEZ.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted two-parameter Weibull and three-parameter Inverted Kumaraswamy (IKum) distributions to hourly wind-speed data from six stations around Lake Van. IKum parameters were estimated using maximum likelihood, least squares, and maximum product of spacing methods; a Monte-Carlo simulation compared the estimators. Final wind-speed fitting performance was evaluated using RMSE, R2, KS, and power density error criteria.
studyKeyFindings: The IKum distribution was preferable to the Weibull distribution in terms of RMSE, R2, and KS criteria for four of six stations, and had lower power density error at five of six stations. Weibull had better goodness-of-fit performance at Tatvan and Muradiye; at Muradiye, IKum nevertheless had a smaller power density error. The authors state that IKum can be considered an alternative to Weibull, particularly when data have a high peak or outlying observations in the right tail.
studyFutureWorks: The behavior of the ML, MPS, and LS estimators should be investigated for small sample sizes, for example n = 30, 50, and 100.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study used the IKum distribution for the first time to model wind-speed data and compared ML, MPS, and LS estimation methods for its parameters.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The authors state that, to their knowledge, no study concerning IKum parameter-estimation methods other than maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods existed in the related literature.

studyMethodsSummary: The study fitted Weibull, Normal, and generalized extreme value distributions to wind data from Adrar, extrapolated wind speeds from 10 m to the 55 m hub height, calculated expected wind-farm performance using the PDFs and the manufacturer power curve, and compared the predicted outputs with SCADA operating data from the Kaberten wind farm.
studyKeyFindings: For the studied case, the three distributions gave comparable estimates of average wind speed, while the GEV distribution was more appropriate for assessing wind-turbine annual energy production. The results may change for other sites with different wind regimes and climates and for other wind-turbine types.
studyFutureWorks: The effect of the power curve should be investigated.
studyLimits: The present work concerns a wind farm located in a desert and hot area; the results may change for other sites with different wind regimes and climates and could be different for other types of wind turbines.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study investigated the influence of Weibull, Normal, and GEV distributions on expected wind-farm performance by comparing predicted outputs with actual operating data.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The impact of wind-speed probability density functions on the assessment of wind-farm performance was not widely investigated.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data recorded at 10 m during 2017–2019 were analysed using Weibull graphical and standard deviation methods. Wind characteristics were extrapolated to 70 m, the methods were evaluated using RMSE, Chi-square error and R2, and five commercial wind turbines were simulated using capacity factor.
studyKeyFindings: Both numerical methods were found appropriate for Weibull-parameter estimation in the study area; however, the standard deviation method gave higher Weibull parameter estimates and higher average monthly wind power density than the graphical method. The Polaris P50-500 had the highest capacity factor among the five simulated commercial turbines for all three years.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There had been no previous studies related to wind-energy potential conducted in the coastline region of Dar es Salaam.

studyMethodsSummary: Wind-speed data collected at meteorological stations in N'Djamena and Faya Airport over five years were processed using Weibull wind-speed distribution modelling, WAsP-based wind-resource mapping, SRTM topographic data, obstacle and roughness modelling, and vertical extrapolation of wind speed to 100 m using a variable coefficient power law.
studyKeyFindings: At 10 m from the ground, the reported mean wind speed and energy density were 3.8 m/s and 99 W/m2 in N'Djamena, respectively, and 5.54 m/s and 246 W/m2 in Faya, respectively. The authors conclude that the Faya site offers the greatest wind potential among the two sites considered. At 100 m, mapped low-potential-zone average wind speeds were reported as 6.95 m/s for N'Djamena and 15 m/s for Faya; high-potential-zone wind speeds were 7.12 m/s in the North-East direction for N'Djamena and 16.4 m/s in the North-North-East direction for Faya.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analysed hourly wind speed, temperature, and air-density measurements at 80 m, fitted a Weibull distribution using the likelihood method, calculated wind-turbine operating hours for five temperature and wind-speed cases, and estimated monthly, seasonal, and annual energy production for one Gamesa G52 wind turbine using a logical temperature equation.
studyKeyFindings: The annual Weibull scale parameter was 6.9 m/s and annual wind velocity was 6.2 m/s. The turbine was most productive in May, with average wind energy of 185.95 MWh. Estimated annual energy production was 1644.75 MWh. Low winds were reported as the principal reason preventing production, while temperature affected production only during summer for limited hours.

studyMethodsSummary: The study analysed hourly wind-speed data measured at 10 m above ground level for 2010–2014 at 12 South African locations. Weibull distributions were fitted to site wind characteristics, and annual energy outputs for two Kestrel small wind turbines were calculated by combining site wind probability distributions with turbine power curves. Economic performance was evaluated using simple payback period, net present value, and levelised cost of energy.
studyKeyFindings: Port Elizabeth had the highest annual energy production for both evaluated turbines, whereas Oudtshoorn, Potchefstroom, and Nelspruit had the lowest annual energy outputs. Cape Peninsula and South Eastern locations had higher probabilities of high wind speeds than the Central and Northern regions. Under the present policies and assumptions considered, the two selected small wind turbines were not economically viable in the locations evaluated because NPVs were below zero and calculated LCOEs were higher than the stated electricity tariff.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study established energy-productivity and economic-viability findings for small wind energy systems at locations in different South African regions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Little or no known research had evaluated how energy and economic performance affected the growth of small wind generation in South Africa.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily wind-speed data measured at 10 m at four Nigerian sites were analysed using a two-parameter Weibull Distribution Function. Weibull parameters, wind power density, most probable wind speed, wind speed carrying maximum energy, turbine energy outputs, and capacity factors were estimated.
studyKeyFindings: Among the four investigated sites, Maiduguri was reported as having the best wind-energy potential. Ilorin, Makurdi, and Gombe were classified as wind power class 1 and described as unsuitable for wind power applications, while Maiduguri was classified as class 2 and may be considered for stand-alone applications. WT3 was reported as the most suitable turbine choice for the sites. The conclusion reports a Maiduguri wind power density of 1097.4 W/m2, which conflicts with Table 3, where the value is 107.485 W/m2.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study additionally selected adequate wind turbines for the selected locations and determined the effect of wind-turbine parameters on capacity factor.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous Nigerian wind-energy studies were concerned with adequately assessing site wind-power potential.

studyMethodsSummary: The study statistically assessed wind potential at Adrar, In Salah, Illizi, and Tamanrasset using Weibull distributions fitted to wind data collected every 3 hours over 5 years at 10 m above ground. It evaluated CALORIUS 37 wind-turbine power and annual energy production while accounting for wind, temperature, latitude, longitude, and altitude data.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull shape parameter ranged from 2.0 at Illizi and Tamanrasset to 2.48 at In Salah, while the scale parameter ranged from 4.6 m/s at Illizi to 6.3 m/s at Adrar. Mean wind speed ranged from 4.1 m/s at Illizi to 5.5 m/s at Adrar. Annual CALORIUS 37 energy production ranged from 4467.6 kWh at Illizi to 8409.6 kWh at Adrar. The authors state that the amount of CO2 that can be avoided ranged from 0.90 TE-CO2 for a natural-gas power plant in Illizi to 2.24 TE-CO2 for a gasoil power plant in Adrar.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly mean wind speed and wind direction data from 38 UK surface observation stations for 1981–2018 were quality controlled and averaged to daily mean wind speeds. Weibull scale and shape parameters were estimated using empirical, maximum-likelihood, and power-density approaches. Wind speeds were extrapolated from 10 m to 100 m using the 1/7th power law when directly applied to wind turbine functions. Weibull parameters were used to estimate wind power density, characteristic wind speeds, capacity factor, and operation probability for two wind turbines. Long-term trends were assessed using the Mann-Kendall test.
studyKeyFindings: The Weibull distribution modeled daily mean wind-speed probability distributions satisfactorily, with correlation coefficients across the observation network between 0.90 and 0.96. Wind power density varied substantially among sites and regions. Statistically significant long-term changes in annual mean wind speed occurred at 15 of 38 stations but only in three of 11 regions. Wind power density was generally higher in winter than in summer, and 36 of 38 stations had at least twice as much wind power density in winter as in summer.
studyLimits: No additional attempt was made to separate different windstorm types because of the nature of the study and the relatively low likelihood of extreme wind-speed occurrence. Data availability may be restricted because MIDAS data were used under license.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provides an updated assessment of long-term and seasonal wind-speed variation across the UK using 1981–2018 data.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous UK wind-speed studies did not clearly state which reported long-term trends were statistically significant, and available assessments did not extend the analysis to 2018.

studyMethodsSummary: The study proposed two variational-Bayesian infinite mixtures of Gaussian distributions, IMoG-I and IMoG-II, based on stick-breaking construction. They were used to fit hourly wind-speed distributions at fourteen Puerto Rico stations and compared with fourteen single distributions, seven homogeneous finite-mixture distributions, and seven heterogeneous finite-mixture distributions using goodness-of-fit indicators.
studyKeyFindings: IMoG-I and IMoG-II generally outperformed the compared single, heterogeneous-mixture, and homogeneous-mixture distributions across the fourteen Puerto Rico datasets. IMoG-II and IMoG-I ranked first and second, respectively, among the compared models. The models automatically determined useful Gaussian components; the optimal number of components was less than 10 for all data considered in this study.
studyFutureWorks: The proposed models will be utilized to estimate wind-speed distributions at unknown locations. The authors also propose studying infinite mixture distributions whose components are Weibull, Gamma, Kappa, Wakeby, or other distributions.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly averaged wind-speed data from thirteen meteorological stations in Chad, covering five consecutive years at 10 m above ground level, were statistically analyzed using a two-parameter Weibull distribution. Wind speed carrying maximum energy, wind power density, wind energy density, and wind-direction patterns were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: Higher wind speeds occurred during generally dry weather conditions from November to May, while lower wind speeds occurred during wet conditions from June to October. Based on yearly averaged data, Abéché was the most recommended site for wind-energy generation, followed by N'Djamena, Pala, Mongo, and Faya-Largeau. The study concluded that most assessed sites are promising only for small-scale applications, whereas Am Timan, Bousso, Bokoro, and Ati were not feasible for wind-energy generation because of weak mean wind speeds of around 1 m/s.
studyFutureWorks: Develop a wind map for other parts of the Saharan region and locations close to Lake Chad using data recorded at various heights above ground level, to develop a wind atlas for Chad.
studyLimits: Some stations had their last observation in late 1978 and were no longer recording wind data consistently. The study used five consecutive years of data; the authors noted that longer observation periods would provide more reliable evaluation and confidence for investors.
studyResearchGapAddressed: The study provided an initial multi-station assessment of wind-energy potential and contributed toward a comprehensive wind map or wind pattern for Chad.
studyResearchGapIdentified: No extensive study had been undertaken to assess wind-energy prospects across Chad, apart from a previous study covering only the single city of N'Djamena.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated five sunshine-hour and two temperature empirical models against measured monthly mean daily global solar radiation; fitted two site-specific models at Owabi.
studyKeyFindings: The proposed sunshine-hour model had R2 0.9098 and lowest MBE -0.0102 MJ m-2 day-1 MPE 0.0585 percent and RMSE 0.0338 MJ m-2 day-1. The proposed temperature model had R2 0.8328 and RMSE 0.9859.
studyFutureWorks: Use ongoing long-term measurements from other Ghana regions to improve solar-potential estimation.
studyLimits: Sunshine-duration data came from Kumasi airport about 20 km from Owabi; coefficients and meteorological inputs are site specific.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Calibrated and compared site-specific sunshine and temperature models for global solar radiation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Inadequate local long-term solar-radiation observations constrain Ghana solar-energy assessment.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed six combined empirical temperature models and a Bayesian neural network using 2006 daily GSR Tmax and Tmin; tested in summer and winter 2007 and generalized in February-July 2012.
studyKeyFindings: Proposed model 5 was most accurate in 2012 with RMSE 1.1431 Wh/m2/day MBE 0.0255 MAE 0.8254 and MPE 1.1006%; BNN generalized less well.
studyFutureWorks: Build larger databases to improve BNN generalization.
studyLimits: Long-term GSR records are sparse; BNN needs a larger training database for long-term generalization.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Develop simple accurate temperature-based models for daily GSR in semi-arid Ghardaia.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Limited solar-radiation records in southern Algeria hinder solar-system design despite widely available temperature observations.

studyMethodsSummary: Calibrated and evaluated 12 existing and one new daily global solar-radiation empirical model using temperature rainfall and relative humidity at six Yucatan stations.
studyKeyFindings: New M5 was best at all stations with R2 0.620-0.706 RMSE 2.30-2.94 MJ/m2/day and MBE -0.054 to 0.303. Bristow-Campbell T2 was best among temperature-only models.
studyFutureWorks: Test and calibrate the new regression relation at additional sites.
studyLimits: Solar-radiation sensor data have missing and erroneous readings; model coefficients require local calibration.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared meteorological-variable models and developed M5 using temperature rainfall and humidity.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Yucatan has sparse reliable solar-radiation records relative to temperature and precipitation observations.

studyMethodsSummary: Calculated beam and diffuse solar exergy using Petela model from monthly Indian radiation temperature and sunshine data; fitted 32 single-predictor models using clearness index and relative sunshine period and ranked them by GPI.
studyKeyFindings: Beam exergy efficiency was 0.9286-0.9365; diffuse 0.7189-0.7499; global 0.7700-0.8912. Power model with clearness index for global exergy-efficiency factor ranked first overall (model 23).
studyFutureWorks: Apply developed correlations to estimate solar exergy for solar-device design and performance assessment.
studyLimits: Models are empirical correlations trained on station data; estimation depends on meteorological input availability.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed and ranked empirical global-solar-exergy models for India.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Solar-system viability needs solar-radiation quality/exergy estimates beyond energy-only analysis.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated 14 existing and six proposed temperature-based empirical models using daily meteorological records from 20 humid subtropical and tropical Chinese radiation stations (1966-2015).
studyKeyFindings: Proposed polynomial P2 was top-ranked single-temperature model; complex P3 and P5 improved accuracy by adding logarithmic precipitation and relative humidity. P2 recommended when only temperature is available.
studyFutureWorks: Test and calibrate proposed relations in other humid climates.
studyLimits: About 1.6% of observations were omitted; model coefficients require calibration and applicability beyond similar climates needs testing.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed temperature-only and complex models and ranked them with a global performance index.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Reliable daily global radiation measurements are sparse while temperature precipitation and humidity are widely available.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed an optimal solar-radiation zoning criterion using k-means clustering of 1970–2017 data from 112 Chinese radiation stations; applied zoning to 1,042 surface meteorological stations, then built zone-level linear clearness-index/relative-sunshine-duration models and cross-validated against station models.
studyKeyFindings: Relative sunshine duration was the optimal zoning criterion. Nine zones were identified, and their zone models achieved good accuracy and generalizability for regions with sunshine-duration data.
studyFutureWorks: Assess changes under future climate conditions and enrich models with additional predictors.
studyLimits: Empirical linear models use limited inputs and results depend on historical station representativeness.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provided nine sunshine-duration-based zones and parsimonious zone models for China.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Regions with only surface meteorological measurements lack reliable daily solar-radiation estimates; complex models give limited accuracy gains.

studyKeyFindings: Proposed models reduced errors by up to 73% versus empirical-model averages; best RMSE was 223.2 J/cm2/day at Tacna.
studyFutureWorks: Use proposed regression models for Peruvian solar and hydrometeorological applications.
studyLimits: Reliable daily solar-radiation estimates are needed where pyranometer data are scarce.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared seven empirical models and proposed multiple-linear regressions across Peru.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Pyranometer data are costly and unavailable at many stations.

studyMethodsSummary: Compared 20 empirical GSR models using 1984–2018 data from six Fiji meteorological stations, calibrated against NASA GEOS/MERRA reanalysis and ground observations at Nadi and Laucala; evaluated with R2, RMSE, mean error and correlation coefficient.
