studyKeyFindings: The electric heater reduced generation-plan deviation and wind curtailment: clear-sky deviation fell to 0%, partial-cloudy deviation fell from 47.49% to 31.74%, and annual wind curtailment was reduced by more than 90% for 151 days.
studyFutureWorks: Study optimal ratios among wind power capacity CSP capacity and TES capacity considering performance and economy.
studyLimits: The case uses scaled BPA wind data, NSRDB irradiation data and steady-state component models; dynamic CSP processes are ignored.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Curtailed wind power is converted by an electric heater into heat stored in CSP thermal energy storage for later generation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing wind-CSP studies operate the subsystems independently and lack additional measures when wind curtailment occurs.

studyMethodsSummary: Used SAM PVsyst HOMER and RETScreen to model and validate grid-connected residential PV wind and PV-wind systems in Thailand using solar irradiance wind speed demand and financial inputs.
studyKeyFindings: PV model annual-yield errors were 3.6% SAM 6.9% PVsyst 5.5% HOMER and -3.9% RETScreen. A 6.6 kW PV system was best in Chaiyaphum; 6.05 kW PV plus 1 kW wind was best in Sa Kaeo; only Chanthaburi supported an economic hybrid among seven sites.
studyFutureWorks: Use local measurements and broader real-system validation.
studyLimits: Model results depend on database weather and limited reference-system data; actual output can diverge from modeled annual values.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Validated four tools and compared PV WTS and hybrid options across nine Thai locations.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Thai PV wind and hybrid applications lacked validated multi-tool comparisons across regions.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed and validated wind farm CSP thermal energy storage electric-heater and power-block submodels; used PSO to optimize capacity ratio TES duration solar multiple and heater capacity for an 80 MWe Zhangbei case.
studyKeyFindings: The optimal configuration had wind-to-CSP ratio 1.91 TES capacity 13 h solar multiple 2.9 and heater capacity 6 MW, giving NPV USD 27.67 million and 15470 tCO2/year reduction.
studyFutureWorks: Test alternative weather pricing and dispatch cases.
studyLimits: CSP validation used SEGS VI output in California and the case relies on assumed pricing dispatch and design parameters.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Stores curtailed wind electricity as heat in CSP thermal energy storage and optimizes configuration with PSO.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Wind curtailment and intermittency reduce the economic performance and stability of high-wind systems.

studyMethodsSummary: Modelled a 2 MW DFIG wind turbine and 50 kW PV system connected through back-to-back converters in MATLAB Simulink; applied vector control P&O and PSO solar MPPT and indirect-speed wind MPPT.
studyKeyFindings: The control strategy maintained DC-link voltage under step-up and step-down wind changes and produced rated 2 MW at 11 m/s; PV MPPT tracked maximum power under constant and real-time irradiance.
studyFutureWorks: Validate the controller experimentally and test broader grid and weather scenarios.
studyLimits: Simulation-only evaluation without hardware experiments or a detailed numerical comparison of P&O and PSO tracking performance.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrated PV at the DFIG converter DC link with independent solar and hybrid wind MPPT.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Efficient stable grid integration and maximum power extraction from combined PV and DFIG wind systems require coordinated control.

studyMethodsSummary: Reviewed national electricity statistics, wind-resource assessments, energy policy, and ongoing or planned wind, geothermal, and hydropower projects; compared CESEN, SWERA, meteorological, and project-site evidence.
studyKeyFindings: Ethiopia had an estimated 10000 MW wind resource but only 52 MW operating wind capacity by December 2012. Eight wind farms totaling 1116 MW were planned, while hydropower supplied 92.7% of electricity in 2010/2011; dry-season winds could complement drought-sensitive hydro.
studyFutureWorks: Collect standardized site measurements; formulate a long-term diversified-energy plan; improve incentives and financing; revise policy to enable more private investment.
studyLimits: National wind maps relied on sparse, nonstandard-height observations and 10 km mesoscale modeling that omitted local effects; reported projects and plans reflect the review's 2012–2013 evidence base.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Synthesized resource maps site measurements policies and the 1116 MW wind-project pipeline to show wind's diversification value.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Sparse reliable wind data and extreme reliance on hydropower limited Ethiopian wind-energy development and exposed supply to rainfall and drought risk.

studyMethodsSummary: DEM and stream-network GIS analysis screened sites by stream order, bed slope, and spacing. SWAT2000 simulated flows for 60 subwatersheds; flow-duration curves at 50%, 75%, and 90% dependability supported theoretical run-of-river potential estimates.
studyKeyFindings: 107 sites on nine streams were identified. At 50% dependability, the estimated theoretical potential was 132.67 MW; 68 micro sites below 0.5 MW provided 10.8% of that capacity. Developing half the potential could reduce emissions by about 125 thousand t CO2.
studyFutureWorks: Undertake geologic, population, demand-center, and site-feasibility studies; assess hybrid solar, biomass, and hydropower supply options.
studyLimits: Rainfall and temperature data were sparse for the watershed; soil mapping at 10 km² grid resolution could miss finer variation; sites are theoretical and require practical feasibility investigation.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrated GIS site identification and calibrated SWAT simulation to provide spatially distributed hydropower potential.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Traditional outlet-based gauged-data assessments can miss potential sites and provide limited spatial coverage.

studyMethodsSummary: Identified barriers through literature review, refined them with 12 experts, linked barriers to strategies using adapted QFD, weighted seven criteria with AHP, ranked 38 strategies with Fuzzy ARASKOR, and compared rankings with nine fuzzy MCDM methods.
studyKeyFindings: Seventy-five barriers and 38 strategies were identified. Policy stability and long-term commitment ranked first, followed by promoting renewable energy as a climate solution and developing training and certification programs.
studyFutureWorks: Test alternative MCDM methods, add evaluation criteria, and use advanced fuzzy representations such as type-2 fuzzy sets.
studyLimits: Results rely on a limited expert panel and Iran-specific contextual data; alternative strategies, criteria, or perspectives may change outcomes.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed and tested an integrated QFD, AHP, and Fuzzy ARASKOR framework in Iran.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Barrier research is fragmented and generally does not link comprehensive barriers to feasible, prioritized mitigation strategies.

studyMethodsSummary: Province-wide survey of Alberta municipal decision-makers, analyzed with descriptive statistics and a theory-informed binary logistic regression that combines the Theory of Planned Behaviour and transition theory.
studyKeyFindings: Economic value was the leading motivation. Key constraints were access to grants and loans, limited provincial support, and concern that projects diminish natural vistas. Visual impact (odds ratio 1.81) and external challenges (odds ratio 0.63) were significant predictors of adoption intention.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct in-depth municipal case studies and examine how broader landscape-level factors incentivize local renewable development.
studyLimits: The unknown survey reach prevents a response-rate calculation; renewable-energy labelling may cause selection bias, and results cover 101 respondents from 74 Alberta municipalities.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Surveyed decision-makers across Alberta and applied a blended behavioural and transition-theory framework.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Municipal community-energy development and direct insights from municipal leaders have received limited empirical attention.

studyMethodsSummary: A UK Department of Trade and Industry study (March–June 2003) applied a National Systems of Innovation framework, technology-maturity stages, and system maps to six technology sectors.
studyKeyFindings: System failures occur chiefly from demonstration to pre-commercial deployment and from pre-commercial to supported commercialisation. Stable policy, niche-market support, stronger risk/reward ratios, knowledge sharing, and skills development are needed.
studyFutureWorks: Develop stronger and more detailed recommendations for overcoming specific system failures and barriers to long-term UK renewable options.
studyLimits: A policy-focused, time-limited snapshot underemphasises learning processes and does not provide a full international comparison.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Mapped actors, knowledge, influence and funding flows and characterized failures along the innovation chain.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Innovation-systems approaches had not been widely applied to UK renewable technologies or systematically related system failures to technology-maturity stages.

studyMethodsSummary: Conceptual specification of carbon lock-in barriers in renewable generation, transmission and distribution grids, storage, and demand response, followed by a policy review of existing instruments and reform needs.
studyKeyFindings: Generation policies are widespread but grid, storage, and demand-response measures remain immature. Carbon lock-out requires simultaneous barrier removal, integrated EU-wide planning, coordinated scenarios, and partly harmonised policy rules.
studyFutureWorks: Develop coordinated, transparent European electricity scenarios and continue research on policy challenges of renewable deployment.
studyLimits: Conceptual policy review; it does not rank barriers or policy responses and recognizes that many areas require further research.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Reviewed policies across generation, grid, storage, and demand barriers and specified an integrated EU policy portfolio.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing renewable-electricity support is fragmented across Member States and insufficiently addresses non-generation components of the electricity system.

studyMethodsSummary: Online questionnaire of renewable project representatives used a five-point barrier-importance scale and quota sampling. Sixty responses were complemented by five face-to-face semi-structured interviews.
studyKeyFindings: Grid connection constraints and lack of capacity were the highest-rated barrier (4.35/5), followed by lengthy permitting (4.16), land/water lease securement (3.90), and limited project finance (3.71).
studyFutureWorks: Examine barriers by technology and investigate government and financial-institution perspectives, including project-risk assessment under differing regulations and procedures.
studyLimits: Barrier relevance varies by technology; quota sampling is non-probabilistic and cannot provide generalisable population estimates or robust sampling-error estimates.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Prioritized 18 barriers with investor/developer survey data and follow-up interviews.
studyResearchGapIdentified: No prior study had examined renewable-deployment barriers in Chile from investors’ perspectives, including Chile-specific mining-concession and grid-regulation issues.

studyMethodsSummary: Stakeholder-centred synthesis of literature and real-world case studies of South Africa’s REIPPPP, Kenya’s Olkaria geothermal project, Rwanda’s Gigawatt Global solar project, and Tanzanian solar mini-grids.
studyKeyFindings: Technical, financial, policy, and socio-cultural barriers are intertwined. Successful initiatives combine stable policy support, innovative financing, capacity building, and broad stakeholder/community engagement.
studyFutureWorks: Develop context-specific regional assessments, support localized research and pilot projects, and strengthen knowledge transfer between research and market deployment.
studyLimits: The synthesis emphasises diverse regional contexts; strategies and barriers vary by country, technology, and stakeholder group.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Synthesized barriers and case-study lessons into coordinated strategies for policy reform, finance, capacity building, and public engagement.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Renewable-energy barriers in Sub-Saharan Africa require an integrated stakeholder perspective spanning governments, private entities, financial institutions, and communities.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied dual state-parameter Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) to extended SAC-SMA, assimilating streamflow only, soil moisture only, or both; Hydrus supplied areal soil-moisture observations.
studyKeyFindings: Combined assimilation gave more accurate soil-moisture and streamflow forecasts, especially at 1–14-day lead times. Streamflow-only assimilation distorted soil moisture; soil-moisture-only assimilation gave inaccurate flow.
studyFutureWorks: Assess remotely sensed soil-moisture products and particle-filter/Markov-chain Monte Carlo approaches.
studyLimits: Only point soil-moisture observations were available, so Hydrus-simulated sub-basin averages were used as observations.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared three dual-EnKF observation-assimilation strategies for state and forecast variation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hydrological DA can update streamflow while producing unvalidated and distorted soil-moisture states.

studyMethodsSummary: Calibrated WRF-Hydro at four USGS gauges then used evolutionary particle-filter Markov-chain Monte Carlo data assimilation to independently and jointly assimilate USGS streamflow and SMAP soil moisture at 36 km 9 km and 1 km.
studyKeyFindings: Joint streamflow and 1-km SMAP assimilation improved streamflow across regimes. During normal flow 1-km SMAP outperformed coarser products; during Hurricane Harvey soil-moisture resolutions had similar effects.
studyFutureWorks: Improve observation quality over water bodies and extend high-resolution multivariate assimilation studies.
studyLimits: SMAP retrievals are degraded over water bodies such as Lake Livingston; point stream gauges provide limited spatial soil-moisture correction.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Evaluated independent and joint assimilation of satellite soil moisture and in-situ streamflow in a distributed WRF-Hydro model.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hyper-resolution hydrologic forecasts have uncertainty in states parameters forcing and observations, while the value of multivariate remote-sensing assimilation was insufficiently tested.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed sequential three-phase multi-metric tuning for control-theory-based data assimilation. A 1D DiffW1D river hydraulic model of the Iron Gate 1 Danube reach is continuously updated by PID-controller correction flows derived from water-level discrepancies.
studyKeyFindings: The PI configuration Kp=10 and Ki=10 substantially improved assimilation: RMSE was 0.02 m at assimilation points and 0.07 m at the validation point. Adding derivative gain offered no benefit up to Kd=1000 and extreme derivative gain caused instability.
studyFutureWorks: Test numerical-model complexity effects and perform individual-controller fine tuning with multi-objective optimization.
studyLimits: The study uses a synthetic test scenario and identical controller gains across all assimilation points.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Uses PID controllers as a simple, control-theory-based data-assimilation method with sequential multi-metric initial tuning.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Uncertain initial and boundary conditions degrade model-driven near-future hydropower forecasting, while standard data-assimilation methods can be slow or difficult to apply operationally.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied ensemble Kalman filtering to an E-HYPE sub-model for the Umeälven catchment. Assimilated in-situ discharge and reservoir inflow plus satellite fractional snow cover, snow water equivalent, actual evapotranspiration, and potential evapotranspiration; assessed ensemble size and 63 single and combined assimilation experiments using KGE gains.
studyKeyFindings: Ensembles of 25 members sufficed for most products, while discharge and reservoir inflow required 100. Thirteen combinations improved both target variables; in-situ observations outperformed satellite products except fractional snow cover, and MODIS potential evapotranspiration did not generally improve target forecasts.
studyFutureWorks: Assess other evapotranspiration products and translate reservoir-inflow prediction gains into economic gains.
studyLimits: Passive-microwave snow-water-equivalent data were unreliable in highland and coastal areas, and MODIS potential evapotranspiration may be biased.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Objectively selects EnKF ensemble size and tests single and multi-product assimilation combinations for discharge and reservoir-inflow prediction.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The value of assimilating multiple satellite and in-situ products at distinct spatial and temporal scales for hydrological target predictions had not been established.

studyMethodsSummary: Assimilated early-April snow-water-equivalent observations at three Refsdal sites into a distributed conceptual Shyft hydrological model using a stochastic EnKF. For 15 snowmelt seasons, forecasts were run for 120 days and benchmarked against an unassimilated base case.
studyKeyFindings: Assimilation improved seasonal inflow forecasts in 7 of 15 years, with large improvements in 2001 and 2010 and only small degradation in 3 years. The lowest forecast MAE (6%) was achieved with Grønebotn and Katledalane observations; Ovridsfjell alone produced the worst MAE (15%).
studyFutureWorks: Develop snow-sampling designs tailored to gridded ensemble updating and improve meteorological forcing and snowmelt modelling.
studyLimits: The sampling scheme was not designed for ensemble updating; precipitation forcing may underestimate solid precipitation.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Tests objective EnKF assimilation of peak-accumulation SWE observations to improve long-lead inflow forecasts.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Manual snow-observation updates in Norwegian hydropower forecasts are labor-intensive, non-reproducible, and lack an objective systematic method.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed SWAT-HDAS by coupling the gridded parallel SWATGP distributed hydrological model with PDAF. Conducted synthetic OSSEs assimilating soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and discharge with an EnKF in the Babaohe River Basin.
studyKeyFindings: Assimilation improved soil-moisture, SWE, and streamflow estimates. More and more-downstream discharge observations improved outlet streamflow estimation; an 18-site configuration was best. Assimilating discharge alone was as good as multivariable assimilation for streamflow in the synthetic experiments.
studyFutureWorks: Extend observation operators for microwave and cosmic-ray soil-moisture observations and assess localization, smoothing, scaling, and observation-error effects.
studyLimits: Experiments used synthetic observations and assumed model and observation error statistics; real applications require realistic error settings and suitable observation scaling.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrates SWATGP and PDAF into SWAT-HDAS and demonstrates multiscale synthetic soil-moisture, snow, and discharge assimilation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Basin-scale hydrological studies need a flexible system that can assimilate multi-source observations into a physically based distributed model at high spatial resolution.

studyMethodsSummary: Compared dynamics-driven Square Root Analysis (SQRA) and data-driven Kalman–Takens filtering in W3RA. Assimilated GRACE terrestrial water storage and AMSR-E/SMOS soil moisture separately and jointly at 5-day resolution over the Murray–Darling and Mississippi basins.
studyKeyFindings: Joint GRACE-plus-soil-moisture assimilation gave the largest improvements. SQRA case 3 was best in Murray–Darling (groundwater RMSE 24.85 mm, correlation 0.80); Kalman–Takens case 6 was best in Mississippi (27.11 mm, 0.84). Kalman–Takens was about six times faster and performed comparably to SQRA.
studyFutureWorks: Assess further data-driven assimilation applications where physical-model error is large.
studyLimits: Physical-model errors can reduce performance of model-driven assimilation; satellite soil moisture mainly updates shallow layers, and data required bias correction.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Assesses SQRA and Kalman–Takens using separate and joint GRACE and satellite soil-moisture assimilations against independent in-situ measurements.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The comparative value of dynamics-driven and data-driven assimilation frameworks for different combinations of satellite water-storage and soil-moisture products was unclear.

studyMethodsSummary: Trained separate feed-forward multilayer-perceptron networks with sigmoid activation functions on monthly Kainji and Jebba reservoir data. Inputs were inflow, storage, elevation, turbine release, net head, plant-use coefficient, tailrace level, and evaporation loss; output was energy generation.
studyKeyFindings: The 8–7–1 networks produced test-set correlations of 0.89 for Kainji and 0.77 for Jebba, indicating reliable energy-generation forecasts from reservoir variables.
studyFutureWorks: Use reservoir-variable forecasts to support hydropower operation and energy prediction.
studyLimits: The study evaluates historical monthly data from only Kainji and Jebba reservoirs.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Uses MLP neural networks to model monthly energy generation as a function of eight reservoir variables.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hydropower reservoir management requires understanding complex relationships between reservoir variables and energy generation.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured monthly river discharge with the velocity-area method, estimated gross hydropower potential with a UNIDO model, and used flow-duration curves to assess flow dependability.
studyKeyFindings: Ovia had the highest annual power yield (61.6189 MW); Ikpoba, Orlie, and Edion yielded 14.7868 MW, 9.819 MW, and 5.4956 MW.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct a comprehensive technical and socioeconomic viability appraisal of small-scale hydropower development.
studyLimits: The study was limited to streamflow analysis.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Generated monthly discharge and hydropower-potential evidence for four Edo State rivers.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hydrological characteristics and small-hydropower potential of most Edo State rivers are not fully understood because reliable discharge data are scarce.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied output-oriented variable-returns-to-scale DEA with an inverted frontier to derive three partial indices and a scaled Hydropower IPAT Index for 53 proposed Brazilian projects. Trained 7–4–1 ANN impact-prediction and 3–3–2 SHP/LHP classification models in SPSS.
studyKeyFindings: All top-10 low-impact projects were SHPs, while 7 of the 10 worst-ranked projects were LHPs. Selected ANN prediction model 5 achieved R²=0.963, test MSE=0.0001, and MAD=0.026; selected classification model achieved 99.0% accuracy.
studyFutureWorks: Include other indicators and theoretical models and compare alternative machine-learning methods.
studyLimits: The index uses a selected set of local IPAT indicators and does not constitute a definitive energy-policy assessment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combines DEA-derived IPAT impact indexing with ANN prediction and SHP/LHP classification for 53 projects.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Brazil lacks standardized, specific criteria to compare and classify hydropower projects by local environmental impact across different production scales.

studyMethodsSummary: Measured Sombriero River surface velocity with a weighted wooden float over a 22 m reach, estimated mean velocity with a 0.6 tolerance factor, calculated cross-sectional area using the trapezoidal rule, calculated power from discharge, head, and efficiency, and performed RETScreen financial simulation.
studyKeyFindings: Measured discharge was 1.99 m³/s. At 3.5 m head and 0.75 efficiency, potential output was 51.25 kW. A run-of-river micro-hydropower scheme was viable at a US$127.61/MWh tariff, with US$920 NPV, 22.6% equity IRR, 19.5% asset IRR, benefit–cost ratio 1.01, and 4 years 6 months equity payback.
studyFutureWorks: Use a standard current meter and 1–2 years of hydrological data, and prepare detailed civil, electro-mechanical, and transmission cost estimates.
studyLimits: Wooden-float measurement and short April–July record limit flow-estimation accuracy; civil works, turbine-generator, hydraulic, and transmission costs need real-time detailed costing.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combines float-method flow measurement, power calculation, and RETScreen financial analysis for a run-of-river micro-hydropower scheme.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The Sombriero River’s discharge, micro-hydropower potential, and financial feasibility had not been quantified for decentralized electricity supply.

studyMethodsSummary: Integrated ten hydro-physical thematic layers with GIS and AHP to create an upper Benue SHP dam-suitability map. Used a semi-automatic ArcGIS contour–stream-order–suitability intersection and SQL query to identify narrow valleys, then evaluated five sites by field survey.
studyKeyFindings: Very high suitability covers 11,111.2 km² (7.5%) of the watershed and high suitability covers 40,327.2 km² (27.4%). Map validation achieved ROC AUC 79.67%; 18 suitable dam sites were selected from 636 narrow valleys. Field/model valley widths correlated at 0.71, though the semi-automatic approach underestimated field widths by 7.1–33.1%.
studyFutureWorks: Use very high-resolution data, especially DEM data, to improve semi-automatic valley-width estimation.
studyLimits: Thematic inputs have varied spatial and temporal resolution; five of 18 sites were field surveyed because other sites were remote or inaccessible.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combines GIS–AHP suitability mapping with semi-automatic narrow-valley identification and field validation for upper Benue SHP dam sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Previous dam-suitability mapping studies often do not explicitly explain how potential sites are spatially identified and selected across large watersheds.

studyMethodsSummary: An annual Choudhury-Budyko water-balance model was regionally calibrated with discharge data from 410 gauges to simulate annual discharge across more than 500,000 river reaches. The model was driven with 15 CORDEX-Africa regional climate models under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 using a delta-change method, then theoretical line and specific hydropower potential were calculated from discharge, reach head, and length.
studyKeyFindings: The most promising theoretical potential is in Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, and south-eastern Nigeria. The ensemble median does not indicate a considerable West Africa-wide decrease in annual discharge over the next decades, though warming increases evapotranspiration and regional rainfall signals are mixed.
studyFutureWorks: Publish interactive ECOWREX map layers and use the results to target sub-basin studies and discharge-measurement campaigns.
studyLimits: Observed discharge records contain gaps, biases, and georeferencing errors; precipitation products also introduce uncertainty. The theoretical potential is an upper limit because it assumes full discharge and head are turbinated and excludes spillway losses and environmental-flow constraints.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provides a region-wide, reach-scale theoretical-potential and climate-impact screening framework.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hydro-meteorological data and spatially complete discharge and hydropower-potential evidence are inadequate across much of West Africa.

studyMethodsSummary: Integrated vertical electrical sounding (VES), Landsat 8 imagery, SRTM DEM, geological mapping, and GIS thematic layers using analytic hierarchy process (AHP) weighted overlay.
studyKeyFindings: The Ogun basin was delineated into high (21%), moderate (31%), low (6%), and very-low (42%) groundwater-potential zones; AHP consistency ratio was 0.04.
studyFutureWorks: Add detailed VES data, well data, and pumping-test results to improve and validate the groundwater-potential map.
studyLimits: VES validation was limited to 20 soundings at Abeokuta and Ewekoro; the RS/GIS map can be pessimistic relative to VES-derived potential.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combined hydrogeophysical observations with remote sensing and GIS multi-criteria mapping and validated against resistivity surveys.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Groundwater occurrence and storage potential in the Ogun drainage basin require spatially integrated assessment.

studyMethodsSummary: Used SRTM DEM ArcHydro GIS PERSIANN-CDR rainfall NIMET validation and NRCS-CN runoff modelling; constructed Q92 flow-duration curves and screened 58 points for slope and head.
studyKeyFindings: Rainfall and discharge correlations were 65% and 63%. Eleven points met 2% slope and 10 m head criteria, with 393.849–16038.194 kW potential at 92% annual exceedance.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct detailed site feasibility and longer-term hydrological monitoring.
studyLimits: Rainfall and flow validation covered only 2018 and site screening remains preliminary.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combined GIS RS and NRCS-CN modeling to assess Oyanmi SHP potential.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Poorly gauged Nigerian rivers lack hydrological information for small-hydropower planning.

studyMethodsSummary: SWAT, interfaced with MapWindow GIS, simulated watershed hydrology; calibrated flow and hydraulic head derived from a digital elevation model were used to calculate theoretical river hydrokinetic potential.
studyKeyFindings: Awun River had the highest estimated potential (154.82 MW); Oyun and Asa were estimated at 98.39 MW and 41.63 MW.
studyFutureWorks: Harness assessed river potential with appropriate technology for nearby communities.
studyLimits: Potential estimates may be affected by turbine design, turbine type, efficiency, deployment mode, and river use.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Applied SWAT in a GIS environment to estimate potential for selected Asa watershed rivers.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Hydrokinetic potential of Nigerian river currents is largely unexplored.

studyMethodsSummary: Constructed a flow-duration curve from seven years of daily flow, subtracted residual flow, modeled turbine efficiency and power-duration curves, integrated annual energy, and compared turbine and head alternatives.
studyKeyFindings: At 46.5 m net head and average flow, a single Kaplan turbine was projected at 8.774 MW, 50018 MWh/year, and 65.1% capacity factor with 148 days at rated output. Minimum-flow configurations could operate for 365 days at 97.8% capacity factor.
studyLimits: Only seven years of flow records were available; the average-flow configuration was not highly dependable and required standby capacity during dry periods.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Quantified flow-dependent turbine performance and energy production for a proposed Opeki River plant.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Nigeria lacks relevant small-hydropower data and a comprehensive inventory of potential sites.

studyMethodsSummary: Used ArcGIS overlay of UN-FAO water areas waterline shapefiles and administrative boundaries across six geopolitical zones; used 200 m–5 km buffers and IDW suitability interpolation.
studyKeyFindings: Mapped high SHP potential in Borno Niger Edo Anambra and Jigawa. The north-east had 151 potential small-dam sites and Yobe 55 inland-water sites; north-west had 95 potential small-dam sites.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct field flow head environmental social and feasibility studies at mapped locations.
studyLimits: The assessment lacks site-level elevation head and flow information and is constrained by data availability GIS expertise and missing environmental and stakeholder data.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Produced national zonal maps and statistics to guide preliminary SHP site prioritization.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Nigeria lacks a comprehensive nationwide ArcGIS assessment of small-hydropower sites and supporting hydrological data.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied ArcHydro remote sensing GIS and NRCS Curve Number rainfall-runoff modelling to 148 drainage-network points; derived flow-duration design discharges and heads; then used SHPRASA for turbine cost and emission screening.
studyKeyFindings: Eighteen of 148 points could yield 677.485–7622.877 kW at 92% flow exceedance, avoid 555.8–6543.0 tCO2/year, and cost GBP 937167.48–4048733.99.
studyFutureWorks: Undertake detailed field and feasibility studies at promising sites.
studyLimits: Screening-level assessment based largely on modeled peak discharge and limited gauge data; detailed engineering and field feasibility remain required.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Established SHPRASA as a GIS and NRCS-CN based SHP screening and sustainability workflow.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Data-scarce river basins lack an efficient basin-wide method to identify technically economically and environmentally viable SHP sites.

studyMethodsSummary: Transferred recent flow from the similar Gumera catchment using an area-ratio approach; simulated daily Beshilo flows with SWAT; calibrated with SUFI-2; screened GIS and field-survey sites using flow, head, spacing, construction, and sediment criteria; built Weibull flow-duration curves; and calculated power at three dependability levels.
studyKeyFindings: Nine run-of-river sites were identified. Total potential was 9.866 MW at 90% dependable flow, 37.765 MW at 75%, and 184.098 MW at 50%. Site 1 was strongest at every level, reaching 2.320, 8.900, and 42.750 MW.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct detailed engineering and economic feasibility assessment of the proposed sites.
studyLimits: The Beshilo River lacked recent gauge records, requiring regionalized Gumera flows. Results require detailed technical and economic feasibility studies before development.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combined catchment-similarity flow transfer, SWAT simulation, GIS screening, and field observations to quantify nine sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Recent observed Beshilo flows are unavailable despite the need to identify hydropower resources for rural electrification and regional power deficits.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied a satellite-driven 0.1 degree VIC hydrological model with routing and a reservoir-operation optimization model to simulate 37 years of GERD inflow storage releases turbine use and generation.
studyKeyFindings: Upper Blue Nile hydrology could support 13629 GWh/year at capacity factor 0.30; in the current configuration eight of 14 turbines would likely be idle annually. The 5150 MW design was judged more reasonable than 6000 and 6450 MW alternatives.
studyFutureWorks: Assess climate and sedimentation impacts and peak-versus-base load operations.
studyLimits: Operational optimization used assumed downstream-damage penalties and did not assess future climate-change or sedimentation effects in detail.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Linked long-term hydrologic simulation to reservoir operation and turbine-capacity scenarios.
studyResearchGapIdentified: GERD's ability to meet declared design generation and whether its capacity is oversized had not been evaluated from Upper Blue Nile hydrology.

studyMethodsSummary: Converted 25 years of discharge records into velocity and power density using SRTM DEM ArcGIS HEC-GeoRAS HEC-RAS and field velocity depth and width measurements.
studyKeyFindings: Maximum extractable power density was 1.4 kW/m2 in Gumara 3.4 kW/m2 in Gilgel-Abay and 2.6 kW/m2 in Bahirdar-Abay; 24.5% 31.7% and 29% of their reaches respectively met velocity thresholds.
studyFutureWorks: Obtain better spatial velocity and turbine-power-curve data.
studyLimits: Historical discharge is not velocity data; bathymetry was limited and HKT power-curve averaging lacks a standardized convention.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Coupled public GIS hydraulic modeling and low-cost field validation to estimate velocity and power density.
studyResearchGapIdentified: River velocity records required for hydro-kinetic turbine assessment are generally unavailable although discharge records exist.

studyMethodsSummary: Integrated ALOS PALSAR terrain data, Sentinel-2 land cover, geology, rainfall and infrastructure layers in ArcGIS Pro; applied AHP weighting and weighted GIS overlay within 10 km of seven existing reservoirs.
studyKeyFindings: Head was the highest-weighted criterion (29.8%), followed by head-to-distance ratio (17.9%), slope (15.9%), TWI (11.7%), lineaments (6.9%), grid proximity (6.3%), river proximity (5.8%), and road proximity (5.6%). Very-high suitability covered 2.6 km2 (0.17%).
studyFutureWorks: Conduct detailed reservoir-pair design capacity environmental and economic evaluations.
studyLimits: A screening study without detailed engineering, economic, environmental, social, or reservoir-pair feasibility; criteria weights are subjective.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Produced a national PHES suitability map using GIS-based MCDA and AHP.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Selecting viable pumped-storage locations around Ethiopian reservoirs requires integrating topographic hydrologic geological and infrastructure constraints.

studyMethodsSummary: Used ArcSWAT with 30 m DEM land cover soil weather and streamflow inputs; calibrated and validated flow; screened fourth-order streams by head and spacing; and used flow-duration curves to estimate theoretical power.
studyKeyFindings: Reported 33 sites in results and 20 in the conclusion. Results reported 3039, 1127, and 805 kW at 90%, 75%, and 50% dependability; the conclusion instead reported 12744, 2538, and 603.1 kW at 50%, 75%, and 90%.
studyFutureWorks: Assess land-cover change river morphology and hydrology and optimize head and spacing criteria.
studyLimits: Site-count criteria and aggregate outputs are internally inconsistent; geological and other nonhydrological feasibility criteria were not assessed.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Applied GIS and SWAT to screen sites and simulate flows along the watershed.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Limited integrated spatial and hydrological evidence for screening hydropower sites in the Temcha watershed.

studyMethodsSummary: Calibrated Poli-Hydro for the Blue Nile and Omo basins, downscaled 21 CMIP5/CMIP6 climate projections, and used Poli-Power and Poli-Price to optimize GERD and GIBE III operation under no-release and environmental-release scenarios through 2100.
studyKeyFindings: GERD production generally increases by mid-century and then moderates by end-century; GIBE III production generally increases. Constrained and unconstrained GERD operation produced similar results, and an approximately five-year GERD filling period performed best.
studyFutureWorks: Use longer and more recent streamflow series, obtain plant energy-production data, and investigate a larger climate-scenario ensemble.
studyLimits: Hydrological, production, and price observations were sparse; only calibration was possible; future GCM, RCP, and SSP projections embed uncertainty.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Coupled hydrological, climate, price, and reservoir-operation models to project GERD and GIBE III production through 2100.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Prospective climate change may alter water availability, reservoir management, and Ethiopian hydropower production.

studyMethodsSummary: Combined 12.5 m DEM-based GIS screening, daily SWAT simulation and SUFI-2 calibration, inverse-distance parameter regionalization, flow-duration curves, the hydropower equation, and AHP-weighted GIS multicriteria ranking.
studyKeyFindings: Identified 103 sites with heads of 20–81 m. Total theoretical potential was 183.16, 125.96, and 33.03 MW at 50%, 75%, and 90% flow exceedance; regionalized SWAT performance was satisfactory at two verification gauges.
studyFutureWorks: Assess run-of-river potential at sub-basin scale and undertake detailed implementation studies for prioritized sites.
studyLimits: Sparse and potentially inaccurate inputs increased hydrological uncertainty, and SWAT reproduced peak flows poorly; the assessment remained a screening-level theoretical analysis.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Transferred calibrated SWAT parameters to ungauged sites and integrated GIS-derived head with dependable flow and multicriteria ranking.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Data scarcity and costly field surveys impede comprehensive multi-site run-of-river assessment in Ethiopian basins.

studyMethodsSummary: ArcSWAT, driven by terrain, land-use, soil, daily meteorological, and observed-flow data, delineated 15 sub-basins and 66 HRUs, calibrated and validated streamflow, and simulated flows at three candidate sites. Q90 flow-duration analysis, DEM-derived gross head, the hydropower equation, and AHP/MCDM were used to estimate and rank theoretical candidates.
studyKeyFindings: Calibration R², NSE, and PBIAS were 0.84, 0.78, and −4.6%; validation values were 0.81, 0.72, and −4.8%. Q90 was 0.37, 0.45, and 0.48 m³/s at sites 1–3; corresponding gross heads were 15, 25, and 20 m and theoretical power was 54.45, 110.36, and 94.18 kW. Site 2 was selected as best.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct detailed river-flow field surveys and update hydrological and meteorological data systems.
studyLimits: Detailed field verification of the full river flow was constrained by budget; authors note the need for improved hydro-meteorological data collection and field survey.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrates calibrated ArcSWAT, geospatial gross-head assessment, dependable-flow analysis, and MCDM site ranking.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The Megecha watershed lacked integrated surface-water modelling and technically ranked hydropower-site evidence.

studyMethodsSummary: A 12.5 m DEM and ArcGIS derived the Furfuro watershed, flow accumulation, Strahler stream order, and potential head. Fourth- and fifth-order streams were screened for at least 8 m head and 1,000 m spacing, and Google Earth Pro head drops were compared with handheld GPS readings at four accessible locations.
studyKeyFindings: Four potential hydropower sites were identified on fourth- and fifth-order streams. Google Earth Pro versus GPS head drops produced R² 0.994 and NSE 0.997, supporting use of DEM, Google Earth, and GPS for head screening.
studyFutureWorks: Assess Furfuro River discharge and undertake technical and economic feasibility studies for hydropower development.
studyLimits: The study estimates head only; it does not report discharge, power capacity, technical feasibility, or economic feasibility for the candidate sites.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provides validated, low-cost geospatial screening of potential head and candidate reaches on the Furfuro River.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Accurate head data and hydropower-potential information are lacking for many Ethiopian perennial rivers.

studyMethodsSummary: ArcGIS, Arc Hydro, HEC-GeoHMS, and Global Mapper derived terrain, river profiles, head, and contributing area. GPS measurements corrected river-profile head; an area-ratio method transferred flow to ungauged sites, Weibull FDCs supplied Q90, technical power and annual energy were calculated, HOMER modeled Alefa Kacha supply at site 8, and AHP ranked nine sites.
studyKeyFindings: Nine run-of-river sites total 660.01 kW technical potential and 5,608.222 MWh/year. Hp site 8 has 151 m corrected head, 0.30 m³/s design flow, 305.87 kW technical potential, and 2,599.04 MWh/year; it ranks first. HOMER reports 4,018,758 kWh/year hydro output versus 483,123 kWh/year load, or 88% excess.
studyFutureWorks: Use the ranking to prioritize detailed micro-hydropower feasibility and development, including surveys and assessments at the selected sites.
studyLimits: Field GPS head validation covered only three sites; flow was transferred to ungauged sites and feasibility relies on available DEM, flow, and assumed efficiency inputs. Detailed field, engineering, environmental, and economic investigation remains needed.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combines geospatial site selection, corrected head, dependable flow, technical potential, rural load simulation, and ranking for nine candidate sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Remote Gilgel-Beles communities lack cost-effective grid access and lack a prioritized micro-hydropower resource and site assessment.

studyMethodsSummary: The study used ten years of daily flow data from MoWE, converted it to mean flow and Weibull FDCs, used QGIS and GPS Visualizer to analyse topography, calculated net head, and estimated theoretical output with a cross-flow turbine at 80% efficiency and an assumed 20 m net head.
studyKeyFindings: Chemoga has the highest theoretical output in high, moist, and mid-range flow at 4,729.20, 3,495.49, and 2,133.08 kW. Wabe has the highest dry and low-flow output at 1,023.37 and 673.35 kW; Wabe also has the largest elevation change, 333.34 m per 11.1 km. Huluka is lower in every condition.
studyFutureWorks: Identify specific small, mini, and micro-hydropower sites along the rivers and assess detailed technical, economic, and environmental feasibility.
studyLimits: Topographic information was not supplied by MoWE, and a 20 m head and 80% cross-flow efficiency were assumed; actual head, efficiency, economics, environmental impacts, and site feasibility require further assessment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provides a scalable FDC-plus-topography framework that compares theoretical hydropower potential under five flow conditions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Many Ethiopian rivers suitable for small-scale hydropower have insufficient flow and topographic potential assessment.

studyMethodsSummary: Mapped 2000, 2010, and 2020 LULC from Landsat, modelled Bui water yield with InVEST using climate, soil, terrain and LULC data, validated yields against Bui-gauge discharge, and compared pre/post daily Black Volta flow with IHA/RVA.
studyKeyFindings: Water yield increased from 3.25 MCM in 2000 to 4.75 MCM in 2020. Forest cover fell from 81.42% to 35.80% while urban cover rose from 10.76% to 41.45%. Bui Dam altered timing and pulses: dry conditions extended 92.43 days, peaks arrived at least 10 days earlier, and low-pulse duration fell from 44.98 to 2.33 days.
studyFutureWorks: Adopt adaptive dam management and integrated water-resource planning that protects environmental flows and ecosystem services.
studyLimits: InVEST is pixel-based and does not explicitly represent baseflow; three benchmark years limit validation; water-yield changes reflect interacting climate, land-use, and dam-operation effects.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrates land-cover change, InVEST water yield, and IHA/RVA evidence to quantify Bui Dam hydrological effects.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Dam planning insufficiently quantifies trade-offs between hydropower operation, water provisioning, natural flow regimes, and riverine ecosystems.

studyMethodsSummary: SWAT simulated flow from remote-sensing, soil, weather, and gauge inputs, calibrated with SUFI-2. Nine sites were screened by head and spacing; FDC/PDC analysis determined firm flow, power and energy, and storage/turbine options were evaluated for a cascade.
studyKeyFindings: Nine sites have combined 7.89 MW firm power. HP1, HP4, and HP7 have annual energy of 28.68, 12.68, and 14.36 GWh and form a recommended 55.72 GWh/year cascade.
studyFutureWorks: Government agencies should explore Densu energy potential and undertake detailed cascade feasibility.
studyLimits: Site data are modelling-based and require detailed technical, environmental, and economic feasibility assessment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provides SWAT-based siting, energy estimates, and a storage-cascade recommendation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Densu small-hydropower investment is constrained by limited hydrological information.

studyMethodsSummary: Used 30 m SRTM DEM and GIS criteria to locate sites; simulated monthly streamflow with SWAT using climate, land-cover, soil, and donor-catchment gauge data; calibrated and validated the model; constructed flow- and power-duration curves at 90% dependability; and assessed run-of-river and dam projects with RETScreen.
studyKeyFindings: Six dam and three run-of-river sites provide 117.72–2356.2 kW firm power and 0.60–12.07 GWh firm energy per site. Dam site 1, run-of-river site 1, and dam site 6 were recommended as a cascade totaling 21.65 GWh annually. Both RETScreen cases were financially viable.
studyFutureWorks: Assess climate-change flows, flood risk, and detailed engineering, geological, and hydrological conditions at the proposed sites.
studyLimits: Daily streamflow was unavailable, so monthly modeled flow and regionalization from the Bamboi donor catchment were used. SWAT may have difficulty resolving localized small-project effects.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Identified and quantified nine Pumpum River sites and evaluated dam and run-of-river financial cases.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Few Ghanaian studies assess both dam and run-of-river small-hydropower siting together with economic feasibility.

studyMethodsSummary: GIS screened Lower Pra sites; calibrated SWAT generated flows; FDC/PDC analysis calculated firm power and energy; storage and Francis-turbine cascade options were assessed.
studyKeyFindings: Ten sites were identified. HP1, HP3 and HP7 provide 12.22, 10.00 and 9.00 MW firm power and 183.77, 157.67 and 141.91 GWh annual energy; their proposed cascade totals 483.4 GWh/year.
studyFutureWorks: Explore Densu Basin potential through detailed feasibility studies.
studyLimits: Potential sites require detailed technical, economic and environmental feasibility assessment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provides SWAT/GIS-based site and cascade evidence.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Ghanaian small-hydropower potential has not been assessed in depth.

studyMethodsSummary: Satellite and in-situ hydroclimatic observations were combined with random-forest models to reconstruct Lake Malawi levels and Shire River discharge. Beta regression quantified discharge-extreme effects on hydropower capacity factor; log-linear OLS related extremes to urban nighttime-light radiance.
studyKeyFindings: A dry discharge extreme reduced total hydropower capacity factor by 9.4 percentage points and monthly urban nighttime lights by 31 percentage points. Random-forest discharge reconstructions had KGE 0.96–0.99 and NSE 0.94–0.99 across gauges.
studyFutureWorks: Integrate hydropower-operation optimization and examine diversified generation and transboundary transmission options.
studyLimits: Satellite-data calibration and interpolation can introduce error; thresholds for extremes are arbitrary; no hydropower-operation or optimization model was used.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Used publicly available satellite data and machine learning to fill discharge-record gaps and assess reliability impacts.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Reliable continuous monitoring of hydropower performance is difficult where hydrological and generation data are sparse.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly production and precipitation data were normalized, split chronologically into 75% training and 25% testing data, and used in grid-searched MLP, LSTM, and sequence-to-sequence LSTM models. Walk-forward validation assessed one-step and twelve-step forecasts.
studyKeyFindings: The differentiated univariate MLP was best in both scenarios: RMSE 4.09 GWh for one-step and 123.84 GWh for twelve-step forecasting. ANN forecasts outperformed ARIMA and ARIMAX in the 2015 comparison.
studyFutureWorks: Use more observations, latent recurrent neural networks, transformers, and super-resolution methods.
studyLimits: The dataset had limited observations; exhaustive grid search is computationally costly for larger datasets.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Evaluated MLP, LSTM, and seq2seq LSTM forecasting designs for Ecuador over 2000–2015.
studyResearchGapIdentified: There were no comparable recurrent-neural-network studies for a medium-size region with a long period of changing installed hydropower capacity.

studyMethodsSummary: Hourly generation from Aslantaş and upstream Ceyhan River HPPs, meteorological reanalysis, market prices, and calendar variables were cleaned and used to train/test CatBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM regressors with 80/20 random sampling. Tree count and learning rate were tuned.
studyKeyFindings: LightGBM was best, with R² 97.07%, RMSSE 0.1217, and 1.240 s runtime at 1,000 trees and learning rate 0.10.
studyFutureWorks: Develop hybrid hydrological-ML approaches, real-time rolling retraining and drift monitoring, and cross-basin testing.
studyLimits: Results are specific to the Ceyhan basin; transferring the framework requires basin-specific retraining and independent validation. ML-only dispatch could be unreliable during extreme inflows.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Introduced basin-aware predictors using upstream HPP generation and benchmarked three tree-based models.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Direct head-to-head benchmarks of CatBoost, LightGBM, and XGBoost for hydroelectricity generation under identical constraints are lacking.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed an improved multilayer neural network with ReLU activation, L2 regularization, Adam optimization, and adaptive inverse normalization; optimized LSSVM hyperparameters with an improved grey wolf algorithm; evaluated both on axial-flow propeller and Francis turbine operating data.
studyKeyFindings: IGWO-LSSVM achieved the best reported relative errors: 1.61% for axial-flow propeller data and 0.41% for Francis data. Adaptive inverse normalization improved neural-network prediction and produced 3.06% and 1.73% best-scenario relative errors, respectively.
studyFutureWorks: Reduce subjectivity in selecting the IGWO optimization range.
studyLimits: The IGWO multi-parameter optimization range still depends on subjective experience and may bias turbine-power predictions; the operational data are confidential.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provided fast data-driven turbine-power predictors for both small- and large-sample operating conditions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Conventional 3D hydrodynamic turbine models have long design cycles and complex solutions, while manual LSSVM parameter selection is uncertain and empirical.

studyMethodsSummary: ANFIS models forecast monthly shares of thermal, hydropower, nuclear, and non-hydropower renewable generation. Single-factor sensitivity analysis and 59,049 multi-factor scenario combinations assess influence mechanisms.
studyKeyFindings: Under the standard scenario in 2025, thermal, hydropower, nuclear, and non-hydropower renewables account for 60.46%, 20.43%, 6.43%, and 12.68%. EHV/UHV transmission primarily benefits hydropower, while rapid urbanization, industrial upgrading, and demand growth increase thermal-power share.
studyFutureWorks: Develop large-scale energy storage, more flexible market mechanisms for peak/frequency regulation, and policy measures beyond UHV projects.
studyLimits: Future indicator scenarios are based on assumptions; energy storage was omitted because samples were insufficient for machine learning.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Modeled generation shares directly rather than using installed-capacity shares as a proxy.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Direct quantitative forecasts of China’s generation structure and systematic evidence on its macro drivers are scarce.

studyMethodsSummary: Split 2005–2017 Karun-III data 80/20 for training/testing; used binary salp swarm optimization for lag selection and continuous SSA for hyperparameters; benchmarked nine standalone and serial hybrid neural/Bayesian models at 1-, 2-, and 3-day horizons; evaluated predictive accuracy and 95% interval uncertainty.
studyKeyFindings: CNNE-MUPE-GPRE was most accurate and least uncertain, with test RMSE of 595, 600, and 612 kW and NSE of 0.93, 0.91, and 0.90 at 1-, 2-, and 3-day horizons. Accuracy declined with horizon. Its 1-day PICP/PINW were 0.99/0.05.
studyFutureWorks: Combine CNNE with BI-LSTM or LSTM for spatiotemporal learning and extend the approach to energy monitoring and early-warning applications.
studyLimits: Forecast skill and uncertainty deteriorated at longer horizons; the study used a single dam and two physical predictors with lagged inputs.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrated convolutional feature extraction, multilayer nonlinear learning, Gaussian-process uncertainty, and salp-based automated selection.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing ANN approaches do not automatically extract time-series features, robustly select inputs and parameters, or quantify predictive uncertainty.

studyMethodsSummary: Calibrated and validated SWAT with observed discharge, generated ten years of spatially distributed flow, ranked dependable years, and combined modeled flow with digital-elevation-model-derived head in GIS to identify candidate sites and calculate theoretical power.
studyKeyFindings: Thirty-three candidate sites were identified; total potential was 3039 kW at 50% dependability, 1127 kW at 75%, and 805 kW at 90%.
studyFutureWorks: Examine candidate sites using geological, environmental, access, demand, and economic criteria and optimize head and spacing thresholds.
studyLimits: Only one river gauging station was available; geological suitability, accessibility, demand, and ability to pay were not evaluated.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Demonstrated a GIS, remote-sensing, and calibrated SWAT workflow for hydrological screening of hydropower sites.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Reliable site assessment in remote hilly terrain is constrained by costly surveys and sparse flow observations.

studyMethodsSummary: Prepared DEM, land-cover, soil, slope, drainage, flow-direction, rainfall, evapotranspiration, and water-yield raster layers; simulated daily hydrology with SWAT using 17 years of data; calibrated and tested parameter sensitivity with SUFI-2; reclassified equal-resolution 5 km2 grids; and applied weighted-sum overlay analysis.
studyKeyFindings: Four hydropower-potential zones and ten tentative SHP sites were identified: seven in the upper catchment and three near the outlet, where optimum suitability occurred. Rainfall and water yield were most important for potential strength, while slope and streams guided site location.
studyFutureWorks: Improve input quality, conduct ground and structural surveys, use climate-scenario data, and add reservoir-operation and dynamic hydrological optimization.
studyLimits: The ten sites are tentative; exact turbine heads, discharges, turbine types, technical feasibility, and structural surveys were not assessed. Model outputs depend on structure and data quality.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Provided an integrated raster-based hydrological and multicriteria screening workflow for a rainfall-dependent inland catchment.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Ground-intensive hydropower surveys are slow and ineffective for initial catchment-scale identification of small-hydropower zones and sites.

studyMethodsSummary: A Visual Basic expert system applied fuzzy C-means clustering to RGB intensity values in IRS-1D LISS III geocoded false-color imagery, then interpreted water bodies, forest/vegetation, habitation, settlements, and snow to screen probable sites.
studyKeyFindings: The remote-sensing method provided a systematic way to extract water-resource and surrounding-feature information for small-hydropower site selection in plains and inaccessible mountains. It was demonstrated for the Ganga and Alaknanda rivers and compared with Survey of India topographic sheets.
studyFutureWorks: Develop a regional flow-duration model and extend the method to water-conveyance facilities such as canal heads and canal drops.
studyLimits: The work did not provide a cost comparison with conventional surveys. Remotely sensed imagery needs interpretation and supporting field data; a regional flow-duration model remains to be developed.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed a VB-based image-classification and expert-system workflow for hydropower resource screening.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Few studies clearly integrate satellite-image interpretation with water-resource and site-selection information for hydropower development in inaccessible hilly terrain.

studyMethodsSummary: State technical capacity, regional grid emission factors, and a 35% plant load factor were used to estimate annual electricity and certified emission reduction potential. A logistic diffusion model projected standard and optimistic capacity, electricity, and CER scenarios to 2020.
studyKeyFindings: India’s technically feasible 10.27 GW small-hydropower potential could generate 31.49 TWh/year and 23.65 million CERs/year at 35% load factor. Projected annual CERs are 7/20 million in standard/optimistic scenarios by 2012 and 13/24 million by 2020.
studyFutureWorks: Introduce supportive policies and use CDM bundling to lower transaction costs and accelerate small-hydropower diffusion.
studyLimits: The assessment is preliminary and macro-level; project additionality, hydrological/geological risk, policy conditions, and plant load factor determine realizable CERs.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Estimated national and state-level small-hydropower CER potential and modeled its diffusion under standard and optimistic conditions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: The CDM potential of Indian small hydropower had not been estimated comprehensively despite its potential to reduce emissions and support rural development.

studyMethodsSummary: Policies, project reports, environmental documents, and secondary data were reviewed. Field visits, interviews with technical experts and developers, and group discussions with local residents assessed project impacts and barriers, using the 48 MW Lower Kalnai project as a case.
studyKeyFindings: Jammu and Kashmir has 20,000 MW hydro potential, but administrative clearances, Indus Treaty constraints, difficult terrain, severe climate, social acceptance, security, and high costs slow development. A 4,000 MW development could meet the state power shortfall; Lower Kalnai’s carbon-credit benefit lowers estimated generation cost from Rs 3.90 to Rs 3.36/kWh.
studyFutureWorks: Conduct mandatory social-impact assessment for projects above 25 MW; use multi-criteria/AHP ranking; establish single-window clearance and improve local participation, monitoring, and benefit sharing.
studyLimits: Impacts and sustainability-factor intensity vary between projects; field evidence is case-specific and needs longer-term social-impact assessment.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Identified RoR-specific sustainability indicators and project-development barriers through field investigation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Most large-hydropower sustainability research concerns reservoir projects, with little evidence on without-reservoir run-of-river projects in the western Himalayan region.

studyMethodsSummary: Compiled Indian rainfall records for 1931–2022, calculated state/subdivision descriptive statistics, compared rainfall with installed hydro capacity, visualized rainfall series, examined basin-area distributions, and assigned qualitative regional hydropower-potential classes from annual-rainfall ranges.
studyKeyFindings: Arunachal Pradesh, Coastal Karnataka, Lakshadweep, Kerala, and Konkan-Goa had the highest rainfall. The Western Ghats, Northeast India, and Himalayan region were classified as high potential; large-basin states were also considered favorable for hydropower development.
studyFutureWorks: Refine rainfall-based analysis with detailed local topographical and hydrological data and integrated water-cycle variables.
studyLimits: Rainfall alone cannot predict hydropower performance; site-specific topography, water availability, flow, storage, infrastructure, snowmelt, and glacial runoff are also required. The reported potential classes are broad regional observations.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Combined long-term rainfall statistics, basin distributions, and installed capacity information to screen favorable Indian regions.
studyResearchGapIdentified: India requires regionally resolved analysis linking long-term rainfall and basin characteristics to hydropower-development suitability.

studyMethodsSummary: Applied SVR and XGBoost to Hawaii reservoir-resource data, optimized each with Aquila, slime mould, and grey wolf algorithms, analyzed input correlations and Delta Moment-Independent sensitivities, and compared test predictions using six statistical metrics.
studyKeyFindings: Standalone XGBoost outperformed SVR. XGBoost-SMA was the best test model with R2=0.9713, RMSE=18.73, and MAE=6.19. System water volume was the most influential input, followed by transmission spurline cost and total dollar per kW.
studyFutureWorks: Incorporate additional datasets and algorithms, including deep learning, and develop real-time prediction systems.
studyLimits: Results depend strongly on input-data quality; only SVR and XGBoost families and one geographic case were tested; hybrid optimization adds computational cost that can hinder real-time use.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Benchmarked standalone and metaheuristically optimized SVR and XGBoost models for Hawaii hydropower capacity.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Traditional regression and autoregressive methods struggle with nonlinear and nonstationary hydropower relationships, while optimized XGBoost hybrids remain underexplored.

studyMethodsSummary: Daily precipitation, streamflow, temperature, and energy production were split 70%/30% for training/testing, with 20% of training for validation. AdaBoost, autoencoder regression, DNN, ESN, LightGBM, and ResNet models were compared; LightGBM feature importance ranked predictors.
studyKeyFindings: LightGBM was the best model: RMSE 98.27, MAE 73.93, AIC 17,100, NSE 0.69, KGE 0.77, R² 0.69, MBE −5.23, bias factor 1.02, and PBIAS 1.51. Streamflow was most important, followed by temperature and precipitation.
studyFutureWorks: Integrate the approach in operational planning, load balancing, and reservoir operation and expand data/model testing.
studyLimits: Results use a limited four-year record at one plant; model generalization under changed climate and operational conditions requires additional testing.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Delivered a multi-model daily benchmark with LightGBM-based feature importance.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Few studies jointly compare AdaBoost, autoencoder regression, DNN, ESN, LightGBM, and ResNet for daily hydropower prediction while explaining hydro-meteorological feature importance.

studyMethodsSummary: A 1,819-record hydropower dataset was split 80%/20%. CatBoost and histogram gradient boosting were run independently and optimized with Hunger Games Search, Chaos Game Optimization, and Archimedes Optimization Algorithm.
studyKeyFindings: CatBoost-HGS was best in testing, with R² 0.90751273, RMSE 45.21301314, MAE 8.89683593, MBE −2.16463953, Willmott index 0.97262189, and Jensen-Shannon divergence 105.508137.
studyFutureWorks: Extend to real-time and regional/global predictions; include climate, economic and environmental information, deep reinforcement learning, and decision-support systems.
studyLimits: Data incompleteness and variable hydropower conditions, especially at under-monitored small plants, complicate model calibration and generalizability.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Integrated CatBoost and HGBoost with three metaheuristic optimizers to improve prediction accuracy and efficiency.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Standalone prediction methods have difficulty representing complex nonlinear relations among physical, economic, and geographic hydropower variables.

studyMethodsSummary: Monthly and quarterly 1993–2019 data were modelled with Gaussian process regression, support vector regression, multiple linear regression, and power regression. Three quarterly seasonal groupings and rainfall-only or multi-weather inputs were evaluated.
studyKeyFindings: Quarterly data outperformed monthly data. Gaussian process regression was best; for quarterly climatic-data Option 1 it achieved R 0.92, MAPE 4.5%, BIAS −0.4, Nash number 0.9, and RSR 0.3.
studyFutureWorks: Apply the selected model with forecast rainfall to predict future power generation at the plant.
studyLimits: The analysis is confined to one hydropower plant and historical meteorological observations; rainfall forecasts and unreported operational reservoir variables may affect practical forecasting.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared four regression techniques across monthly and quarterly meteorological input formulations.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Regression-based prediction using the full set of relevant weather indices at Samanalawewa had been limited.

studyMethodsSummary: Conducted a SALSA-structured Web of Science literature review with snowballing; synthesized rural renewable-energy transition problems, prosumption and cooperative options, barriers and motives, policy responses linked to technology-adoption theory, and success factors.
studyKeyFindings: Socio-political and regulatory barriers now dominate as renewable-energy costs decline. Effective initiatives depend on locally specific strategic, institutional, and physical capacities. Regulatory reform, prosumer participation, fair competition, information, training, privacy protection, and tailored economic and non-economic policy packages are needed.
studyFutureWorks: Tailor policy packages to local adoption stages, community capacities, and adopter characteristics; phase instruments as technology diffusion advances.
studyLimits: The review is qualitative and the same policies can perform differently across communities because local capacities and conditions vary.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Produced rural-specific barrier, motive, policy, and success-factor frameworks for community renewable-energy initiatives.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Existing research emphasizes urban renewable adoption and lacks an integrated rural-community analysis of barriers, drivers, success factors, and policies.

studyMethodsSummary: Compared 105 literature sunshine-duration models and calibrated seven new regression models using Kipp and Zonen pyranometer data from Mugla University (2007-2015).
studyKeyFindings: "Only models 24 and 35 met ±10% error limits; new models reduced errors below 0.8 and semester-specific cubic/quadratic models performed best."
studyFutureWorks: Use semester-specific models and extend calibration to other Turkish sites.
studyLimits: Solar measurements are difficult to obtain and model validity declines in winter.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed calibrated annual and semester regression correlations for Mugla.
studyResearchGapIdentified: No prior empirical correlation was available for Mugla despite high solar potential.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated 72 empirical models in nine categories using diffuse and global radiation and meteorological data from 10 Chinese stations; calibrated 1966-2000 and validated 2001-2015.
studyKeyFindings: Best daily models were VIII-3 in NWC, IV-3 in QTP NEC NC, and III-2 in CSC; best monthly models were IV-3, VIII-3, VII-7, VIII-5, and IV-5 respectively.
studyFutureWorks: Apply recommended region-specific models in solar thermal and photovoltaic design.
studyLimits: Diffuse radiation measurements are sparse and the best model varies by climate and time scale.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared model categories and identified climate- and timescale-specific best models.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Only 17 of 726 Chinese stations record diffuse radiation.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed M-01, M-02, and M-03 using 15 years of India Meteorological Department data for 20 locations split equally into training and validation sets.
studyKeyFindings: M-03, using sunshine duration, latitude, altitude, and relative humidity, was the most transferable model and had a maximum MPE magnitude of 11.8935%.
studyFutureWorks: Validate the developed models at additional locations.
studyLimits: Performance varies by location and climatic conditions.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Developed and validated a higher-order four-variable model across diverse Indian locations.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Measured solar-radiation coverage is limited and existing equations do not generalize reliably across India.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated 42 temperature-based solar-radiation models across six Moroccan climatic zones using long-term meteorological data and optimized them with SVM decision-tree Gaussian and linear regression learners.
studyKeyFindings: Optimized models achieved R2 of 0.80-0.95 for all skies and 0.95-0.98 for clear skies.
studyFutureWorks: Use optimized temperature models for Moroccan solar-project decisions.
studyLimits: Performance varies by climate zone and sky condition.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared least-squares and machine-learning optimization of temperature-based models.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Solar measurements are sparse and model transferability is uncertain.

studyMethodsSummary: Calibrated and evaluated 21 sunshine-based empirical models at 51 Iranian weather stations using 2007-2017 daily radiation data, linear and nonlinear regression, and ordinary Kriging maps.
studyKeyFindings: Regression models 4 and 12 performed best for climate zones C and F; linear model 15 had highest national correlation.
studyFutureWorks: Use calibrated models and radiation maps for solar-energy planning.
studyLimits: Radiation measurements are costly and unavailable at many Iranian stations.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Calibrated sunshine-based models and interpolated monthly radiation maps.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Many stations lack radiation instruments.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated six temperature-based global solar-radiation models using four years of measurements at URERMS Adrar under varied desert weather conditions.
studyKeyFindings: Model M4 performed best with R2 = 0.87; dust effects varied with soil quality.
studyFutureWorks: Use temperature-based models to estimate available solar energy in Adrar.
studyLimits: Solar-radiation estimates in Saharan environments are affected by weather and dust.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared six temperature-based models against URERMS observations.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Dust and atmospheric conditions complicate surface radiation prediction.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed linear quadratic and logarithmic hybrid regression models using ambient temperature sunshine duration and relative humidity for Jubail Industrial City.
studyKeyFindings: Quadratic model performed best with r = 0.939 R2 = 0.925 and MAPE = 6.17%.
studyFutureWorks: Use the quadratic hybrid model for solar-energy planning in Jubail.
studyLimits: Site-specific solar-radiation data are needed for Jubail energy planning.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared three hybrid regression models against measured GHI.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Few local radiation measurements motivate empirical estimation.

studyMethodsSummary: Developed empirical models for monthly mean daily global solar radiation at Eskisehir using 2011-2014 measurements of radiation sunshine temperature pressure wind and humidity.
studyKeyFindings: Evaluated models with nine statistical tests including MAPE MBE RMSE and R2 for solar-application planning.
studyFutureWorks: Use calibrated empirical models for Eskisehir solar engineering and forecasting.
studyLimits: Reliable local radiation estimates are needed for Eskisehir solar applications.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared empirical model estimates with measured Eskisehir radiation.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Radiation data availability is limited and models are site specific.

studyMethodsSummary: Evaluated seven empirical daily solar-radiation models at 13 Peruvian stations using 1990-2004 calibration and 2004-2010 validation data; proposed multiple-linear models added precipitation and relative humidity.
studyKeyFindings: Proposed models reduced errors by up to 73% versus empirical-model averages; best RMSE was 223.2 J/cm2/day at Tacna.
studyFutureWorks: Use proposed regression models for Peruvian solar and hydrometeorological applications.
studyLimits: Reliable daily solar-radiation estimates are needed where pyranometer data are scarce.
studyResearchGapAddressed: Compared seven empirical models and proposed multiple-linear regressions across Peru.
studyResearchGapIdentified: Pyranometer data are costly and unavailable at many stations.
